Preface

A JSON Web Token is three pieces of base64url text joined by dots. That is the whole format. Everything difficult about tokens happens around that format: which algorithm you pinned, which key you verified with, whether the claim you read was the one that was signed, and what you do on the day a key has to be replaced while requests keep arriving.

This book is about github.com/kataras/jwt, a JWT and JWKS implementation for Go with no dependencies. It covers what the package does, and it spends at least as long on why the API is shaped the way it is. An API you can predict is worth more than one you have to look up, and the only way to make it predictable is to say what it was worried about.

Who this is for

You write Go, and something in your system hands out tokens or accepts them. You do not need to have read RFC 7519. Chapter 1 builds the format from nothing, and every chapter after that assumes only what came before it.

If you already know JWT well, skip to Chapter 5 for the algorithm trade-offs, Chapter 7 for key rotation, or Chapter 12, which is the honest list of this package’s sharp edges.

What this book is not

It is not a reference. The reference is go doc, and it is generated from the source, which means it cannot drift. This book is the part go doc cannot give you: the order to do things in, the reason a default is what it is, and the failure that made somebody choose it.

It is also not a security course. It will tell you that verifying a signature proves who wrote a token and nothing else about whether you should trust its contents, and it will show you the code that gets that wrong. It will not teach you threat modelling.

How the code in here was checked

Every signature quoted in this book was compared against the package source, not remembered. That sounds like a low bar. It is not: the package’s own documentation contained a dozen examples that could not compile, including four that showed the wrong number of return values and three that referenced a type which does not exist. Prose is not compiled, so nothing catches this for you.

Where a chapter says a call returns a particular error, that error was produced and read. Where it quotes a benchmark number, that benchmark was run on the machine named beside it.

The shape of the book

Chapters 1 to 4 are the parts every user needs: the format, signing and verifying, claims, and time. Chapters 5 to 7 are about keys, which is where real systems spend their difficulty. Chapters 8 to 11 cover validation, revocation, HTTP, and payload encryption. Chapter 12 is the sharp edges. Chapters 13 and 14 are testing and performance.

Read 1 to 4 in order. After that, take what you need.

A note on the word secure

This book avoids calling anything secure. A token is signed, or it is not. A signature verifies under a key, or it does not. A claim was covered by that signature, or it was not. Those are checkable. “Secure” is a summary of somebody’s judgement about a whole system, and a library cannot make that judgement for you.

Where this book does make a recommendation, it says what the recommendation protects against and what it costs. You can then disagree with it on purpose rather than by accident.

Chapter 1

What a Token Is

A JSON Web Token is a string with two dots in it. Before any of this package’s API makes sense, it is worth taking one apart by hand, because almost every mistake people make with tokens comes from a wrong mental model of what those three pieces are and which of them the signature covers. This chapter builds the format from nothing, decodes a real token character by character, and then states precisely what verifying one does and does not tell you.

Three segments and two dots

Here is a complete token, produced by this package with the shared key sercrethatmaycontainch@r$:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImthdGFyYXMifQ.HxPZbhkeH0DtRAOJH_1F0YnbmxJvNQiaLzFHBQ-QLtc

Split it on the dots and you get three parts:

Part Decoded What it is
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9 {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} The header. Says how the token was signed.
eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImthdGFyYXMifQ {"username":"kataras"} The payload. Your claims.
HxPZbhkeH0DtRAOJH_1F0YnbmxJvNQiaLzFHBQ-QLtc 32 raw bytes The signature.

The first two are JSON documents that have been base64url encoded. The third is not text at all: it is the raw output of a signing function, encoded the same way so it survives being put in a URL or an HTTP header.

That is the entire compact serialization. There is no length prefix, no version marker and no envelope. A parser splits on ., expects exactly three parts, and goes from there.

Why base64url and not base64

Standard base64 uses + and / in its alphabet and pads with =. All three characters mean something in a URL, so a token pasted into a query string or a cookie would need escaping, and something in the chain would eventually escape it twice.

Base64url swaps + for - and / for _, and JWT drops the padding entirely. RFC 7515 requires that: the padding carries no information, since the length of the encoded text already tells a decoder how many bytes came in.

Dropping the padding is why decoding a segment is slightly more than a library call. The standard decoder wants input whose length is a multiple of four. This package handles it by removing padding rather than adding it:

func Base64Decode(src []byte) ([]byte, error) {
	src = bytes.TrimRight(src, padStr)

	buf := make([]byte, base64.RawURLEncoding.DecodedLen(len(src)))
	n, err := base64.RawURLEncoding.Decode(buf, src)
	return buf[:n], err
}

The obvious alternative, appending = characters until the length divides by four, is a trap, and this package fell into it for years. Chapter 12 explains what went wrong: the short version is that bytes.Split hands back a final segment that still owns the whole token’s spare capacity, so appending to it writes past the end of the caller’s buffer. Trimming has no such problem, needs no allocation, and turned out to be faster.

Taking a token apart in Go

You do not have to do any of that by hand. Decode parses a token without checking anything:

unverified, err := jwt.Decode(token)
if err != nil {
	return err
}

fmt.Printf("header:  %s\n", unverified.Header)
fmt.Printf("payload: %s\n", unverified.Payload)

header:  {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
payload: {"username":"kataras"}

The type it returns is called UnverifiedToken, and the name is doing real work. Nothing in that struct has been checked. The signature was decoded but not tested. The header says HS256 because the sender wrote HS256, not because anybody agreed.

Use Decode when you need to look at a token before you can verify it: reading the kid to work out which key to fetch, or logging which issuer a rejected token claimed. Do not use it to read claims you are going to act on.

What the signature covers

This is the part worth being precise about. The signature is computed over the header and the payload in their encoded form, joined by a dot:

signature = Sign(key, base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload))

Three consequences follow, and each one is a bug somebody has shipped.

The signature covers the header. An attacker cannot change alg without invalidating it. That is what makes the header trustworthy after verification, and it is why this package will carry a verified header forward into an enriched token but never an unverified one.

The signature covers the encoded bytes, not the decoded JSON. Two payloads that parse to the same object can have different signatures, and one signature is valid for exactly one byte sequence. You cannot re-serialize a payload and keep the signature. That is why adding a claim to an existing token means signing a new token, which is what Enrich does.

The signature covers nothing else. Not the transport, not the time you received the token, not who sent it to you. A signed token that is valid for somebody else is still a valid token when it arrives from an attacker who stole it.

What verifying proves, and what it does not

When Verify returns without an error, you have learned exactly one thing:

Somebody holding the key you supplied produced these exact header and payload bytes.

That is worth a lot, and it is less than people assume. Here is the same statement turned into the questions it does and does not answer.

Question Does verification answer it?
Were these bytes produced by a holder of the key? Yes.
Have the claims been modified since? No, they have not. Verification proves that.
Is the token within its validity window? Only because this package also checks exp and nbf. That is claim validation, not signature verification.
Was it issued for me? No. Check aud yourself, or with Expected.
Was it issued by who I think? No. Check iss.
Is the person presenting it the person it was issued to? No. Nothing in a bearer token can tell you that.
Has it been revoked? No. See Chapter 9.

The last two are where real incidents come from. A JWT is a bearer credential: possession is the whole authorization. If it leaks, whoever holds it is you, until it expires.

The compact form is not encryption

Base64 is an encoding, not a cipher. Anyone holding a token can read its payload with a one-line command:

echo 'eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImthdGFyYXMifQ' | base64 -d

{"username":"kataras"}

People put things in payloads that they would not put in a URL, on the reasoning that the token looks opaque. It is not opaque. Treat the payload as public. Put an identifier in it and look the rest up on your side.

If you genuinely need the payload hidden from the person carrying it, Chapter 11 covers the package’s AES-GCM support, along with the cases where it does not help.

Summary

A JWT is three base64url segments separated by dots: a header saying how it was signed, a payload of claims, and a signature over the first two in their encoded form. Base64url exists so the result survives a URL, and JWT drops the padding, which is why decoding trims rather than pads.

Verification proves that a holder of your key produced those exact bytes. It does not prove the token is for you, is from who you expect, is still wanted, or is being presented by its owner. Those are separate checks, and the rest of this book is largely about making them.

The payload is readable by anyone holding the token. Encoding is not encryption.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7519: JSON Web Token: the format itself, including the registered claim names.
  • RFC 7515: JSON Web Signature: the compact serialization and exactly what the signing input is. Section 5.1 is the one to read.
  • RFC 4648 section 5: base64url, and why the padding is optional.
  • jwt.io: paste a token in and see it split. Useful for a token you did not produce, and a good demonstration that the payload is public.

Chapter 2

Signing and Verifying

Two functions carry almost all of the traffic in this package: Sign produces a token, and Verify turns one back into claims or refuses to. Everything else is either a variation on those two or a way of choosing the key they use. This chapter covers both in full, and then spends most of its length on one design decision that follows from Chapter 1: the algorithm is something you pass in, and it is never read out of the token you are checking.

The two functions

Here are both signatures, copied from the source rather than from memory:

func Sign(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, claims any, opts ...SignOption) ([]byte, error)

func Verify(alg Alg, key PublicKey, token []byte, validators ...TokenValidator) (*VerifiedToken, error)

The first two parameters have the same shape in both, in the same order, because signing and verifying are the same operation seen from two sides. Both return byte slices rather than strings, since a token is going into an HTTP header or a cookie and Sign joins three byte slices to build it anyway.

PrivateKey and PublicKey are declared as = any. They are aliases, not distinct types, so the compiler will not stop you handing an *rsa.PrivateKey to Verify. The price is a runtime failure instead of a build failure: a mismatched key comes back as ErrInvalidKey, and passing "secret" where []byte("secret") was needed produces expected a string: jwt: invalid key. What you get is one function covering HMAC secrets, RSA and ECDSA key pairs and Ed25519 keys with no generics and no per-algorithm entry points. Chapter 5 goes through which key type each algorithm wants.

A complete program

This compiles and runs against the package as it stands. Nothing has been elided.

package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"time"

	"github.com/kataras/jwt"
)

type userClaims struct {
	Username string `json:"username"`
	Role     string `json:"role"`
}

func main() {
	sharedKey := []byte("sercrethatmaycontainch@r$")

	token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, sharedKey,
		userClaims{Username: "kataras", Role: "admin"},
		jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	verified, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, token)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	var claims userClaims
	if err := verified.Claims(&claims); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	fmt.Printf("token: %s\n", token)
	fmt.Printf("user:  %s (%s)\n", claims.Username, claims.Role)
	fmt.Printf("left:  %s\n", verified.StandardClaims.Timeleft())
}

token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImthdGFyYXMiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4iLCJpYXQiOjE3ODY4NzQ4NjAsImV4cCI6MTc4Njg3NTc2MH0.6I8OqoqQPJffSoY3NphOfS5ntrYcoLACpYHe58xUWPk
user:  kataras (admin)
left:  15m0s

Three things there are worth naming. jwt.HS256 appears twice, once on each side, and both are written out by you: that is the subject of the next section. jwt.MaxAge(15 * time.Minute) is a SignOption, and it sets exp and iat from the current time, which is why the payload holds two claims the struct never declared (Chapter 3 covers sign options, Chapter 4 covers time). And verified.Claims(&claims) unmarshals the payload a second time: Verify already parsed it once into StandardClaims, but it has no idea what your struct looks like, so your own claims cost one more json.Unmarshal.

Why the algorithm is a parameter

A JWT header names its own algorithm. The obvious implementation reads that name and picks the verifier to match. Do not write that implementation, and this package makes it awkward to write by accident.

Consider a service that verifies with an RSA public key and reads alg from the token to decide what to do. An attacker takes a genuine token, replaces the header with {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, and computes an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the new header-and-payload using the RSA public key bytes as the shared secret. The public key is public: it is on your JWKS endpoint, or in a certificate, or in a repository.

The service now does exactly what it was told. The header says HS256, so it runs HMAC-SHA256, and the key it has to hand is the RSA public key. The MAC matches, because the attacker computed it with the same bytes. One asymmetric key pair has become a shared secret everybody already has, and the attacker can mint any claims they like.

That is the algorithm-confusion attack. It has been in the JWT security literature since 2015 and keeps reappearing, because the vulnerable design reads as the reasonable one: the token says how it was signed, so believe it.

This package will not let you believe it. Verify takes alg as its first argument, and the token’s header never chooses the verifier. Pass jwt.RS256 and an RSA public key, hand the forged token to it, and the result is ErrTokenAlg, returned before any signature is computed. The forged signature is never checked against anything, because the header did not survive the earlier test.

The trade-off is that you have to know your own algorithm at the call site. For a service issuing its own tokens that is free. For one consuming tokens from an identity provider that rotates algorithms it is not, and that is what VerifyWithHeaderValidator and the Keys registry exist for (Chapters 6 and 7). Both still keep the choice explicit: a HeaderValidator returns the Alg to use, so the selection is code you can read rather than a lookup keyed on attacker-controlled text.

What compareHeader actually does

The check that rejects the forged header is compareHeader in token.go, and it does not parse JSON at all.

At package initialisation, token.go fills a map called fixedHeaders, one fixedHeader entry per built-in algorithm. Each entry holds three byte slices: raw, the header JSON, encoded, its base64url form, and reversed, the same JSON with the two fields in the opposite order. For HS256, raw and reversed are {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} and {"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256"}, both 27 bytes. Verification base64-decodes the incoming header and runs bytes.Equal against one of them. There is no alg field to extract, because nothing is ever extracted.

Two cheap tests decide which form to compare against. A decoded header shorter than 25 bytes is accepted only at exactly 15, the length of {"alg":"HS256"}, a header with no typ at all. Otherwise, if byte index 2 is t the header started {"typ" and the reversed form is used. Everything else goes against the standard order. Then bytes.Equal, and ErrTokenAlg if it differs.

This is strict, and it is worth seeing how strict. Each of these was signed with the correct HS256 key and passed to jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token):

Header Result
{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} accepted
{"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256"} accepted
{"alg":"HS256"} accepted
{"alg":"HS256","typ":"jwt"} ErrTokenAlg
{"alg":"HS256", "typ":"JWT"} ErrTokenAlg
{"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256","kid":"a"} ErrTokenAlg

One space and a lowercase jwt are both fatal, and so is a kid, which is a perfectly ordinary header field. That is a real cost: a token from another implementation that formats its header differently is rejected even though its signature is fine. What you get for it is that the parsing step an attacker would need to influence does not exist. There is no field ordering to confuse, no duplicate-key handling to exploit, no Unicode escape to smuggle a second alg through. The comparison is against 27 bytes your process chose at startup.

When you need the flexibility back, supply a HeaderValidator:

type HeaderValidator func(alg string, headerDecoded []byte) (Alg, PublicKey, InjectFunc, error)

The package-level CompareHeader variable holds the strict implementation and is used when you pass none. Replacing it is how kid support works, and it is why a validator returns a PublicKey too: having read the header, it can also choose the key.

What a VerifiedToken gives you

Verify returns *VerifiedToken, which is five fields and one method.

type VerifiedToken struct {
	Token          []byte
	Header         []byte
	Payload        []byte
	Signature      []byte
	StandardClaims Claims
}

func (t *VerifiedToken) Claims(dest any) error

Token is the original bytes you passed in, unchanged. Keep it if you will pass the token onward or key a blocklist entry on it. Signature is the decoded signature, 32 bytes for HS256, useful mainly for logging.

Header and Payload are base64-decoded JSON. For the program above they read {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} and {"username":"kataras","role":"admin","iat":1786874860,"exp":1786875760}. This header is trustworthy in a way the one from Decode is not, because the signature covered it and the signature verified. StandardClaims is a Claims struct filled from the payload during verification, with its time claims already checked. Chapter 3 walks its fields.

Claims(dest) unmarshals Payload into anything JSON can fill: a tagged struct, a jwt.Map, a type with its own UnmarshalJSON. It calls the package-level Unmarshal variable, so replacing that replaces the behaviour everywhere, which is how UnmarshalWithRequired is switched on in Chapter 3. It re-parses on every call, so if you need three views of one payload, unmarshal once into a struct holding all three sets of fields.

Decode versus Verify

Decode splits a token and base64-decodes the pieces. It checks no signature, no expiry and no algorithm. The result is an UnverifiedToken, with Header, Payload and Signature fields, its own Claims(dest any) error, and two header helpers that cache what they read:

func Decode(token []byte) (*UnverifiedToken, error)

func (t *UnverifiedToken) Alg() (Alg, error)
func (t *UnverifiedToken) Kid() (string, error)

There are two honest uses for this.

Deciding which key to fetch. You cannot verify until you have the key, and the kid naming that key is inside the token, so reading it first is unavoidable. What makes it safe is that the value is used only as a lookup, and the verification that follows decides whether the token is real. A kid naming a key you do not have produces ErrUnknownKid, and a kid naming the wrong key produces a signature failure.

Reporting on tokens you rejected. When verification fails and you want to log which issuer the token claimed, Decode is the only way to see it. Log it as a claim, not a fact.

Everything else is a mistake waiting for its incident. unverified.Claims(&user) followed by trusting user.Role is the whole vulnerability, in two lines that look like normal code. If your reason for reaching for Decode is that the token comes from a trusted internal source, “internal” describes your network and the payload describes what somebody typed.

The errors a failed verification returns

Verification can fail in about a dozen ways, and services that map them to HTTP status codes end up maintaining a list of sentinels that drifts out of date. Classify in classify.go collapses them into the five values an application actually branches on:

func Classify(err error) ErrorKind

switch jwt.Classify(err) {
case jwt.KindNone:
	// carry on
case jwt.KindExpired:
	http.Error(w, "token expired", http.StatusUnauthorized) // the client can refresh
default:
	http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
}

Here is what the common failures produce. Every row was run.

Failure Error Classify
Verify(alg, key, nil) ErrMissing KindMalformed
Not three dot-separated parts ErrTokenForm KindMalformed
Longer than MaxTokenSize ErrTokenSize KindMalformed
Header does not match ErrTokenAlg KindInvalid
Payload altered, or the wrong secret ErrTokenSignature KindInvalid
Key of the wrong type ErrInvalidKey KindInvalid
exp in the past ErrExpired KindExpired
nbf in the future ErrNotValidYet KindExpired
iat in the future ErrIssuedInTheFuture KindExpired
Expected{Issuer: ...} did not match ErrExpected KindRejected
A required claim was absent ErrMissingKey KindRejected

Classify uses errors.Is, so a wrapped error still classifies, and anything it does not recognise comes back as KindInvalid, the conservative reading of an unrecognised verification failure. Two categories land somewhere you might not expect: a payload that is not JSON, and a base64 error out of a segment that is not base64 at all, both come back KindMalformed. Neither is one of this package’s sentinel errors: the first is unexported and the second is a base64.CorruptInputError, so Classify matches them specially.

KindExpired is the one distinction worth surfacing to a client of your own, since refreshing is a fix the client can apply. For anybody else, return the same body for every failing kind. Telling an attacker whether a token was expired, forged or revoked is information given away for nothing.

A custom header replaces the whole header

SignWithHeader lets you put your own fields in the header:

func SignWithHeader(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, claims any, customHeader any, opts ...SignOption) ([]byte, error)

The package’s own documentation describes those fields as being merged with the standard ones. They are not. Here is the whole implementation from token.go:

func createCustomHeader(header any) ([]byte, error) {
	b, err := Marshal(header)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return Base64Encode(b), nil
}

Your value is marshalled and encoded. Nothing adds alg, nothing adds typ, and whatever you pass is the entire header.

token, _ := jwt.SignWithHeader(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, jwt.Map{"sub": "1"},
	jwt.Map{"kid": "key-1"})

unverified, _ := jwt.Decode(token)
fmt.Printf("%s\n", unverified.Header) // {"kid":"key-1"}

That token is signed correctly, and jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, token) rejects it with ErrTokenAlg, because the strict comparison from earlier finds no match. Restating the standard fields does not save you, for a reason worth knowing about:

jwt.SignWithHeader(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, claims,
	jwt.Map{"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT", "kid": "key-1"})
// header: {"alg":"HS256","kid":"key-1","typ":"JWT"}

encoding/json sorts map keys, so kid lands between alg and typ and the byte comparison fails. Raw JSON in the exact standard order fares no better: the header is then {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"key-1"}, still not one of the three forms compareHeader knows.

The conclusion is short. Signing with a custom header commits you to verifying with a HeaderValidator. VerifyWithHeaderValidator takes one, and Keys.ValidateHeader is a ready-made one that reads kid and picks the key. Chapter 7 covers it.

What Sign accepts as claims

The claims parameter is any, and it goes through the package-level Marshal variable:

var Marshal = func(v any) ([]byte, error) {
	if b, ok := v.([]byte); ok {
		return b, nil
	}

	return json.Marshal(v)
}

Three cases follow from those five lines.

A struct. Tag the fields and json.Marshal handles it. Embed jwt.Claims to get the registered claims into the same object.

A map. jwt.Map is = map[string]any, an alias, so any map[string]any works with no conversion. Key order in the payload is alphabetical, which is what encoding/json does with maps.

Raw bytes. A []byte is returned unchanged and becomes the payload verbatim: the fast path for a payload you already hold, and unvalidated. This signs and hands out a token whose payload is not JSON:

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, []byte(`{"not":"validated"`))
// err is nil

Verifying it returns jwt: payload is not a type of JSON, which jwt.Plain exists to suppress if a non-JSON payload is what you meant. If you would rather find out at signing time, pass at least one SignOption: that routes the value through Merge, which runs json.Valid on raw strings and byte slices and returns ErrNotJSONObject. Chapter 3 goes into Merge.

The size ceiling

Decode and every Verify variant refuse a token longer than MaxTokenSize, declared as var MaxTokenSize = 64 * 1024, before parsing it.

Verification allocates in proportion to the token it is handed, and the token arrives from whoever is calling. Without a ceiling, one unauthenticated request can ask your process for as much memory as it can send. The refusal is ErrTokenSize, which classifies as KindMalformed.

The default of 65536 bytes sits far above anything ordinary. A JWT with a handful of claims is a few hundred bytes, and one carrying an x5c certificate chain in its header might reach a few kilobytes. If you know your own tokens are small, set jwt.MaxTokenSize = 8 * 1024 during startup, before any concurrent verification begins. It is a plain package variable read without a lock, so changing it while requests are in flight is a data race.

Summary

Sign(alg, key, claims, opts...) and Verify(alg, key, token, validators...) are the two calls, and the algorithm is the first argument to both because you choose it, not the token.

That choice closes the algorithm-confusion attack, where a token’s header is rewritten to HS256 and signed with the RSA public key everybody already has. The mechanism is compareHeader, which base64-decodes the header and runs bytes.Equal against one of three precomputed forms for the algorithm you named. It never parses alg, so there is no parse to influence, and it is strict enough that one extra space or a kid is a rejection.

A VerifiedToken carries the original bytes, the decoded header, payload and signature, a populated StandardClaims, and a Claims(dest) method. Decode gives you the same pieces with nothing checked, which is right for reading a kid before you have a key and wrong for everything you act on. Classify sorts a dozen sentinel errors into five kinds, and KindExpired is the one worth telling a client about.

A custom header replaces the whole header rather than merging into it, so signing with one commits you to a HeaderValidator. Raw []byte claims are passed through unvalidated unless a SignOption sends them via Merge.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7519 section 6: unsecured JWTs, and why alg: none needs a deliberate decision rather than a default.
  • RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices: section 3.1 is the algorithm-confusion attack and the recommendation this package implements.
  • RFC 7515 section 4.1.1: the alg header parameter, including the requirement that recipients reject algorithms they do not expect.
  • pkg.go.dev/github.com/kataras/jwt: the generated reference, which cannot drift from the source the way prose can.
  • encoding/json: the marshalling rules behind jwt.Marshal, including the map key ordering that breaks a restated custom header.

Chapter 3

Claims

A payload is a JSON object, and the names in it are claims. Seven of them are registered by RFC 7519 and this package models those in a struct called Claims; everything else is yours. The interesting part is not either half on its own but how the two get joined into one object, because the answer explains a performance choice, a duplicate key you may see in your own tokens, and a parser that will accept a numeric sub but refuses a structured one.

The Claims struct, field by field

Here is the whole type from claims.go, tags included:

type Claims struct {
	NotBefore int64    `json:"nbf,omitempty"`
	IssuedAt  int64    `json:"iat,omitempty"`
	Expiry    int64    `json:"exp,omitempty"`
	ID        string   `json:"jti,omitempty"`
	OriginID  string   `json:"origin_jti,omitempty"`
	Issuer    string   `json:"iss,omitempty"`
	Subject   string   `json:"sub,omitempty"`
	Audience  Audience `json:"aud,omitempty"`
}

The Go names and the JSON names differ on purpose. The three-letter forms are what goes on the wire, because that is what RFC 7519 registered and what every other implementation looks for. The longer forms are what you read in your own code.

Field Claim What it holds
NotBefore nbf Seconds since the epoch before which the token is not valid.
IssuedAt iat Seconds since the epoch at which the token was signed.
Expiry exp Seconds since the epoch after which the token is refused.
ID jti A unique identifier for this token.
OriginID origin_jti The jti of the token this one came from.
Issuer iss Whoever minted the token.
Subject sub The principal the token is about, usually a user.
Audience aud Who the token is for, as an Audience.

Every tag carries omitempty, so a zero field is left out of the payload rather than written as 0 or "". That is what makes a Claims value usable as a partial template, and it is also why validation treats zero as absent. Chapter 4 covers what that means for time.

origin_jti is not a registered claim. The other seven are in the IANA JSON Web Token Claims registry. This one is a convention of this package: it links a refresh token to the access token issued alongside it, so revoking one can revoke the other. SignPair sets it for you and Chapter 9 covers the revocation side. Send a token carrying origin_jti to somebody else’s service and expect them to ignore it.

Three methods read the time fields, all covered in Chapter 4:

func (c Claims) Age() time.Duration      // Expiry - IssuedAt, the designed lifetime
func (c Claims) ExpiresAt() time.Time    // time.Unix(c.Expiry, 0)
func (c Claims) Timeleft() time.Duration // Expiry - Clock().Unix()

Custom claims in a struct of your own

Your own claims are an ordinary Go struct with JSON tags. Nothing in the package needs to know about the type. Pass a value of it to Sign, and read it back with VerifiedToken.Claims:

type sessionClaims struct {
	Username string   `json:"username"`
	Scopes   []string `json:"scopes"`
}

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, sharedKey,
	sessionClaims{Username: "kataras", Scopes: []string{"read", "write"}},
	jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute))

verified, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, token)

var claims sessionClaims
err = verified.Claims(&claims)

Claims takes a pointer and hands it to the package-level Unmarshal. Fields the payload does not mention are left at their zero value, which is the standard encoding/json behaviour and is why the next-to-last section of this chapter exists: if absence has to be an error, you have to ask for that.

A jwt.Map works too, and is right when the claim set is not known at compile time:

var m jwt.Map
err = verified.Claims(&m)
fmt.Printf("%T\n", m["iat"]) // json.Number

Numbers come back as json.Number, not float64, because the default Unmarshal builds a json.Decoder and calls UseNumber() on it. Call .Int64() on the result rather than asserting to float64.

Combining custom claims with standard ones

You have two ways to get registered claims into the same payload as your own.

Embed jwt.Claims. The fields are promoted and encoding/json inlines them, so one struct marshals to one flat object:

type userClaims struct {
	Username string `json:"username"`
	Role     string `json:"role"`
	jwt.Claims
}

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, userClaims{
	Username: "kataras",
	Role:     "admin",
	Claims:   jwt.Claims{Subject: "user-42", Issuer: "auth.example.com"},
}, jwt.MaxAge(time.Hour))

{"username":"kataras","role":"admin","iss":"auth.example.com","sub":"user-42","iat":1700000000,"exp":1700003600}

Pass them as sign options. That is the variadic fourth parameter of Sign, and a SignOption is one method:

func Sign(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, claims any, opts ...SignOption) ([]byte, error)

type SignOption interface {
	ApplyClaims(*Claims)
}

type SignOptionFunc func(*Claims)

signToken starts with a zero Claims, calls ApplyClaims on each option in the order you gave them, and merges the result with your claims. Because each option writes into the same struct, a later option overwrites an earlier one that sets the same field:

jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, jwt.Map{}, jwt.Issuer("first"), jwt.Issuer("second"))
// payload: {"iss":"second"}

Claims itself implements SignOption, through an ApplyClaims that copies only the fields that are set:

func (c Claims) ApplyClaims(dest *Claims) {
	if v := c.NotBefore; v > 0 {
		dest.NotBefore = v
	}
	// ... and so on for the other seven fields
}

The test is > 0 for the numbers and non-empty for the strings, so jwt.Claims{} as an option contributes nothing and a partially filled one contributes only what it names. That is what lets you keep a package-level template of your issuer and audience and pass it to every call.

One asymmetry follows. ApplyClaims will not write a zero, so a Claims option cannot clear a field an earlier option set. NoMaxAge exists precisely because of that: it is a SignOptionFunc assigning 0 to Expiry and IssuedAt directly, which no Claims value can do.

jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, jwt.Map{"a": 1}, jwt.MaxAge(time.Hour), jwt.NoMaxAge)
// payload: {"a":1}

The sign-option shorthands

Before signoptions.go, the only sign options were MaxAge, NoMaxAge, Audience and Claims. Setting a jti or an iss on its own meant writing a SignOptionFunc by hand, and downstream packages did, which put this library’s type into signatures that were meant to hide it. Seven shorthands now set one field of Claims each:

func ID(id string) SignOptionFunc
func OriginID(id string) SignOptionFunc
func Issuer(issuer string) SignOptionFunc
func Subject(subject string) SignOptionFunc
func NotBefore(t time.Time) SignOptionFunc
func IssuedAt(t time.Time) SignOptionFunc
func ExpiresAt(t time.Time) SignOptionFunc

The three taking a time.Time call t.Round(time.Second).Unix(), so a timestamp with nanoseconds in it lands on a whole second, which is what the format stores anyway.

Alongside them are the four originals. MaxAge(d) sets exp to now plus d and iat to now, both from the Clock variable. NoMaxAge clears both. Audience is the []string type itself, which implements ApplyClaims so you can pass it directly. And Claims, as above. One behaviour of MaxAge is worth stating outright: if maxAge <= time.Second it returns NoMaxAge, so jwt.MaxAge(500 * time.Millisecond) produces a token with no expiry at all rather than one that expires immediately. Chapter 4 comes back to it.

Put together:

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, sharedKey, jwt.Map{"role": "admin"},
	jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute),
	jwt.Issuer("auth.example.com"),
	jwt.Subject("user-42"),
	jwt.ID("tok-1"),
	jwt.OriginID("tok-0"),
	jwt.Audience{"api.example.com"},
	jwt.NotBefore(time.Unix(1700000000, 0)),
)

{"role":"admin","nbf":1700000000,"iat":1700000000,"exp":1700000900,"jti":"tok-1","origin_jti":"tok-0","iss":"auth.example.com","sub":"user-42","aud":["api.example.com"]}

Your claims come first, then the accumulated standard ones in the field order of the Claims struct. That is not encoding/json being clever. It is the next section.

How Merge splices

Merge is what joins your claims to the standard ones, and it does not build a map and re-encode it:

func Merge(values ...any) ([]byte, error)

For each value it obtains JSON bytes, checks that the first byte is { and the last is }, strips both, and keeps the inside. At the end it joins the pieces with commas and wraps the lot in one pair of braces. Two objects go in and one comes out, with no intermediate map[string]any and no reparse. That is why it is fast, and it is also why this happens:

jwt.Merge(jwt.Map{"iss": "a"}, jwt.Claims{Issuer: "b"})
// {"iss":"a","iss":"b"}

The claim appears twice, because nothing looked at the names: looking at the names is the expensive part that was skipped on purpose.

Be clear about what that costs. RFC 8259 says the names in an object “should be unique” and that behaviour is unpredictable when they are not, so a payload like this is legal JSON but not what the specification prefers. encoding/json resolves it last-wins, so Go reads b, and so does anything else built on encoding/json, including VerifiedToken.StandardClaims:

token, _ := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, jwt.Map{"iss": "from-claims"}, jwt.Issuer("from-option"))
// payload:  {"iss":"from-claims","iss":"from-option"}
verified, _ := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token)
// verified.StandardClaims.Issuer == "from-option"

A first-wins parser elsewhere reads from-claims, and both parsers are within their rights. If a token you issue is going to be read by something you did not write, do not put the same claim in two places. Set iss in your claims object or in a sign option, not in both.

Merge does check the two cases it cannot vouch for. A string or a []byte is spliced in verbatim rather than marshalled, so those two are run through json.Valid:

_, err := jwt.Merge(`{"broken"}`)
// part: 1: jwt: value is not a JSON object

That is ErrNotJSONObject, which Classify reports as KindMalformed. The error names the part number rather than the value, because claims carry personal data and formatting the offending value into an error puts it in whatever you log. Anything that came out of json.Marshal skips the json.Valid scan, since it is valid by construction.

Nil values are skipped and empty objects are dropped, so Merge(nil, jwt.Map{}, jwt.Map{"a": 1}) returns {"a":1} and merging nothing at all returns {}.

The Audience type

aud is the one registered claim whose type is ambiguous in the specification. RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 says it is an array of strings, then says that in the special case of one value it “MAY be a single case-sensitive string”. Both forms are in the wild, so Audience, which is a []string, gives itself an UnmarshalJSON that looks at the first byte and branches:

switch data[0] {
case '"': // it's a single string.
	// unmarshal into a string, wrap it in a one-element slice
case '[': // it's an array of strings.
	// unmarshal into []string directly
}

So "aud":"api.example.com" and "aud":["api.example.com"] both arrive as Audience{"api.example.com"}, and your code never has to care which the sender used. Anything else, a number or an object, falls through the switch and leaves the audience nil without an error. That is a quiet outcome for a malformed claim, and worth a length check or an Expected validator if aud matters to you.

Marshalling only goes one way. jwt.Claims{Audience: jwt.Audience{"one"}} writes {"aud":["one"]}, an array even for a single value, which is the form the specification prefers.

Contains is the membership test RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 actually asks for:

func (aud Audience) Contains(value string) bool

if !verified.StandardClaims.Audience.Contains("api.example.com") {
	return errors.New("token is for somebody else")
}

The rule in the specification is that the recipient must identify itself with a value in the audience. Not that it is the only value, and not that it is the first. A token good for ["api.example.com", "admin"] is good for the API and good for the admin panel, and each of them checks for its own name. Comparison is exact and case sensitive, because audience values are identifiers rather than prose: Audience{"api.example.com"}.Contains("API.example.com") is false. Expected calls Contains for you if you would rather express the check as a validator, and String joins the values with spaces for logging.

The second-chance parser

verifyToken unmarshals the payload into a Claims struct with the standard library. When that fails, it tries once more with a looser struct before giving up:

type claimsSecondChance struct {
	NotBefore json.Number `json:"nbf,omitempty"`
	IssuedAt  json.Number `json:"iat,omitempty"`
	Expiry    json.Number `json:"exp,omitempty"`
	ID        string      `json:"jti,omitempty"`
	OriginID  string      `json:"origin_jti,omitempty"`
	Issuer    any         `json:"iss,omitempty"`
	Subject   any         `json:"sub,omitempty"`
	Audience  Audience    `json:"aud,omitempty"`
}

json.Number for the timestamps and any for the two identity claims. toClaims then converts, and what it accepts and refuses is the point.

A float timestamp is accepted. Some authorities emit "exp":2000000000.5, off by a fraction of a second. toUnix parses through Float64 and truncates, so that arrives as 2000000000. This is the case the loose struct was written for.

A numeric identity claim is accepted and rendered as text. {"sub":12345} gives you Subject of "12345". Issuers that write a numeric subject exist, and tolerating them is the other reason for the second pass.

A structured identity claim is refused. {"sub":{"a":1}} returns ErrTokenForm, as jwt: invalid token form: sub: expected a string but got map[string]interface {}. That is a fix rather than a feature: the conversion used to format the value with %v, which turned that payload into the subject map[a:1], so an application treating Subject as a principal identifier accepted a token whose subject was not a principal at all. A boolean fails the same way.

A timestamp no int64 can hold is refused. {"exp":1e30} returns jwt: invalid token form: exp: out of range: 1e30. This is the other repair, and it mattered more. json.Number.Float64 reports an error for text float64 cannot hold, and Go leaves a float-to-integer conversion undefined when the value does not fit. Both used to be discarded. An exp of 1e400 came out as a negative int64, failed the “greater than zero” test the old validation used, and was read as no expiry at all. A token claiming an absurd expiry became a token that never expired. toUnix now checks math.IsNaN, math.IsInf and both int64 bounds before converting.

When the second pass also fails to parse, verification reports an unexported error whose message is jwt: payload is not a type of JSON. jwt.Plain is the validator that suppresses it, for tokens whose payload is deliberately not JSON. {"iat":"notanumber"} lands here, since a string will not go into a json.Number.

Required fields

encoding/json has no notion of a required field. A claim that is absent leaves your struct field at its zero value, and a missing username is indistinguishable from an empty one.

The package adds an opt-in check driven by a required option in the JSON tag. Switch it on by replacing the package-level Unmarshal, which every Claims method routes through:

func UnmarshalWithRequired(payload []byte, dest any) error

jwt.Unmarshal = jwt.UnmarshalWithRequired

type strictClaims struct {
	Username string `json:"username,required"`
	Role     string `json:"role"`
}

It unmarshals normally and then walks the destination with reflection, descending into nested structs. Any exported field whose tag contains ,required and whose value is zero produces jwt: token is missing a required field: "Username". That is ErrMissingKey, which Classify reports as KindRejected. HasRequiredJSONTag exposes the tag test if you want to run it yourself over a reflect.StructField.

Two limits are worth stating. The check is on the Go value rather than the JSON, so a claim present but empty ("username":"") fails exactly as an absent one does. And the message names the Go field, Username, rather than the JSON name username, which is a nuisance when you are matching an error against a payload. Set jwt.Unmarshal once at startup, for the same reason as MaxTokenSize: it is a package variable read without a lock.

Summary

Claims holds the seven registered claims RFC 7519 defines, under Go names that differ from the wire names (Expiry is exp, ID is jti), plus OriginID, which serializes as origin_jti and is this package’s own convention for linking a refresh token to its access token. Every field carries omitempty, so zero means absent throughout.

Your own claims are any struct with JSON tags, read back with VerifiedToken.Claims(&dest). Combine them with the registered ones by embedding jwt.Claims, or by passing sign options: Claims implements SignOption through an ApplyClaims that copies only non-zero fields, and signoptions.go adds ID, OriginID, Issuer, Subject, NotBefore, IssuedAt and ExpiresAt for setting one claim at a time. Later options win.

Merge joins the two objects by stripping braces and splicing raw JSON, which is why it is quick and why a claim set in two places appears twice in the payload. Go reads the last one, a first-wins parser somewhere else reads the first, so set each claim in exactly one place. Raw string and []byte fragments are checked with json.Valid and rejected with ErrNotJSONObject.

Audience unmarshals from either a string or an array, always marshals as an array, and Contains is the RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 membership test. The second-chance parser tolerates a float timestamp and a numeric sub, returning ErrTokenForm for a structured sub or a timestamp no int64 can hold, and UnmarshalWithRequired turns a ,required tag into ErrMissingKey.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7519 section 4.1: the registered claim names, one subsection each. Section 4.1.3 is the audience rule that Contains implements.
  • IANA JSON Web Token Claims registry: the live list of registered names, and the place to check before inventing one.
  • RFC 8259 section 4: JSON objects, and the paragraph on duplicate names that explains why Merge output is parser-dependent.
  • encoding/json: struct tags, omitempty, embedded struct inlining, and the last-wins behaviour on duplicate keys.
  • json.Number: what UseNumber gives you and why .Int64() beats a float64 assertion on a timestamp.

Chapter 4

Expiry and Time

A bearer token is valid until it is not, and the only thing deciding when that moment arrives is a number in the payload. RFC 7519 makes every one of the time claims optional, which means the default state of a JWT is permanent. This chapter covers the three time claims, the exact rules this package applies to them, the two validators that exist because clocks disagree, and one function whose name points the opposite way from what it does.

The three time claims

RFC 7519 registers three claims that carry a time, all of them as seconds since the Unix epoch, and all three are listed as optional.

Claim Name Meaning Section
exp Expiration Time When the token stops being valid. 4.1.4
nbf Not Before When the token starts being valid. 4.1.5
iat Issued At When the token was created. 4.1.6

In this package they are three fields on Claims:

type Claims struct {
	NotBefore int64 `json:"nbf,omitempty"`
	IssuedAt  int64 `json:"iat,omitempty"`
	Expiry    int64 `json:"exp,omitempty"`
	// ... iss, sub, aud, jti, origin_jti
}

exp is the one that matters for security. It puts a ceiling on the damage a leaked token can do, because a stolen bearer credential is the holder’s credential until it expires and nothing about the token itself can tell you it was stolen.

nbf is for tokens minted ahead of the moment they are supposed to work: a subscription that starts at midnight, a batch job whose credentials are prepared in the previous run. Most systems never set it.

iat is metadata rather than a control. It tells you how old a token is and lets a verifier notice a clock that is badly wrong. It bounds nothing by itself.

Verify checks all three when they are present. There is no option to turn that off, and the check runs after the signature, so the values being checked are values your key covered.

Why zero means absent

Read validateClaims in claims.go. It is short, and every line is a decision:

func validateClaims(t time.Time, claims Claims) error {
	now := t.Round(time.Second).Unix()

	if claims.NotBefore != 0 {
		if now < claims.NotBefore {
			return ErrNotValidYet
		}
	}

	if claims.IssuedAt != 0 {
		if now < claims.IssuedAt {
			return ErrIssuedInTheFuture
		}
	}

	if claims.Expiry != 0 {
		if now > claims.Expiry {
			return ErrExpired
		}
	}

	return nil
}

The three fields are int64 tagged omitempty. That tag makes a Claims value with no expiry serialize to a payload with no exp key, and it also makes zero unrepresentable as a real value: nothing in the round trip distinguishes “the issuer did not set this” from “the issuer set this to 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z”. So zero is read as absent and the claim is skipped.

Every other value is present and gets checked, negative ones included. A token carrying "exp": -1 expired one second before the epoch, and now > claims.Expiry is true for any clock set after 1969, so Verify returns ErrExpired.

Both comparisons are strict, and the reference time is rounded to the nearest second. A token is therefore accepted from the exact second named by its nbf, which is what RFC 7519 asks for, and still accepted during the exact second named by its exp, which is a second more generous than a strict reading of “the current time MUST be before exp”. The RFC allows small leeway of this kind. In practice it means every window is a whole number of seconds wide, and sub-second precision does not exist anywhere in this format.

That sounds obvious and it was not always the code. The test used to be claims.Expiry > 0, which reads as “if an expiry was set” and behaves as “if the expiry is after 1970”. Under that rule a negative exp counted as no expiry at all, so a token that should have been rejected outright verified and stayed valid forever. toUnix reaches the same place from another direction: it converts a JSON number to int64, and a float too large for int64 used to land on the most negative value the type can hold, so an "exp" of 1e400 produced an immortal token. Both are fixed, and toUnix now returns an error wrapped in ErrTokenForm for anything out of range.

One asymmetry to know about. Claims.ApplyClaims, which runs when you pass a Claims value as a SignOption, copies each timing field only if v > 0. A template Claims carrying a negative Expiry is therefore ignored on the way in, while a token arriving with a negative exp is treated as expired on the way out.

Setting a lifetime with MaxAge

You will rarely fill Expiry in by hand:

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, claims, jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute))

MaxAge sets two claims, not one:

func MaxAge(maxAge time.Duration) SignOptionFunc {
	if maxAge <= time.Second {
		return NoMaxAge
	}

	return func(c *Claims) {
		now := Clock()
		c.Expiry = now.Add(maxAge).Unix()
		c.IssuedAt = now.Unix()
	}
}

iat comes along with exp because the two are read together. An exp with no iat tells a reader when the token dies but not how long it was meant to live, which is what Claims.Age() reports.

Now the guard at the top. Any duration of one second or less returns NoMaxAge, and NoMaxAge is not a no-op:

var NoMaxAge SignOptionFunc = func(c *Claims) {
	c.Expiry = 0
	c.IssuedAt = 0
}

It zeroes both fields, omitempty drops them, and the token goes out with no exp and no iat. State that plainly, because it is the sentence people need: a zero MaxAge in a configuration file produces permanent tokens, and no call in the chain returns an error. Sign succeeds. Verify succeeds, tomorrow and next year. Nothing logs anything.

The route into that is short. A KeyConfiguration carries a MaxAge time.Duration field with json, yaml, toml and ini tags, and Keys.SignToken applies it only under if k.MaxAge > 0. Leave MaxAge out of the YAML, or write MaxAge: 0, and the option is never added. Write MaxAge: 1s and the option is added and then erases itself. Two different mistakes, one result.

If your claims are a Map rather than a struct, the equivalent is func MaxAgeMap(maxAge time.Duration, claims Map), which mutates the map in place and returns nothing:

claims := jwt.Map{"user_id": "12345", "role": "admin"}
jwt.MaxAgeMap(15*time.Minute, claims)

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, claims)

Two differences from MaxAge. It will not overwrite an exp already in the map, so a caller who set one keeps it. And for a duration of one second or less it returns without touching the map rather than zeroing anything, so the failure here is “no expiry was added” rather than “an expiry was removed”. Both end at a token with no exp.

Requiring an expiry

RFC 7519 leaves exp optional and this package follows the RFC. If you want the stricter rule, ask for it:

verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.RequireExpiry)

RequireExpiry is a TokenValidatorFunc value, not a function returning one, so it takes no arguments. Its body does three things in order: return any error that arrived from earlier validation, return ErrMissingExpiry if standardClaims.Expiry == 0, otherwise return nil. That first step matters. A token that has genuinely expired already failed with ErrExpired, which this validator passes through, so it only ever sees the missing case. The error message is jwt: token has no expiry.

Add it wherever you accept tokens you did not mint, and to your own issuer’s verification too, because that is what catches the configuration mistake above on the day it ships rather than on the day somebody audits the key store.

There is a second reason, about revocation. A blocklist entry has to be kept until the token would have expired anyway, at which point it can be dropped. A token with no expiry has no such point, so its revocation record can never be collected. Chapter 9 goes into it.

Clock skew and the order of validators

Two machines rarely agree on the time to the second. An issuer whose clock runs two minutes fast mints a token whose iat is in the future from the verifier’s point of view, and validateClaims rejects it with ErrIssuedInTheFuture even though nothing is wrong with it. There are two validators for this, and the difference between them is not obvious from the names.

func Future(dur time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc
func Skew(d time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc

Future opens with if errors.Is(err, ErrIssuedInTheFuture) and does nothing for any other error. It rescues iat, and only iat. Now look again at validateClaims: it checks nbf first and returns as soon as that check fails. An issuer that sets nbf equal to iat, which several do, produces a skewed token that fails with ErrNotValidYet, and Future passes that error straight through. The rescue never happens.

This is not hypothetical. Four call sites across two services depended on Future and worked only because the identity provider they talked to happens to omit nbf. A change at the provider would have broken all four at once.

Skew(d) is the one to reach for:

verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute))

It switches on the error it was handed and accepts either ErrNotValidYet or ErrIssuedInTheFuture when the claim falls within d of now. A non-positive d passes the error through unchanged, so Skew(0) is a safe no-op rather than a validator that accepts everything.

Tolerance in the other direction is deliberately not offered. There is no option to accept a token that expired thirty seconds ago. Extending the life of a credential that has run out is a policy decision about your system, not a correction for a clock, and if you want it you should write it where a reviewer can see it.

Validator order is load-bearing. Verify runs validators in the order you pass them, handing each one the error the previous produced, and it breaks out of the loop at the first validator that returns non-nil. A validator that rescues an error must therefore come before one that would refuse it. Almost every built-in validator, Expected among them, opens with if err != nil { return err }, which is the correct way to respect an earlier failure and also the reason ordering matters:

// Correct: Skew clears the skew error, then Expected checks the issuer.
jwt.Verify(alg, key, token, jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute), jwt.Expected{Issuer: "us"})

// Wrong: Expected returns ErrNotValidYet, Verify breaks, Skew never runs.
jwt.Verify(alg, key, token, jwt.Expected{Issuer: "us"}, jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute))

If you keep validators in a slice and want to append at a call site, Validators saves you the conversion loop and preserves order:

jwt.Verify(alg, key, token, jwt.Validators(app.Validators, jwt.Skew(time.Minute))...)

One consequence of the early return in validateClaims deserves a sentence. When Skew clears an nbf failure, the iat and exp checks for that token never ran, because validateClaims returned before reaching them. In practice that only matters for a token whose exp is earlier than its nbf, which nobody meant to issue, but it is worth knowing that a cleared error is a skipped check rather than a passed one.

Leeway is stricter than it sounds

Leeway reads like a tolerance. It is the opposite.

func Leeway(leeway time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc

The whole of its logic is one comparison, guarded by err == nil and Expiry > 0:

if Clock().Add(leeway).Round(time.Second).Unix() > standardClaims.Expiry {
	return ErrExpired
}

It moves the clock forward by leeway and then asks whether the token has expired. So jwt.Leeway(30 * time.Second) rejects, with ErrExpired, any token that will expire within the next thirty seconds. It narrows the acceptance window instead of widening it.

The name comes from the caller’s problem rather than the token’s. You are about to start work that will take a while: a database transaction, a chain of calls to three services, a batch that runs for twenty seconds. Beginning that with a credential that dies halfway through leaves you with a partial write and a 401 you cannot retry. Leeway is how you insist on a token with enough life left to finish. Note the two guards: it does nothing at all for a token with no exp, and it never rescues an earlier error, only refuses.

Replacing the clock in tests

Every time comparison in this package goes through one package-level variable:

var Clock = time.Now

validateClaims, MaxAge, MaxAgeMap, Leeway, Future, Skew and Claims.Timeleft all call it. Replace it and you control the package’s idea of now, which is how you test expiry without sleeping:

func TestExpiredToken(t *testing.T) {
	original := jwt.Clock
	t.Cleanup(func() { jwt.Clock = original })

	base := time.Date(2024, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
	jwt.Clock = func() time.Time { return base }

	token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, jwt.Map{"sub": "user"}, jwt.MaxAge(time.Hour))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	jwt.Clock = func() time.Time { return base.Add(2 * time.Hour) } // past the expiry

	if _, err = jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token); !errors.Is(err, jwt.ErrExpired) {
		t.Fatalf("expected ErrExpired but got: %v", err)
	}
}

t.Cleanup is doing real work there. A test that leaves Clock pointing at a fixed instant breaks every later test that expects real time, and the failure surfaces somewhere else entirely.

Set it once, at startup. Clock is read without a lock, from whichever goroutine is verifying, so assigning to it while requests are in flight is a data race and the race detector will say so. That rules out swapping the clock in a test that runs in parallel with others: keep those serial, or build the token you need from explicit Claims values and leave the global alone. The same applies to CompareHeader, ReadFile, Marshal, Unmarshal and MaxTokenSize.

Reading time off a verified token

Three methods on Claims answer the questions you will actually ask:

func (c Claims) Age() time.Duration
func (c Claims) ExpiresAt() time.Time
func (c Claims) Timeleft() time.Duration

Age is exp minus iat: the lifetime the issuer intended, not the time elapsed since issuance. It does not consult the clock. With either claim missing it returns whatever the subtraction produces, so check for zero before you trust it.

ExpiresAt converts exp to a time.Time at second precision. With no exp you get time.Unix(0, 0), the epoch, which is emphatically not “no expiry” if you feed it to a comparison.

Timeleft is exp minus Clock(), so it is the one that moves. Positive means the token is still good, negative means it has expired, and zero means either that it expires exactly now or that there is no exp at all. Those last two are indistinguishable in the return value, which is a good reason to pair it with RequireExpiry:

verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.RequireExpiry)
if err != nil {
	return err
}

claims := verifiedToken.StandardClaims
if left := claims.Timeleft(); left < 2*time.Minute {
	log.Printf("token for %s expires at %s, %s left",
		claims.Subject, claims.ExpiresAt().Format(time.RFC3339), left)
}

StandardClaims is a field on *VerifiedToken, already parsed. Your own claims come out separately through verifiedToken.Claims(&dest).

Choosing lifetimes

There is no correct number, but there is a shape, and it comes from one fact: you cannot un-issue a JWT. Verification is a signature check and a clock comparison, neither of which asks anything else, which is the whole reason a JWT scales and the reason a token stays good until it expires whatever happens in between.

Access tokens: minutes. Five to fifteen is the usual range. This is the token that travels on every request, gets logged by proxies, sits in browser memory, and shows up in crash reports. A short lifetime gives a leak a deadline. The cost is refresh traffic and the client-side machinery to handle a 401 mid-flight without losing the user’s work.

Refresh tokens: days to weeks. Seven days is a common default. This token is presented rarely, to one endpoint, and can be stored somewhere better guarded. The cost is that it becomes the thing worth stealing, which is why it should be revocable: keep its jti and check a blocklist when it is presented. Chapter 9 covers that, and the pairing is common enough that the package ships a TokenPair type for it.

Anything you cannot revoke: as short as you can stand. For a token minted for one operation, a machine-to-machine call or a signed download link, the lifetime should cover the operation and no more.

Permanent tokens: almost never. If you need a credential that does not expire you also need a way to revoke it, which means a lookup on every request, which means the JWT is buying you nothing over an opaque random string in a database. Use the database.

One more number to set deliberately: the tolerance you pass to Skew should be smaller than your shortest token lifetime, or you have quietly extended it. On hosts running NTP, a minute or two is generous, and reaching for ten usually means a clock is broken somewhere and the tolerance is hiding it.

Summary

exp, nbf and iat are all optional in RFC 7519, so a token with none of them is a valid token that never expires. Verify checks all three when they are present, after the signature. Zero means absent, because int64 plus omitempty leaves nothing else to mean it. Every other value is checked, negative ones included, so exp: -1 is expired rather than unbounded.

MaxAge(d) sets both exp and iat, and for any d of one second or less it returns NoMaxAge, which clears both. A zero MaxAge in a config file therefore yields permanent tokens silently. RequireExpiry is the check that catches it, and it returns ErrMissingExpiry.

For clock skew use Skew(d), which covers nbf and iat. Future(d) covers only iat, and since validateClaims returns at the first failed check it cannot rescue a token whose issuer set nbf. Validators run in the order given and Verify stops at the first error, so a rescuing validator must come first. Leeway(d) is stricter rather than looser: it rejects tokens expiring within the next d.

Clock is a package variable, ideal for tests, read without a lock, so set it before anything concurrent starts. Age(), ExpiresAt() and Timeleft() read the claims you have already verified.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7519 section 4.1.4: the exp claim, including the sentence that makes it optional and the note about leeway between clocks. Sections 4.1.5 and 4.1.6 cover nbf and iat.
  • RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices: the operational advice RFC 7519 leaves out, including why a claim you did not validate is not a claim you know.
  • pkg.go.dev/github.com/kataras/jwt: the generated reference for MaxAge, Leeway, Skew, Future and RequireExpiry.
  • pkg.go.dev/time#Duration: what 2*time.Minute is, and why a time.Duration written as a bare integer is nanoseconds.

Chapter 5

Choosing an Algorithm

The alg argument you pass to Sign and Verify decides more than which mathematics runs. It decides who can mint tokens, how large every token is, whether the same claims produce the same bytes twice, and what your key material looks like on disk. This chapter goes through the six families the package implements, states what each one requires and costs, and ends with a recommendation you can disagree with on purpose.

The six families

Every algorithm in the package is a package-level variable of type Alg, and the interface has three methods:

type Alg interface {
	Name() string
	Sign(key PrivateKey, headerAndPayload []byte) ([]byte, error)
	Verify(key PublicKey, headerAndPayload []byte, signature []byte) error
}

PrivateKey and PublicKey are both aliases for any. That is what lets one interface carry a []byte secret and an *rsa.PrivateKey, and it is also why a key of the wrong type is a runtime error rather than a compile error. The next section deals with that.

Family Names Sign key Verify key RFC
HMAC-SHA2 HS256 HS384 HS512 []byte the same []byte 7518 3.2
RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 RS256 RS384 RS512 *rsa.PrivateKey *rsa.PublicKey 7518 3.3
ECDSA ES256 ES384 ES512 *ecdsa.PrivateKey *ecdsa.PublicKey 7518 3.4
RSA-PSS PS256 PS384 PS512 *rsa.PrivateKey *rsa.PublicKey 7518 3.5
Unsecured NONE ignored ignored 7518 3.6
EdDSA EdDSA ed25519.PrivateKey ed25519.PublicKey 8037

The number in an HMAC, RSA or PSS name is the SHA-2 variant and nothing else. RS512 is not a bigger RSA key than RS256: both use whatever key you hand them and both produce a signature the width of the modulus. ECDSA is the exception, because the curve and the hash move together:

ES256 Alg = &algECDSA{"ES256", crypto.SHA256, 32, 256}
ES384 Alg = &algECDSA{"ES384", crypto.SHA384, 48, 384}
ES512 Alg = &algECDSA{"ES512", crypto.SHA512, 66, 521}

The last two fields are the coordinate width in bytes and the curve size in bits. Note the final line: ES512 uses P-521, not a 521-typo and not a 512-bit curve. The name follows the hash, the curve does not, and 66 bytes is what 521 bits rounds up to.

RSA-PSS is the same RSA key as PKCS#1 v1.5, with different padding:

PS256 Alg = &algRSAPSS{"PS256", &rsa.PSSOptions{SaltLength: rsa.PSSSaltLengthAuto, Hash: crypto.SHA256}}

A *rsa.PrivateKey works with both families. What you cannot do is verify a PS256 token with RS256 or the reverse: the padding differs, so the signature does not check out, and the header comparison would refuse it first anyway.

Symmetric or asymmetric

This is the decision. Everything else in the chapter is detail.

With HMAC, the key that verifies a token is the key that signs one. There is no separate public half. Any service you give the verification key to can mint tokens indistinguishable from yours, and your Verify call will accept them, because they are correct.

Say that plainly, because it is easy to walk past. If you run an auth service and six APIs, and all seven share an HS256 secret, then all seven are your auth service. A bug in the least careful of them, a leaked environment variable in a container image, a contractor with read access to one repository: any of those is a signing key. Nothing in the token can tell you afterwards which of the seven produced it, because the signature proves possession of a key that all seven possess.

With RSA, ECDSA or EdDSA the split is real. The issuer holds the private key and mints tokens; everybody else holds the public key and can only check them. That public key can be published, put in a config map, served from a JWKS endpoint, or checked into a repository.

The trade is honest in both directions. Asymmetric verification costs more CPU and produces larger tokens, and you now have a key pair to generate, distribute and rotate, which is Chapters 6 and 7. HMAC is faster, the key is a byte slice you can generate with one call, and there is nothing to parse. The question is not which is stronger. It is whether everything that verifies your tokens is allowed to issue them.

HMAC is a reasonable choice inside one trust boundary. One process signing and verifying its own session tokens, or two services under the same deployment with the same owner, is a fine place for HS256. The moment a third party verifies, or a verifier lives somewhere you would not put a signing key, you want the split. And note the thing HMAC cannot do at all: every holder of the key is equally the author, so if you ever have to answer “which service issued this token”, the token itself will not tell you.

Key types and wrong keys

Each Sign and Verify begins with a type assertion, and a wrong type yields ErrInvalidKey.

func (a *algHMAC) Sign(key PrivateKey, headerAndPayload []byte) ([]byte, error) {
	secret, ok := key.([]byte)
	if !ok {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("expected a string: %w", ErrInvalidKey)
	}
	// ...
}

The most common mistake in the whole package is right there. HS256 wants []byte, and a Go string is not a []byte:

_, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, "my-secret", claims)         // ErrInvalidKey
_, err = jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, []byte("my-secret"), claims)  // fine

The error text reads “expected a string”, which is misleading, since a string is exactly what it will not take. Match on the wrapped error rather than the message: errors.Is(err, jwt.ErrInvalidKey).

The asymmetric implementations follow the same shape with one addition. RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA all check for a nil key after the assertion:

publicKey, ok := key.(*rsa.PublicKey)
if !ok || publicKey == nil {
	if privateKey, ok := key.(*rsa.PrivateKey); ok && privateKey != nil {
		publicKey = &privateKey.PublicKey
	} else {
		return ErrInvalidKey
	}
}

The nil test is not decoration. A nil pointer stored in an interface makes the interface itself non-nil, so an *rsa.PublicKey(nil) passes the assertion and then panics inside crypto/rsa. It got there through a registered Key whose Public field was a typed nil, and from that point any token naming that kid crashed the process. EdDSA has the matching version: ed25519.PrivateKey.Public() slices the key at [32:], so the length check has to run before the call rather than after.

The fallback in that snippet is deliberate. All three asymmetric families accept a private key where a public one is expected and extract the public half themselves, which is a convenience for the single-process case where you hold both. It does not work in reverse. There is no way to sign with a public key.

Two more refusals worth knowing. algECDSA.Sign compares the key’s curve against the algorithm’s curveBits and returns ErrInvalidKey when they differ, so signing with ES256 and a P-384 key fails outright rather than producing something a verifier rejects later. And algECDSA.Verify checks len(signature) != 2*a.keySize before doing any arithmetic, because the JWS form is the fixed-width r || s concatenation rather than a DER structure.

Sizes and cost

Signature width is fixed by the algorithm, so token size is predictable. These were measured by signing the same three-claim payload with each algorithm, using a freshly generated 2048-bit RSA key:

Algorithm Signature Whole token
none 0 bytes 105 chars
HS256 32 bytes 149 chars
HS384 48 bytes 170 chars
HS512 64 bytes 192 chars
ES256 64 bytes 192 chars
EdDSA 64 bytes 192 chars
ES384 96 bytes 234 chars
ES512 132 bytes 282 chars
RS256 and PS256 256 bytes 448 chars

RSA is the outlier, and the reason is structural: an RSA signature is the width of the modulus, so a 2048-bit key gives 256 bytes whatever the hash, and a 4096-bit key gives 512. An RS256 token is roughly three times the size of an ES256 one carrying identical claims. For a token that rides in a header on every request that is real bandwidth, and for anything that has to fit in a 4 KB cookie it can be the deciding constraint.

For cost, the package’s benchmark suite covers HS256 only. On windows/arm64:

BenchmarkSign_Map-12       489426     2500 ns/op    1528 B/op    23 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_Struct-12    580483     2179 ns/op    1392 B/op    21 allocs/op
BenchmarkVerify-12         431294     2620 ns/op    1376 B/op    18 allocs/op

Almost all of that is JSON and base64, not HMAC. The same suite measures golang-jwt at 4713 ns/op and go-jose at 7460 ns/op for the equivalent verification, which tells you about the packages rather than about SHA-256.

Per-algorithm numbers are not in the suite, so measure them on your own hardware rather than trusting a table in a book. What you can rely on is the shape, which follows from the mathematics rather than the implementation. HMAC is the cheapest at both ends by a wide margin, because it is one hash. RSA is lopsided: signing performs a private-key operation across the full modulus and is the slowest operation in the set, while verification uses the public exponent, usually 65537, and is among the fastest. ECDSA is the reverse, cheap to sign and dearer to verify. EdDSA is quick at both and needs no entropy at signing time.

Pick on the ratio your system actually has. A gateway verifying ten thousand tokens a second against an issuer minting fifty cares about verification cost; a batch job minting a million tokens cares about the other end.

Determinism and golden tests

Sign the same header and payload twice with the same key. Do you get the same token? It depends on the family, and the answer was measured rather than assumed:

Family Same bytes twice?
HMAC Yes
RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 Yes
EdDSA (Ed25519) Yes
RSA-PSS No
ECDSA No

HMAC is a hash of the input. PKCS#1 v1.5 padding is fixed, so rsa.SignPKCS1v15 is deterministic even though it takes an io.Reader. Ed25519 derives its nonce from the message and the private key by design, which is one of the reasons the scheme exists: there is no per-signature random value to get wrong. PSS and ECDSA both draw from rand.Reader on every call, PSS to salt the padding and ECDSA to pick a nonce, and in both cases repeating that value would leak the private key. The randomness is not optional and not a flaw.

The consequence lands in your test suite. A golden test that pins an expected token string works for HS256, RS256 and EdDSA, and cannot work for ES256 or PS256:

// Fine for HS256, RS256, EdDSA.
if string(token) != want {
	t.Fatalf("token changed:\n got %s\nwant %s", token, want)
}

// Required for ES256, PS256: verify instead of comparing.
if _, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.ES256, publicKey, token); err != nil {
	t.Fatal(err)
}

The package’s own golden tests take exactly this split: where they can pin bytes they pin bytes, which is what caught the header casing bug in the next section, and where they cannot they verify and check the claims. If you are choosing partly for testability, the deterministic algorithms are easier to assert on, which is a genuine if minor point in favour of EdDSA over ECDSA.

The none algorithm

RFC 7518 section 3.6 defines an unsecured JWT: the alg header reads none, the signature segment is empty, and nothing is proved. The package implements it in three short methods, of which this is the interesting one:

func (a *algNONE) Name() string {
	return "none"
}

Lowercase, because that is what the RFC says. It returned "NONE" until v0.2.0, which no other implementation recognises, so tokens produced here were not valid unsecured JWTs anywhere else and conforming tokens naming none were never accepted here. Both directions were broken, which is a small argument for byte-exact golden tests. Sign returns nil, nil, and Verify returns ErrTokenSignature unless the signature is empty.

Now the part that matters. The classic JWT attack is to take a signed token, rewrite its header to {"alg":"none"}, drop the signature, and hand it back. It works against any library that reads the algorithm out of the token. This one does not:

verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token)

The algorithm is an argument. The default CompareHeader builds the expected header from that argument and compares bytes:

expectedHeader := createHeaderRaw(alg)
if !bytes.Equal(expectedHeader, headerDecoded) {
	return nil, nil, nil, ErrTokenAlg
}

createHeaderRaw("HS256") is the 27-byte literal {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}. There is no parse and no lookup. A header reading {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"} is 26 bytes that cannot equal those 27, so it fails with ErrTokenAlg before any signature check runs. The comparison also accepts the reversed field order some libraries emit, and a 15-byte header with no typ, but each of those is likewise built from the algorithm you pinned. A Verify call that named a real algorithm can never accept an alg: none token.

Enrich refuses NONE outright, both in the package-level function and in UnverifiedToken.Enrich:

if alg == NONE {
	return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: refusing to enrich under the unsecured algorithm", ErrTokenAlg)
}

Enriching means adding claims and signing the result. Doing that under none produces a token with your claims, your structure and no signature: the shape of a credential without being one. There is no legitimate use, so it is refused rather than documented.

If you genuinely want an unsecured token, for a client-side preferences blob where tampering costs nothing, pass jwt.NONE to Sign and Verify explicitly and be certain no authorization decision reads it. The source file listing the algorithms marks NONE, and also HS256, HS384 and HS512, with the comment // Not recommended.

Writing your own Alg

Alg is exported, so you can implement it. Reasons that come up: an HSM or KMS that holds the private key and exposes a signing call, an algorithm the package does not ship, or a wrapper around one that already works.
