The wrapper is the easiest case, because embedding jwt.Alg supplies the two methods you are not changing:

// timed wraps an algorithm and reports how long each signing operation took.
type timed struct {
	jwt.Alg
	observe func(name string, d time.Duration)
}

func (a timed) Sign(key jwt.PrivateKey, headerAndPayload []byte) ([]byte, error) {
	start := time.Now()
	defer func() { a.observe(a.Alg.Name(), time.Since(start)) }()

	return a.Alg.Sign(key, headerAndPayload)
}

Pass it as you would any algorithm: jwt.Sign(timed{Alg: jwt.ES256, observe: record}, key, claims). Name and Verify come from the embedded value, so the header still reads ES256 and the token verifies with plain jwt.ES256 anywhere else. A KMS-backed implementation is the same shape with a real Sign body, and it has to return the JWS signature form, which for ES256 is the 64-byte r || s concatenation rather than the DER structure most signing APIs hand back.

Three things to get right.

The name goes into the header, and the header is built by concatenation. Nothing escapes it, so Name() is validated before it gets there. encodeToken opens with checkAlgName, which requires a name of 1 to 64 characters drawn only from a-z, A-Z, 0-9 and the four punctuation marks -, +, . and _, returning a wrapped ErrTokenAlg otherwise. That is the character set JWA uses for algorithm names, not an allowlist of the built-in ones, so a sensible custom name still works. Without the check, an implementation returning a name containing a double quote could inject header fields of its own choosing into a token signed with somebody else’s key. Your Name() should return a constant.

Verification must be constant time in whatever you compare. If you compare bytes yourself, use hmac.Equal or crypto/subtle, not bytes.Equal.

Implement AlgParser if your keys come from files or a registry. It is the optional second interface, and Keys uses it to turn PEM bytes into key objects:

type AlgParser interface {
	Parse(private, public []byte) (PrivateKey, PublicKey, error)
}

All the built-in asymmetric algorithms implement it. HS256 does not, because there is nothing to parse.

One limit to note: UnverifiedToken.Alg() resolves a name through parseAlg, which only searches the built-in list, so it returns ErrTokenAlg for a custom name. Signing and verification are unaffected, since you pass the Alg value directly. Code that inspects an unverified token to decide what to do with it is affected, and the fix is a custom HeaderValidator. Chapter 6 covers those.

What to pick

EdDSA, when you control both ends. 64-byte signatures, 32-byte public keys, fast at both signing and verification, deterministic, and no per-signature randomness to get wrong. It is the newest of the set, which is the whole of its downside: older JWT libraries may not support it, and HSM coverage is thinner than for RSA and ECDSA. If your issuer and your verifiers are all your own Go services, that downside does not apply to you.

RS256 or ES256, when you must interoperate. RS256 is the most widely implemented asymmetric JWT algorithm in existence; every library, every gateway, every identity provider handles it. Choose it when an unknown third party has to verify, or when you are consuming tokens from a provider that offers it. ES256 gives you the same interoperability almost everywhere with a token a third of the size, so prefer it when you can check that your consumers support it. Both are fine choices, and the difference between them is bandwidth rather than strength.

HMAC only inside one trust boundary. HS256 is fast, simple, and requires a key at least 32 bytes of real entropy, which jwt.MustGenerateRandom(32) will give you. Use it when the same owner runs everything that touches the key, and stop using it the moment that stops being true. A password, a config default, or a phrase somebody typed is not a key; RFC 7518 requires a key at least as long as the hash output for a reason.

PS256 over RS256 when both ends are modern. PSS has better proofs and no known weaknesses in its padding, where PKCS#1 v1.5 has a long history of implementation problems. The catch is support: PSS is less widely implemented, and OpenSSL uses distinct key OIDs to stop a key being reused across the two schemes. Pick PSS for a new closed system, and RS256 when interoperability decides.

ES384, ES512, HS512 and the rest: only if something requires them. Larger hashes and curves cost bytes and cycles and buy margin above what the rest of your system provides. If a compliance document names one, use it. Otherwise the 256-bit variants are not the weak link. NONE: no.

Whatever you choose, pin it: pass the algorithm to Verify rather than letting a header choose. And write the choice down with its reason, because the next person to touch it will otherwise change it to whatever the first search result recommends.

Summary

Six families: HMAC (HS256, HS384, HS512), RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (RS*), RSA-PSS (PS*), ECDSA (ES256, ES384, ES512), EdDSA (Ed25519), and NONE. The number names the hash, except in ECDSA where it moves with the curve, and ES512 uses P-521.

The real decision is symmetric or asymmetric. With HMAC every verifier can also mint tokens that your own Verify will accept, and nothing in the token says which holder produced it.

Key types are checked by assertion at the top of every Sign and Verify, and a wrong type returns ErrInvalidKey. A Go string for an HMAC key is the common case. The asymmetric implementations also check for typed nils, because a nil pointer in an interface asserts successfully and then panics.

Signatures are 32 to 64 bytes for HMAC, 64 to 132 for ECDSA, 64 for Ed25519, and the width of the modulus for RSA, which is 256 bytes at 2048 bits. RSA signing is the slowest operation in the set and RSA verification among the fastest. HMAC, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and Ed25519 produce identical bytes for identical input; RSA-PSS and ECDSA randomise, so golden tests that pin a token string cannot be written for them.

NONE names itself none, per RFC 7518 section 3.6. Because header comparison is byte-exact against the algorithm you pinned, an alg: none token can never be accepted by a Verify call naming a real algorithm, and Enrich refuses NONE outright.

Recommendation: EdDSA where you control both ends, RS256 or ES256 where you must interoperate, HMAC only inside one trust boundary.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7518: JSON Web Algorithms: sections 3.2 to 3.6 define every algorithm here, including the minimum HMAC key lengths and the none algorithm.
  • RFC 8037: how Ed25519 is used in JOSE, which is where the name EdDSA comes from.
  • RFC 8032: Ed25519 itself, including why its signatures are deterministic.
  • RFC 8725 section 3.1: perform algorithm verification, which is the practice this package enforces by making alg an argument. Section 3.2 covers choosing among them.
  • NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: the key-length equivalence tables, if you want to argue about 2048-bit RSA against P-256 with numbers.
  • pkg.go.dev/crypto/ed25519 and pkg.go.dev/crypto/ecdsa: the Go implementations these algorithms call, including the key types you have to supply.

Chapter 6

Keys and Rotation

A system with one signing key has no way to replace it. Every token in flight was signed with that key, every verifier holds that key, and the moment you swap it every outstanding token becomes invalid at once. This chapter is about the mechanism that removes the constraint: a key identifier in the header, a registry mapping identifiers to keys and algorithms, and the ordering that lets a new key take over while the old one is still verifying traffic.

The flag day problem

Chapters 2 and 3 passed the key as an argument: jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, secret, claims) on one side, jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, secret, token) on the other. That works until you need a different key, and then there are two ways to replace it and both are bad. Deploy the new key everywhere at the same instant, and every process that verifies must restart in lockstep with every process that signs, while any token issued a moment before the switch fails on the other side. Or accept a window where verification is broken and hope it is short.

That coordinated restart is a flag day. It scales with the number of services holding the key, it cannot be rehearsed safely, and it turns key replacement into an event rather than a routine. The predictable result is that keys never get replaced, so a leaked key has no recovery path except the flag day you have been avoiding. What breaks the deadlock is letting a verifier hold several keys, and letting the token say which one signed it.

The kid header and the Keys registry

kid is a header parameter registered by RFC 7515 section 4.1.4. It is a hint, not a credential: it names a key, and the receiver decides what that name means. The value is an arbitrary case-sensitive string, so dates, version counters and random identifiers all work. What matters is that it stays stable for the life of a key and is never reused for another. The registry is a map, and each entry is a Key:

type Keys map[string]*Key

type Key struct {
	ID      string        // Unique identifier for this key
	Alg     Alg           // Algorithm implementation for this key
	Public  PublicKey     // Public key for verification (can be nil for HMAC)
	Private PrivateKey    // Private key for signing (required for signing)
	MaxAge  time.Duration // Optional: automatic token expiration
	Encrypt InjectFunc    // Optional: payload encryption function
	Decrypt InjectFunc    // Optional: payload decryption function
}
Field What it holds
ID The kid written into the header when this key signs, and the map key it is found under. Register keeps the two in agreement.
Alg An Alg value such as jwt.RS256, not a string. The most important field here: it binds one algorithm to this key, on your side rather than the sender’s.
Public, Private The key material. Both types are aliases for any, so the concrete type is whatever the algorithm expects: *rsa.PrivateKey for RS256, *ecdsa.PrivateKey for ES256, ed25519.PrivateKey for EdDSA, []byte for the HMAC family. A verify-only registry leaves Private nil.
MaxAge When greater than zero, adds an expiry to every token this key signs, which saves repeating jwt.MaxAge(...) at each call site.
Encrypt, Decrypt A payload cipher, covered in Chapter 11. Setting either one makes this key unusable for enrichment and for configuration export, both of which need the plain payload.

Registering takes four arguments, and Get reads a key back:

func (keys Keys) Register(alg Alg, kid string, pubKey PublicKey, privKey PrivateKey)
func (keys Keys) Get(kid string) (*Key, bool)

keys := make(jwt.Keys)
keys.Register(jwt.RS256, "signing-2024-01", &rsaPrivate.PublicKey, rsaPrivate)
keys.Register(jwt.ES256, "signing-2024-06", &ecdsaPrivate.PublicKey, ecdsaPrivate)

Register overwrites an existing entry with the same identifier without complaint. That is deliberate, and it also means a copy-pasted line with an unedited kid silently discards a key, surfacing later as ErrUnknownKid on tokens you expected to verify. Get returns a pointer into the map, so mutating the result mutates the registry, which is the supported way to set MaxAge, Encrypt or Decrypt after Register.

Signing and verifying through the registry

Signing names the key. The header it produces carries both parameters, kid first, and an unregistered identifier returns ErrUnknownKid before any crypto runs:

func (keys Keys) SignToken(kid string, claims any, opts ...SignOption) ([]byte, error)

token, err := keys.SignToken("signing-2024-06", userClaims{Sub: "u-1", Role: "admin"},
	jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute))
// header: {"kid":"signing-2024-06","alg":"ES256"}

On MaxAge precedence. SignToken prepends the key’s MaxAge to the options you passed, and options apply in order, so the last one wins. A key registered with a one hour MaxAge and signed with jwt.MaxAge(time.Minute) produces a token expiring in one minute. The method’s own doc comment claims the opposite. What is written here is what the code does, measured by reading exp off the signed token.

Verification does not name a key. It reads one out of the header. VerifyToken unmarshals into your struct and hands back only an error; Verify returns the token itself, for when you need the raw bytes to forward, a claim outside the standard set, or StandardClaims to give to a blocklist:

func (keys Keys) VerifyToken(token []byte, claimsPtr any, validators ...TokenValidator) error
func (keys Keys) Verify(token []byte, validators ...TokenValidator) (*VerifiedToken, error)

verifiedToken, err := keys.Verify(token)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
var claims userClaims
err = verifiedToken.Claims(&claims)

Both run the same path. Verify exists because without it every caller who wanted the token hand-wrote jwt.VerifyWithHeaderValidator(nil, nil, token, keys.ValidateHeader, validators...), including the two leading nils, which are the algorithm and key arguments the header validator makes redundant.

Three errors are worth knowing by name: ErrEmptyKid when the header carries no kid, ErrUnknownKid when it carries one you have not registered, and ErrTokenAlg when the header’s algorithm disagrees with the registered one. All three are decided before any signature work happens.

ValidateHeader binds the kid to an algorithm

Everything above rests on one method, which satisfies the HeaderValidator function type. Given a decoded header it parses kid and alg, looks the key up, and returns the algorithm, the public key and the decryption function to use. A key registered with no algorithm returns ErrInvalidKey rather than dereferencing a nil interface. The line that matters is the last one here:

func (keys Keys) ValidateHeader(alg string, headerDecoded []byte) (Alg, PublicKey, InjectFunc, error)

if h.Alg != key.Alg.Name() {
	return nil, nil, nil, ErrTokenAlg
}

The algorithm comes from the registry, and the header’s alg is only permitted to agree with it. Consider what that prevents. An attacker takes a token whose kid is signing-2024-06, a key you registered as ES256, rewrites the header to say RS256, and signs with an RSA key of their own. A naive implementation reads RS256 from the header, fetches the key material for that kid, and attempts a verification it was never meant to attempt. Here the header is rejected with jwt: unexpected token algorithm before the signature is examined. The same check covers the downgrade where alg is replaced with none, and the RS256-to-HS256 confusion where a published public key is submitted as an HMAC secret.

This is the security property of the whole chapter, and it fits in one line: the token chooses which key, and the registry chooses which algorithm. The sender picks an entry from a list you wrote, and everything about that entry comes from your side. The alg parameter is a further constraint: when it is not empty the header must match it as well, which pins verification to a single algorithm across a registry holding several.

HMAC in a registry

HMAC signs and verifies with the same bytes, so an HS256 key has no separate public half. Register accepts nil there and fills it in:

keys.Register(jwt.HS256, "internal", nil, []byte("sercrethatmaycontainch@r$"))

// inside Register:
if pubKey == nil {
	if _, symmetric := alg.(*algHMAC); symmetric {
		pubKey = privKey
	}
}

Without that, nil travelled from Register through ValidateHeader into algHMAC.Verify, whose type assertion on []byte failed, and every token naming that identifier was rejected with ErrInvalidKey. The package’s own documented example passed nil. The substitution happens only for HMAC: passing nil as the public key for RS256 leaves it nil, which is correct, since an RSA key with no public half can sign and cannot verify.

Mixing symmetric and asymmetric keys in one registry works for signing and verifying, and breaks two export paths. Keys.JWKS() and Keys.Configuration() both walk every entry and fail on the first they cannot encode: unsupported public key type: []uint8 from the first and jwt: unsupported private key type: []uint8 from the second. An HMAC secret has no PEM encoding and no place in a public key set, so refusing is right. It is also all or nothing, so if you plan to publish a JWKS, keep HMAC keys in a separate registry.

Enriching a token the registry signed

Chapter 3 introduced Enrich, which adds claims by verifying a token and signing a new one. The registry has its own version, taking no key and no algorithm:

func (keys Keys) EnrichToken(plainToken []byte, extraClaims any) ([]byte, error)

enriched, err := keys.EnrichToken(token, jwt.Map{"tenant": "acme"})

The missing parameters are the point. It calls keys.ValidateHeader, which checks the signature under the registered key and binds the kid to the registered algorithm, and only then re-signs. An earlier version signed the incoming header and payload with a registered private key before checking anything, which made the method a signing oracle for anyone who could reach it. The verified header is carried through unchanged, so the enriched token still names the same key and verifies through the same registry on the way back in. Keys with Encrypt or Decrypt set are refused, because enrichment merges claims into a payload it has to read.

Keys from a configuration file

Keys usually arrive as text rather than as Go values. Two types cover that:

type KeysConfiguration []KeyConfiguration

type KeyConfiguration struct {
	ID            string        `json:"id" yaml:"ID" toml:"ID" ini:"id"`
	Alg           string        `json:"alg" yaml:"Alg" toml:"Alg" ini:"alg"`
	Private       string        `json:"private" yaml:"Private" toml:"Private" ini:"private"`
	Public        string        `json:"public" yaml:"Public" toml:"Public" ini:"public"`
	MaxAge        time.Duration `json:"max_age" yaml:"MaxAge" toml:"MaxAge" ini:"max_age"`
	EncryptionKey string        `json:"encryption_key" yaml:"EncryptionKey" toml:"EncryptionKey" ini:"encryption_key"`
}

The four tag sets mean one document loads from JSON, YAML, TOML or INI without a wrapper type. Note the asymmetry: JSON and INI use lowercase names with underscores, YAML and TOML use the Go field names, so check the struct rather than guessing. Load turns the text into keys, and MustLoad is the same with a panic instead of an error, for keys embedded in the binary where a failure means the process cannot start anyway. Three things about Load deserve attention.

func (c KeysConfiguration) Load() (Keys, error)
func (c KeysConfiguration) MustLoad() Keys

An unrecognised algorithm name is an error, and the error names the key. The loop over the built-in algorithms used to start at RS256 and keep it when nothing matched, so "alg": "RSA256" produced a working RS256 key and confusing failures much later. Parse failures are labelled the same way, which matters once a file holds five keys:

jwt: load keys: id="api": unknown algorithm "RSA256"
jwt: load keys: id="api" alg="RS256": parse: RSA: private key: private key: malformed or missing PEM format (RSA)

EncryptionKey must be hex-encoded. It goes through hex.DecodeString before reaching GCM, so the string in your file is twice the length of the key it represents: 32 hex characters for AES-128, 48 for AES-192, 64 for AES-256. Anything else fails at load with jwt: load keys: decode encryption key (hex): encoding/hex: invalid byte: U+007A 'z'.

Quoted strings are unquoted. Public and Private are each passed through strconv.Unquote, and the result is used when it succeeds, which is what lets a PEM block sit on one line with \n escapes inside a JSON file.

Two convenience methods round out the type. Get is a linear scan by identifier. Clone copies the slice and every entry, so production.Clone() gives you a development variant you can edit without touching the original. Every field is a string or a time.Duration, so that copy is deep in the way that matters, and KeyConfiguration.Clone does the same for one entry.

func (c KeysConfiguration) Get(kid string) (KeyConfiguration, bool)
func (c KeysConfiguration) Clone() KeysConfiguration

Loading keys from PEM

When keys are files on disk, each algorithm family has a loader. The RSA set is representative:

func MustLoadRSA(privateKeyFilename, publicKeyFilename string) (*rsa.PrivateKey, *rsa.PublicKey)
func LoadPrivateKeyRSA(filename string) (*rsa.PrivateKey, error)
func LoadPublicKeyRSA(filename string) (*rsa.PublicKey, error)
func ParsePrivateKeyRSA(key []byte) (*rsa.PrivateKey, error)
func ParsePublicKeyRSA(key []byte) (*rsa.PublicKey, error)

The pattern repeats per family. Parse* takes bytes, Load* reads a file and calls Parse*, MustLoad* loads a pair and panics on failure. ECDSA has MustLoadECDSA, LoadPrivateKeyECDSA, LoadPublicKeyECDSA, ParsePrivateKeyECDSA and ParsePublicKeyECDSA. EdDSA has MustLoadEdDSA, LoadPrivateKeyEdDSA, LoadPublicKeyEdDSA, ParsePrivateKeyEdDSA and ParsePublicKeyEdDSA. Reading goes through a package variable, jwt.ReadFile, defaulting to os.ReadFile; replacing it loads keys from an embedded filesystem or a secret manager without touching the call sites.

The accepted formats are wider than the names suggest. ParsePrivateKeyRSA tries PKCS#1 and falls back to PKCS#8. ParsePublicKeyRSA and ParsePublicKeyECDSA try PKIX and fall back to parsing the block as a certificate and taking the public key out of it, so a .crt file works where you might expect a bare public key. Going the other way, RSA private keys come out as PKCS#1 (RSA PRIVATE KEY), ECDSA as SEC1 (EC PRIVATE KEY), Ed25519 as PKCS#8 (PRIVATE KEY), and all three public types as PKIX (PUBLIC KEY). Those two encoders are what Configuration is built on, the inverse of Load:

func EncodePrivateKeyToPEM(key PrivateKey) (string, error)
func EncodePublicKeyToPEM(key PublicKey) (string, error)

func (key *Key) Configuration() (KeyConfiguration, error)
func (keys Keys) Configuration() (KeysConfiguration, error)

The result marshals straight to JSON, and the round trip holds: keys exported this way and reloaded verify tokens signed by the originals. Keys with encryption attached are refused, since Encrypt and Decrypt are functions and cannot be written to a file, and a key with no Alg is refused with ErrInvalidKey.

MustLoadHMAC will not tell you the file was missing

The HMAC loaders break the pattern above, and the difference is dangerous. The argument is a filename or the key itself, and the whole implementation is short enough to read at once:

func LoadHMAC(filenameOrRaw string) ([]byte, error) {
	if fileExists(filenameOrRaw) {
		// load contents from file.
		return ReadFile(filenameOrRaw)
	}

	// otherwise just cast the argument to []byte
	return []byte(filenameOrRaw), nil
}

Now read it against a typo. Two calls, one with the right path and one with the last two letters transposed:

key, err := jwt.LoadHMAC("_testfiles/hmac.key")
// err = <nil>, len(key) = 32
key, err = jwt.LoadHMAC("_testfiles/hmac.kye")
// err = <nil>, key = "_testfiles/hmac.kye"

The second call succeeds. Your HMAC secret is now the 19-byte string _testfiles/hmac.kye, built entirely from characters an attacker can guess, and nothing reported a problem. Tokens sign, tokens verify, tests pass. The only symptom is that anybody who knows your repository layout can forge tokens. MustLoadHMAC is affected identically, because its panic can only fire on an error and there is no error to fire on. A deployment that lost its mounted secret volume gets a guessable key rather than a crash, the reverse of what a Must function is for.

Do not pass a path to these functions. If the key lives in a file, call os.ReadFile yourself and check both the error and the length, rejecting anything under 32 bytes for HS256. Keep LoadHMAC for what it is good at: a key supplied inline, from an environment variable, where there is no file to be wrong about.

The registry is a plain map

Keys is map[string]*Key with no mutex anywhere near it. Concurrent reads are fine, and reading is all verification does. Concurrent writes are not, and neither is a write racing a read. Register writes. The intended shape is to build the registry during startup, from a KeysConfiguration.Load or a series of Register calls, and never touch it again. After that every goroutine reads, and no lock is needed because nothing writes.

This is a real constraint and the package does not pretend otherwise. A mutex inside Keys would put a lock acquisition on every verification in every program, to serve the minority who change keys at runtime. Chapter 7 covers KeySet, which is the type for that minority: it holds a Keys behind an atomic pointer, swaps the whole map on refresh, and satisfies the same HeaderValidator interface, so it drops into the same call sites. If your keys come from somebody else’s JWKS endpoint, that is the type you want. For runtime registration against a local registry, build a new Keys, populate it, and swap the whole value behind your own atomic.Pointer or sync.RWMutex. Mutating the live map is the thing to avoid.

A rotation in four steps

Here is the sequence that makes a key replacement invisible to traffic. The property being exploited throughout is that verifiers can hold many keys while signers use exactly one.

Step one: add the new key, verify only. Deploy it to every service that verifies, alongside the old one. Nothing signs with it yet. Wait until this deployment has reached every verifier, because skipping the wait is the only way to break a rotation.

keys := make(jwt.Keys)
keys.Register(jwt.ES256, "2024-01", &oldPublic, nil)
keys.Register(jwt.ES256, "2024-06", &newPublic, nil)

Step two: start signing with the new key. On the issuing service, change one string, so that keys.SignToken("2024-06", claims, jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute)) replaces the call naming 2024-01. From that instant new tokens name 2024-06, and every verifier already knows it. Tokens signed a second earlier name 2024-01 and still verify. There is no window.

Step three: wait out the old tokens. The longest-lived token signed with the old key expires after its MaxAge. Wait longer than that. If you issue refresh tokens with a seven-day lifetime under the same key, the wait is seven days, not fifteen minutes. Chapter 4 has the arithmetic once skew allowances are involved.

Step four: retire the old key. Remove the registration and deploy. Tokens still naming 2024-01 now fail with ErrUnknownKid, the correct answer for a credential signed by a key you deliberately withdrew.

The whole sequence is three deploys of ordinary code. Nothing has to happen at the same instant, each step is reversible until step four, and at no point is a valid token rejected. Practise it on a schedule and it stays routine; leave it until a key leaks and you will be doing it for the first time under pressure. A leak is a different problem, incidentally: you want the old key to stop working immediately, so you run steps one, two and four back to back and accept that every token signed with it is rejected. That is the outcome you were avoiding in the planned case, and here it is the point.

Summary

A single signing key cannot be replaced without a coordinated restart of everything holding it, which is why keys that cannot be rotated usually are not. kid in the header names the key. Keys maps those names to a Key holding an algorithm, key material, an optional MaxAge and optional payload encryption. Register adds one and fills in the public half for HMAC, where both halves are the same bytes. SignToken writes the identifier into the header; VerifyToken and Verify read it back out.

ValidateHeader is where the safety comes from. The token selects a key by name, the algorithm comes from the registry, and the header’s alg is only ever allowed to agree with what you registered. A rewritten alg is rejected with ErrTokenAlg before any signature is examined.

KeysConfiguration loads keys from JSON, YAML, TOML or INI. An unknown algorithm name is an error naming the offending key, and EncryptionKey must be hex-encoded. Configuration goes the other way, through EncodePrivateKeyToPEM and EncodePublicKeyToPEM. LoadHMAC and MustLoadHMAC treat a path that does not exist as the key itself and return no error, so read the file yourself.

Keys has no lock and is meant to be built at startup. For keys that change while the process runs, use KeySet. A rotation is: publish the new key to verifiers, switch signing to it, wait out the old tokens, remove the old key.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7515 section 4.1.4: the kid header parameter in full. It is four sentences long, and the one about the value being a case-sensitive string is the one people get wrong.
  • RFC 7518: the algorithm names this package matches against, and the key size requirements for each.
  • RFC 8017: PKCS#1, the format ParsePrivateKeyRSA tries first. RFC 5958 is PKCS#8, the format it falls back to and the one Ed25519 private keys use here.
  • pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509: the parsers underneath every Parse* function. pkg.go.dev/github.com/kataras/jwt is the generated reference for every signature quoted here.

Chapter 7

JWKS

Chapter 6 gave every key a name and put that name in the header. This chapter is about how the names and the keys travel between machines. A JSON Web Key Set is the format almost every identity provider uses to publish its public keys over HTTP, and this package can produce one, consume one, and keep a consumed one current while the process runs. It also refuses several things when fetching, and each refusal exists because of a specific way the naive version fails.

What a key set is

RFC 7517 defines two things. A JWK is a JSON object describing one cryptographic key. A JWKS is a JSON object with a single member, keys, holding an array of them. That is the whole container:

{
  "keys": [
    {
      "kty": "RSA",
      "kid": "signing-2024-01",
      "use": "sig",
      "alg": "RS256",
      "n": "uGCsN_H_19DmAEz-OokW7VzP07cZHp41zfShi37N80IPhwaT_JSGzerqjVxt0p2lerBIJg2BPFtOLTQ",
      "e": "AQAB"
    },
    {
      "kty": "EC",
      "kid": "signing-2024-06",
      "use": "sig",
      "alg": "ES256",
      "crv": "P-256",
      "y": "P9N3oC-gFahsyubWhsH-ELO3c6KLh8UCVDIY8NtR6SI",
      "x": "7z0-SC3-OWY_b0ihYuayoh67zt70l-tXsyZKUGIQoho"
    }
  ]
}

The Go type is JWK. Four members appear on every key and the rest depend on the key type:

Member Applies to Meaning
kty all Key type: RSA, EC or OKP. It decides which of the members below are present.
kid all The identifier a token’s kid header names. This is the link back to Chapter 6.
use all sig for signature keys, enc for encryption. This package always writes sig.
alg all The algorithm the key is for: RS256, ES256, EdDSA and so on.
crv EC, OKP Curve name: P-256, P-384, P-521 or Ed25519.
n, e RSA Modulus and public exponent, base64url encoded. e is almost always AQAB, which is 65537.
x, y EC The coordinates of the public point, base64url encoded.
x OKP The 32-byte Ed25519 public key itself. There is no y.

Members that do not apply to a key type are omitted, not emitted empty. That is what the omitempty tags on Crv, N, E, Y and X are for. An earlier version published EC keys with empty n and e and RSA keys with an empty crv, which RFC 7517 does not permit and which some consumers reject outright. The four common members carry no omitempty, so they are always present. The values are base64url without padding, the same encoding Chapter 1 covered, applied to the big-endian bytes of each number.

Nothing in a JWKS is secret: these are public keys, and their purpose is to be downloadable by anyone who needs to check a signature. What matters is integrity, not confidentiality, which is why the transport rules later in this chapter are strict.

Publishing your own keys

If you issue tokens that other services verify, publish a key set and let them fetch it. The alternative is emailing PEM files around, which works exactly once and then becomes the reason nobody rotates.

One method converts a registry into a key set. Only the public halves are read, so a registry holding private keys is safe to pass. The convention is to serve the result at /.well-known/jwks.json, and to build the body once at startup rather than per request, because the document changes only when a key is added or retired:

func (keys Keys) JWKS() (*JWKS, error)

func jwksHandler(keys jwt.Keys) (http.HandlerFunc, error) {
	set, err := keys.JWKS()
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	body, err := json.Marshal(set)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
	etag := `"` + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8]) + `"`

	return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/jwk-set+json")
		w.Header().Set("ETag", etag)
		w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=3600")

		if r.Header.Get("If-None-Match") == etag {
			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNotModified)
			return
		}

		w.Write(body)
	}, nil
}

RFC 7517 registers application/jwk-set+json for this document. Most providers send application/json instead, and no consumer this package talks to checks either way, so send the registered one.

On the ordering. Keys is a map, and ranging over a map in Go yields a different order each time, so JWKS() sorts the result by kid with slices.SortFunc and strings.Compare before returning it. Without that sort the same registry produced a different byte sequence on every call. Any ETag computed from the body would then change on every request, every conditional request would miss, and a document that genuinely changes twice a year would be re-downloaded by every client on every poll. Sorting makes the body a pure function of the registry, which is what makes the handler above work.

One limit carried over from Chapter 6: a registry containing an HMAC key fails here with unsupported public key type: []uint8, because a shared secret has no public half to publish. Keep symmetric keys in a separate registry from the one you serve.

Generating a single JWK

The per-key conversion is exported, for when you are assembling a set by hand or publishing one key from a store this package does not manage:

func GenerateJWK(kid string, alg string, publicKey PublicKey) (*JWK, error)

jwk, err := jwt.GenerateJWK("2024-06", "ES256", &privateKey.PublicKey)
// {"kty":"EC","kid":"2024-06","use":"sig","alg":"ES256","crv":"P-256","y":"LnZi...","x":"quCA..."}

It accepts *rsa.PublicKey, *ecdsa.PublicKey, ecdsa.PublicKey and ed25519.PublicKey, and returns unsupported public key type: %T for anything else. The alg argument is passed through untouched for RSA and ECDSA, so it is on you to pass one that matches the key: nothing stops you labelling a P-256 key ES512, and a consumer that trusts the label will then reject every token it signs. Ed25519 ignores the argument and always writes EdDSA, because there is nothing else it could be.

Fetching somebody else’s keys

Two functions read a key set over HTTP:

func FetchJWKS(client HTTPClient, rawURL string) (*JWKS, error)
func FetchPublicKeys(url string) (Keys, error)

FetchPublicKeys is the whole job in one call: fetch, parse, convert. It returns a Keys, the same registry type from Chapter 6, so everything that worked there works here:

keys, err := jwt.FetchPublicKeys("https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json")
if err != nil {
	return err
}

var claims userClaims
err = keys.VerifyToken(token, &claims)

FetchJWKS is the lower half, returning the parsed *JWKS before conversion. Use it when you want the raw set, or when you need control over the request. Its first argument is an interface with one method, which *http.Client satisfies, and so does a wrapper of your own that adds an Authorization header for a private endpoint, records a metric, or returns a canned response in a test. Passing nil uses the package’s own client, described in the next section.

type HTTPClient interface {
	Get(string) (*http.Response, error)
}

func (set *JWKS) PublicKeys() Keys

PublicKeys is the conversion step. It walks the array, resolves each alg against the built-in algorithms, converts the key material, and builds a Key with the kid as its identifier. Keys it cannot handle are skipped silently: an unrecognised alg, an unsupported kty, base64url that does not decode. That is deliberate, so a set containing one key type you do not support still yields the ones you do. It is also why a set this package understands nothing in comes back as an empty map with no error at all, and KeySet below turns exactly that case into an error.

What the fetch refuses to do

The fetching path is small and most of it is refusals. Each one replaced a default that was wrong in a specific way.

A 15 second timeout. The default client used to be http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout at all. An endpoint that accepted the connection and then said nothing held the calling goroutine for the lifetime of the process. If you pass your own HTTPClient, set a timeout on it yourself, because the package cannot reach inside your implementation to add one.

HTTPS, except on loopback. A key set fetched over plain HTTP can be replaced in transit by anyone on the path, and the replacement keys will then verify the attacker’s tokens, which turns the whole verification step into theatre. Loopback is allowed because that is where a local identity provider runs while you develop, and the exemption is exactly four hostnames: localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1 and [::1].

_, err := jwt.FetchJWKS(nil, "http://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json")
// jwt: jwks: refusing to fetch keys over "http": use https

At most five redirects, each re-checked. http.Client follows up to ten redirects by default and does not care where they go, including from HTTPS to plain HTTP. The package’s client caps at five and runs the same scheme check on every hop, so a provider cannot be redirected off a secure origin partway through.

One megabyte, on both reads. MaxJWKSSize is 1 << 20. The response length is chosen by the host being fetched from, which on this path is precisely the host whose keys you have not established yet, so an unbounded io.ReadAll hands a stranger control of your memory. The limit wraps the body before both the error read and the JSON decode. A key set of a few dozen keys is a handful of kilobytes, so a megabyte leaves room to spare.

body := io.LimitReader(resp.Body, MaxJWKSSize)
if resp.StatusCode >= 400 {
	b, _ := io.ReadAll(body) // a truncated body is still worth reporting.
	return nil, &HTTPError{StatusCode: resp.StatusCode, Body: b}
}

The error body is on a field, not in the message. A status of 400 or above returns an *HTTPError, whose Error() is jwt: jwks: status code: 404 and nothing more:

type HTTPError struct {
	StatusCode int
	Body       []byte
}

var httpErr *jwt.HTTPError
if errors.As(err, &httpErr) && httpErr.StatusCode == http.StatusNotFound {
	return errors.New("no key set at that address")
}

Keeping those bytes out of the message is the point. An error string almost always ends up in a log, and the remote host chooses every byte of that body, newlines and terminal escape sequences included. Putting it in the message hands a stranger a log line to write. Read the field yourself when you want the detail, and treat it as untrusted text when you do. The type was unexported until recently, which meant callers could not tell a 404 from a 503 even though the package’s own documentation showed them doing it.

KeySet keeps the keys current

FetchPublicKeys is one GET. It has no cache, no expiry, and no way to fetch again when a token names a key it has not seen. Every service verifying against somebody else’s keys has to build that part, and two that were examined did not: one called FetchPublicKeys inside a constructor, so the whole fleet failed with ErrUnknownKid until restarted whenever the issuer rotated, and the other pasted the provider’s public key into a configuration file as PEM. KeySet is that missing piece:

func NewRemoteKeySet(url string, options ...RemoteKeySetOption) (*KeySet, error)

keySet, err := jwt.NewRemoteKeySet("https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
	jwt.WithRefreshInterval(15*time.Minute),
	jwt.WithMinRefreshInterval(time.Minute),
)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
defer keySet.Close()

verifiedToken, err := keySet.Verify(token, jwt.Expected{Issuer: "https://auth.example.com/"})

The first fetch happens before the constructor returns, so a URL that is wrong, unreachable or serving nothing usable fails at startup rather than on the first request. Three options adjust it:

Option Default Effect
WithRefreshInterval(d) 1 hour How often the background goroutine refetches. Zero disables the timer entirely, which is reasonable for a provider that rotates rarely.
WithMinRefreshInterval(d) 1 minute The shortest gap between two fetches triggered by an unknown key.
WithHTTPClient(c) the 15 second client above The client used for every fetch.

The methods are few. Keys returns the current map, which you must not modify. Refresh fetches now regardless of the timers. ValidateHeader is the same interface Keys implements in Chapter 6, so a KeySet drops into jwt.VerifyWithHeaderValidator anywhere a registry did, and Verify is that call with the nils already filled in. Close stops the background goroutine, is safe to call more than once, and leaves the keys readable afterwards.

func (ks *KeySet) Keys() Keys
func (ks *KeySet) Refresh() error
func (ks *KeySet) ValidateHeader(alg string, headerDecoded []byte) (Alg, PublicKey, InjectFunc, error)
func (ks *KeySet) Verify(token []byte, validators ...TokenValidator) (*VerifiedToken, error)
func (ks *KeySet) Close() error

Two triggers, and why the second is rate limited. The timer is the ordinary one. The interesting trigger is in ValidateHeader: when the current map has no key for the token’s kid, it refetches once and tries again. That is what makes somebody else’s rotation invisible to you. The provider publishes the new key before signing with it, and the first token carrying the new kid causes the refetch that closes the gap, with no restart and no configuration change.

That second trigger is an outbound request caused by an inbound one, which is a shape worth being careful with. A token naming a key that will never exist is a request anybody can send, so without a floor a stream of them becomes a stream of requests to your identity provider, from your address, at whatever rate the sender chooses. WithMinRefreshInterval is that floor, and the slot is claimed before the fetch rather than after, so a burst of goroutines all hitting an unknown kid produces one request between them rather than one each.

Reads take no lock. The map is swapped whole through an atomic.Pointer, and a verification already in flight keeps reading the map it started with. That is the reason this is a separate type instead of locking inside Keys: a mutex there would cost every verification in every program to serve the callers who rotate at runtime.

Failures are quiet on purpose. A failed refresh leaves the previous keys in place, because a provider having a bad five minutes should not take your verification down with it, and the keys you already hold are almost certainly still correct. The background goroutine swallows both the error and any panic, since nothing is recovering above it, so if you want to know about refresh failures, call Refresh yourself on your own schedule and handle its error.

ErrKeySetEmpty. PublicKeys skips keys it cannot convert, so an endpoint serving a set this package does not understand yields an empty map and no error. Refresh treats a zero-length result as a failed refresh and returns ErrKeySetEmpty, which NewRemoteKeySet surfaces at startup. Without it the operator sees unknown kid on every request and goes looking for a token problem, when the actual fault is that the key fetch is returning nothing usable.

AWS Cognito

Cognito publishes a key set per user pool, at a URL built from the region and the pool identifier. Fetching it once is one call:

func FetchAWSCognitoPublicKeys(region, userPoolID string) (Keys, error)

It returns an AWSCognitoError when Cognito answers with a status of 400 or above and a JSON body this package can parse, carrying the status and the message Cognito sent. That message is quoted and prefixed, jwt: aws cognito: status code: 400: "User pool does not exist.", for the same reason HTTPError keeps its body off the message: the text comes from a remote host and ends up in your logs. Like FetchPublicKeys, it fetches once and never again, so a pool that rotates its signing key leaves the result stale until you call again.

The character allowlist. Both arguments are interpolated into the URL that is then fetched, so both are checked first. A region of evil.com/x would move the request to a host of the caller’s choosing, and whatever came back would be used to verify tokens. The check is an allowlist rather than an escape, because neither field has any business containing something that needs escaping: letters, digits and hyphens, plus underscore for the pool identifier, since Cognito writes those as us-east-1_AbC123:

_, _, err := jwt.NewCognitoKeySet("us east 1", "us-east-1_AbC123", appClientID)
// jwt: aws cognito: region contains an unexpected character ' '

For anything longer-lived than a script, use the KeySet constructor instead. Its middle return value is the part that matters: an Expected validator holding the issuer, https://cognito-idp.{region}.amazonaws.com/{userPoolId}, and the audience, which is your app client identifier.

func NewCognitoKeySet(region, userPoolID, appClientID string, options ...RemoteKeySetOption) (*KeySet, Expected, error)

keySet, expected, err := jwt.NewCognitoKeySet("us-east-1", "us-east-1_AbC123", appClientID)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
defer keySet.Close()

verifiedToken, err := jwt.VerifyWithHeaderValidator(nil, nil, token,
	keySet.ValidateHeader, expected, jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute))

Why the signature and the clock are not enough. A Cognito user pool can have many app clients, and every one of them gets tokens signed by the same pool key. A token minted for a different app client of the same pool therefore has a valid signature under a key in your key set, an issuer you recognise, and an expiry in the future. If you check only the signature and the timestamps, you accept it, and whatever that other client is allowed to do, its users can now do to you. Both services examined for this chapter verified the signature and the clock and nothing else, which is why the constructor hands you the checks rather than leaving them as an exercise. Skew is in the example because Cognito omits nbf and its clock can run slightly ahead of yours; Chapter 4 covers what that allowance costs. If you pass an empty appClientID, the returned Expected carries only the issuer, and you are back to accepting tokens for any client in the pool.

Summary

A JWKS is a JSON object with one member, keys, holding JWK objects. Each JWK carries kty, kid, use and alg, plus the members its key type needs: n and e for RSA, crv, x and y for EC, crv and x for Ed25519. Members that do not apply are omitted rather than emitted empty.

Keys.JWKS() builds a set from a registry, reading only public halves and sorting by kid so the serialized body is stable between calls, which is what makes ETag caching work. Serve it at /.well-known/jwks.json, built once at startup. GenerateJWK does one key at a time. FetchPublicKeys fetches, parses and converts in one call, returning the same Keys type Chapter 6 used; FetchJWKS is the half below it and takes an HTTPClient; JWKS.PublicKeys() skips anything it cannot convert rather than failing the whole set.

The fetch enforces a 15 second timeout, HTTPS outside loopback, five redirects each re-checked, and a one megabyte cap on both the error body and the decode. HTTPError carries the response body on a field rather than in the message, because a remote host chooses those bytes and error strings end up in logs.

KeySet keeps a fetched set current. It refreshes on a timer and again when a token names an unknown kid, with the second trigger rate limited because anybody can send such a token. Reads are lock-free, failed refreshes keep the previous keys, and an empty result is ErrKeySetEmpty. NewCognitoKeySet returns the key set together with the issuer and audience checks, because a Cognito token minted for a different app client of the same pool has a valid signature under a key you hold.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7517: JSON Web Key and JSON Web Key Set. Section 4 is the member list; appendix A has worked examples of each key type.
  • RFC 7518 section 6: how the key material is encoded per key type, including why e is normally AQAB.
  • RFC 8037: the OKP key type and the Ed25519 curve.
  • RFC 7638: JWK thumbprints, a way to derive a kid from the key material so two parties compute the same one.
  • RFC 9110 section 8.8.3: ETag, and what a strong validator means for the handler above.
  • Verifying a JSON Web Token (AWS): Amazon’s own list of the checks a Cognito token needs, including the audience check.
  • pkg.go.dev/github.com/kataras/jwt: the generated reference for every signature quoted here.

Chapter 8

Validators

Verify checks a signature and three timestamps. Every other question your application has about a token, which issuer minted it, which audience it names, whether somebody logged out two minutes ago, arrives through one interface with one method. This chapter covers that interface, the validators the package ships, and one property of the loop that runs them: it stops at the first error. That decides the order your validators have to be in, and getting it backwards produces a chain that reads correctly and never runs.

The interface and its function form

Two declarations, both in verify.go:

type TokenValidator interface {
	ValidateToken(token []byte, standardClaims Claims, err error) error
}

type TokenValidatorFunc func(token []byte, standardClaims Claims, err error) error

func (fn TokenValidatorFunc) ValidateToken(token []byte, standardClaims Claims, err error) error

token is the whole token exactly as it arrived: header, payload and signature, dots included, not the payload and not decoded. standardClaims is the parsed Claims value, the seven registered claims plus origin_jti, and nothing else from the payload reaches you here.

err is the third parameter and the one that makes this interface unusual. It is the verdict so far: whatever claims validation produced, or whatever the previous validator returned. A validator receives the state of the decision and returns the new one, which is what lets it clear an error rather than only add one.

TokenValidatorFunc is the closure form. Leeway, Future and Skew each return one, RequireExpiry and Plain are one, and Expected and *Blocklist are types carrying the method. All go in the same variadic slot of Verify, and none ever runs for a token whose signature failed, since decodeToken returns early on any signature or format problem.

The chaining rule

The whole mechanism is the last third of verifyToken in verify.go:

if err == nil { // do not proceed if we have a JSON error.
	err = validateClaims(Clock(), standardClaims)
}
for _, validator := range validators {
	// A token validator can skip the builtin validation and return a nil error.
	if err = validator.ValidateToken(token, standardClaims, err); err != nil {
		break
	}
}

Read the assignments rather than the shape. Going into the loop, err holds one of three things: nil, errPayloadNotJSON if the payload would not parse, or a timing error from validateClaims. Note the guard on that call: when the payload is not JSON the timing checks never run at all, which matters two sections from here. Inside the loop, err is both the value passed in and the variable assigned, and whatever comes out is what Verify returns. So trace the first iteration. Validator one returns non-nil, the loop breaks, nothing else runs. Validator one returns nil, so validator two is handed nil. There is no third path.

A validator only ever receives a non-nil error when it is first in the list. Stated as a program rather than an argument, over a token that expired an hour ago:

spy := func(name string) jwt.TokenValidatorFunc {
	return func(_ []byte, _ jwt.Claims, err error) error {
		fmt.Printf("%s saw err=%v\n", name, err)
		return err
	}
}
jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, expired, spy("first"), spy("second"), spy("third"))
// prints exactly one line: first saw err=jwt: token expired

The second and third spies print nothing. On a token that passes, all three run and all three see nil. Three consequences follow.

A rescuing validator has to come first. Skew, Future and Plain work by turning one specific error into nil. Anywhere but position one they are handed nil, and returning nil for nil changes nothing:

// Correct: Skew clears the nbf failure, then Expected checks the subject.
jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute), jwt.Expected{Subject: "u1"}) // <nil>
// Wrong: Expected passes ErrNotValidYet through, the loop breaks, Skew never runs.
jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Expected{Subject: "u1"}, jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute))
// -> jwt: token not valid yet

Both compile and both look like a validator chain, and the second silently rejects every token from an issuer whose clock is a minute fast.

A later validator cannot repair an earlier failure. Once any validator returns an error verification is over, and nothing downstream can overturn that decision.

The prologue every built-in validator opens with is unreachable except in position one. Expected, RequireExpiry and *Blocklist all start with if err != nil { return err }. Write it in your own anyway: it is correct where it runs, and whoever reorders the chain next year will not read your code first.

The package’s own documentation got this wrong until v0.2.0. The doc comment on Plain said to place it last, “so it can catch JSON errors that other validators might depend on”. Run jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, plain, jwt.Expected{Issuer: "us"}, jwt.Plain) over a non-JSON payload and the result is jwt: payload is not a type of JSON: Expected returned the error it was handed, and Plain never executed. The comment now says the opposite, which is the useful reminder that advice about ordering is worth testing rather than trusting.

Expected, field by field

Expected is a distinct type over the same struct as Claims, so you fill it the same way:

type Expected Claims

func (e Expected) ValidateToken(token []byte, c Claims, err error) error

Each field is checked only when it is set, which is what makes partial validation possible, and the error names the claim:

Field Claim Checked when Error
NotBefore nbf > 0 jwt: field not match: nbf
IssuedAt iat > 0 jwt: field not match: iat
Expiry exp > 0 jwt: field not match: exp
ID jti non-empty jwt: field not match: jti
Issuer iss non-empty jwt: field not match: iss
Subject sub non-empty jwt: field not match: sub
Audience aud non-empty jwt: field not match: aud ("admin")

All of them wrap ErrExpected, so errors.Is(err, jwt.ErrExpected) matches and Classify returns KindRejected. OriginID has no check: the field exists because Expected is Claims, and ValidateToken never reads it. The timestamp fields are exact equality against a Unix second, useful in a test over a token you minted and rarely what a handler wants.

The audience row is the one entry in that table that is not equality. Each audience you ask for has to appear somewhere in the token’s list, which is what RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 asks of a recipient, so neither order nor extra audiences matter:

for _, expected := range e.Audience {
	if !c.Audience.Contains(expected) {
		return fmt.Errorf("%w: aud (%q)", ErrExpected, expected)
	}
}
// Token carries aud: ["api", "web", "mobile"].
jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Expected{Audience: jwt.Audience{"web"}})           // <nil>
jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Expected{Audience: jwt.Audience{"mobile", "api"}}) // <nil>
jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Expected{Audience: jwt.Audience{"admin"}})
// -> jwt: field not match: aud ("admin")

This used to compare the two lists for equal length and equal order, so an identity provider adding a second audience broke every recipient at once. What the membership test does not do is tell you the token was meant only for you: ["api", "partner-api"] passes a check for api, the RFC’s intent. If your rule is stricter, compare StandardClaims.Audience yourself.

A zero-value Expected validates nothing, and the call site cannot tell. The line jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, jwt.Expected{}) returns nil for any token that verifies. It has a validator in it, it passes review, and it checks no claim. The usual route to it is a config struct whose Issuer was never populated, so check that the string is non-empty when you load your configuration. The validator will not complain on your behalf.

Plain, for a payload that is not JSON

Nothing in RFC 7515 requires a JWS payload to be JSON. This package assumes it is, and when the assumption fails it sets an unexported error before the validator loop, so the only way to act on it is with a validator:

var errPayloadNotJSON = errors.New("jwt: payload is not a type of JSON")

var Plain = TokenValidatorFunc(func(token []byte, standardClaims Claims, err error) error {
	if err == errPayloadNotJSON {
		return nil // skip this error entirely.
	}
	return err
})

Pass it first and the payload comes back raw: for a token signed over just some text, jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, plain, jwt.Plain) returns nil and verifiedToken.Payload is that text.

Understand what you gave up. validateClaims is guarded by if err == nil and runs before the loop, so when the payload does not parse the timing checks never happened, and Plain clearing the error afterwards does not send the verifier back to run them. A token verified with Plain has a checked signature and no time bound at all, which also makes Plain followed by any claim-based validator pointless. Plain then Expected{Issuer: "us"} returns jwt: field not match: iss, and Plain then RequireExpiry returns jwt: token has no expiry, both from the zero Claims. errPayloadNotJSON is not a name Classify knows, so it comes back as KindInvalid rather than KindMalformed.

Reach for Plain when you verify tokens some other system minted with a non-JSON payload, and not to make a parse failure go away in your own tokens, where it is the finding.

Leeway, Skew, Future and RequireExpiry

Four validators that exist because of clocks and defaults. Chapter 4 works through the timing rules; here is what the chaining rule adds to them.

func Leeway(leeway time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc
func Skew(d time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc
func Future(dur time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc
var RequireExpiry = TokenValidatorFunc(...)

Leeway reads like a tolerance and behaves as the opposite. Its whole body is one comparison, which moves the clock forward and then asks whether the token has expired:

if Clock().Add(leeway).Round(time.Second).Unix() > standardClaims.Expiry {
	return ErrExpired
}

A token minted with MaxAge(30*time.Second) verifies on its own and returns jwt: token expired under jwt.Leeway(time.Minute). The name comes from the caller’s problem rather than the token’s: you are about to start something slow, and beginning it with a credential that dies halfway through leaves a partial write and a 401 you cannot retry. Two guards. It does nothing for a token with no exp, and it is wrapped in if err == nil, so it only refuses.

Skew(d) rescues both ErrNotValidYet and ErrIssuedInTheFuture when the claim falls within d of now. Future(dur) rescues only ErrIssuedInTheFuture, and since validateClaims checks nbf first and returns at the first failure, an issuer that sets nbf equal to iat produces a skewed token Future cannot help: with nbf and iat a minute ahead, jwt.Future(2*time.Minute) still returns jwt: token not valid yet while jwt.Skew(2*time.Minute) returns nil.

Both rescue, so both belong first, and a non-positive d makes Skew a no-op that passes the error through. RequireExpiry is a value rather than a function, so it takes no arguments: it returns ErrMissingExpiry for a token whose Expiry is zero, catching a MaxAge of zero quietly producing permanent tokens. It refuses rather than rescues, so put it after anything that rescues.

Collecting validators with Validators

func Validators(values ...any) []TokenValidator

This exists because of a Go rule that surprises people once each. TokenValidatorFunc implements TokenValidator, but a []TokenValidatorFunc is not assignable to a []TokenValidator: one element is a function value, the other a two-word interface value, so converting the slice would mean building a new backing array. Go declines to do that implicitly, and every call site holding one kind and needing the other grew the same copy loop:

jwt.Verify(alg, key, token, jwt.Validators(app.Validators, jwt.Skew(time.Minute))...)

It accepts a TokenValidator, a TokenValidatorFunc, a bare func(token []byte, standardClaims Claims, err error) error, a []TokenValidator or a []TokenValidatorFunc, flattens the slices and drops nils, preserving order.

The cost is in the signature: values ...any means the compiler checks nothing. Pass a string, or a typed nil matching none of the cases, and it is dropped without a word. A chain that silently lost its blocklist looks like one that never had it, so if you build validator lists dynamically, compare len() against what you expected.

Writing your own

A validator sees only the registered claims, so checking one of your own means decoding the payload inside the validator:

// ErrWrongTenant reports a token minted for a different tenant.
var ErrWrongTenant = errors.New("myapp: token is for another tenant")

// TenantValidator accepts only tokens whose "tenant" claim matches Want.
type TenantValidator struct{ Want string }

// ValidateToken implements jwt.TokenValidator.
func (v TenantValidator) ValidateToken(token []byte, standardClaims jwt.Claims, err error) error {
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	decoded, err := jwt.Decode(token)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var claims struct {
		Tenant string `json:"tenant"`
	}
	if err = decoded.Claims(&claims); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if claims.Tenant != v.Want {
		return fmt.Errorf("%w: %q", ErrWrongTenant, claims.Tenant)
	}
	return nil
}

Over a token carrying "tenant": "acme", TenantValidator{Want: "acme"} returns nil and TenantValidator{Want: "globex"} returns myapp: token is for another tenant: "acme".

jwt.Decode verifies nothing, and chapter 1 tells you not to trust what it returns. Inside a validator the situation is different: decodeToken already checked the signature over these exact bytes, so the payload you re-read is the payload your key covered. The cost is a second base64 decode and JSON parse per request, small next to the signature check, and there is no cheaper hook, because the parsed payload is not handed to validators. VerifyEncrypted decrypts after decodeToken, so a validator calling jwt.Decode(token) there gets ciphertext.

The error wraps a sentinel with %w and names the package that produced it, so callers can use errors.Is(err, ErrWrongTenant). What you cannot do from outside is make Classify return a category of your choosing: anything it does not recognise comes back as KindInvalid. To land in KindRejected alongside ErrBlocked and ErrExpected, wrap both, which Go 1.20 allows:

return fmt.Errorf("%w: %w", ErrWrongTenant, jwt.ErrExpected)
// errors.Is matches both; jwt.Classify returns KindRejected

The cost is a message reading myapp: token is for another tenant: jwt: field not match. Use it when the classification drives a response you care about.

Classify, and what to tell the client

Verification fails in about a dozen distinct ways, and a handler mapping them to status codes ends up maintaining a list of sentinels that drifts. Classify collapses them into five values, KindNone for success and the four below, and ErrorKind.String() gives the lowercase name for a log line or a metric label:

Kind Meaning Examples
KindMalformed Not a usable JWT. ErrMissing, ErrTokenForm, ErrTokenSize
KindInvalid Well formed, not ours. ErrTokenSignature, ErrTokenAlg, anything custom
KindExpired Right token, wrong time. ErrExpired, ErrNotValidYet, ErrIssuedInTheFuture
KindRejected Verified, refused by policy. ErrBlocked, ErrExpected, ErrMissingExpiry

Classify uses errors.Is, so a wrapped error still classifies, and the default arm is KindInvalid because the conservative reading of an unrecognised verification failure is that the token is unacceptable.

Return the same body for every failing kind. The kinds are for your logs, your metrics and your own decisions, not for the response:

if kind := jwt.Classify(err); kind != jwt.KindNone {
	log.Printf("rejected token: kind=%s err=%v", kind, err)
	http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
	return
}

Telling somebody their token was expired rather than forged, or revoked rather than signed by a key you do not hold, hands them a free oracle: they learn whether a token they carry was ever real, and whether a stolen session has been noticed. The defensible exception is a first-party client that must know when to refresh, and even there the distinction belongs in a field you control rather than in two error strings.

Summary

A validator is one method taking the token bytes, the parsed registered claims and the error so far, and returning the new error. Verify runs them in order, hands each one the previous result, and breaks at the first non-nil error, so a validator only ever receives a non-nil error when it is first in the list. Rescuing validators (Skew, Future, Plain) must come first or they do nothing, and no validator can undo an earlier failure. That rule is why the package’s own advice to place Plain last was wrong, and why it changed in v0.2.0.

Expected checks each field only when it is set, and its audience check is membership per RFC 7519 section 4.1.3, so extra audiences and a different order both pass. A zero-value Expected validates nothing while looking at the call site as though it does. Plain clears errPayloadNotJSON and with it every timing check. Leeway(d) is stricter than its name: it rejects tokens expiring within the next d.

Validators(values ...any) exists because Go will not convert []TokenValidatorFunc to []TokenValidator; it flattens, preserves order and drops nils, at the cost of compile-time checking. Your own validator decodes the payload with jwt.Decode and wraps a sentinel of its own. Classify sorts the result into five kinds for your logs, and the client gets the same body whichever kind it was.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7519 section 4.1.3: the aud claim, and the sentence that makes the recipient’s check a membership test.
  • RFC 8725: section 3.1, on validating every claim.
  • pkg.go.dev/github.com/kataras/jwt#TokenValidator: the generated reference for the interface and every built-in implementation.
  • go.dev/blog/go1.13-errors: errors.Is and %w.

Chapter 9

Revoking Tokens

A signed token is a promise you cannot take back. Once it leaves your server, every service holding your verification key will accept it until its expiry passes, and nothing in the format lets you change your mind. That is the price of a credential that verifies without a round trip. This chapter covers what to do when you need to change your mind anyway: why short lifetimes are the first answer, what a blocklist costs, and the two ways people get one wrong.

Why a token cannot be taken back

Verification is a local computation. A service holding the public key checks a signature and reads some claims, and at no point does it ask you whether the token is still wanted. That is the whole appeal: no database lookup, no network call, no shared session store.

It is also the whole problem. When a user logs out, when an account is suspended, when a laptop is stolen, the tokens already issued keep working. Deleting the token from the client is a request, not a guarantee: whoever has a copy still has a valid credential.

There is no revocation in RFC 7519, and there could not be. Anything that let an issuer withdraw a token would require the verifier to ask, and a verifier that asks is a session store with extra steps.

Short lifetimes come first

The cheapest answer is to make the window small. A token that lives fifteen minutes is a credential an attacker can use for at most fifteen minutes, and no infrastructure is required to achieve that:

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, claims, jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute))

This is not a complete answer, and it is worth being honest about why. Fifteen minutes is a long time if the token grants a wire transfer. It is also the window during which a suspended account still works, which is difficult to explain to whoever suspended it.

What short lifetimes do is bound the damage and reduce how often you need anything else. Reach for a blocklist for the cases the window does not cover, not for every logout.

The blocklist

A blocklist is a set of tokens the server refuses even though they still verify. This package ships an in-memory one:

blocklist := jwt.NewBlocklist(1 * time.Hour)
defer blocklist.Close()

// On logout.
verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token)
if err != nil {
	return err
}

if err = blocklist.InvalidateToken(verifiedToken.Token, verifiedToken.StandardClaims); err != nil {
	return err
}

// On every subsequent request. Blocklist implements TokenValidator.
verifiedToken, err = jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token, blocklist)
// err is now jwt.ErrBlocked

The argument to NewBlocklist is the garbage collection interval, not a lifetime. Entries are removed once the token they refer to has expired on its own, because after that point the signature check rejects it anyway and the entry is dead weight. Pass zero to disable the background sweep and call GC yourself.

NewBlocklistContext takes a context if you would rather stop the goroutine that way. Close stops it either way, and matters more than it looks: NewBlocklist passes context.Background(), so without Close the goroutine and its ticker live for as long as the process. That is fine for one blocklist created at startup and wrong for one created per test or per tenant.

The rest of the surface is small:

Method What it does
InvalidateToken(token []byte, c Claims) error Adds an entry. Returns ErrMissing for an empty token.
ValidateToken(token []byte, c Claims, err error) error The TokenValidator implementation. Returns ErrBlocked when the entry is present.
Has(key string) (bool, error) Whether a key is blocked.
Del(key string) error Removes an entry.
Count() (int64, error) How many entries are held.
GC() int Runs one sweep and returns how many entries it removed.

Choosing the key

An entry is stored under a key derived from the token, and which key you use is the decision that matters most here.

func DefaultBlocklistKey(token []byte, c Claims) string {
	if c.ID != "" {
		return c.ID
	}

	return BytesToString(token)
}

The jti claim when the token has one, and the whole token otherwise. Give every token a jti. The fallback works, and it keeps a complete bearer credential, signature included, in memory for as long as the entry lives. A memory dump of a process holding a hundred blocked sessions is a hundred usable tokens.

token, err := jwt.Sign(jwt.HS256, key, claims,
	jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute),
	jwt.ID(uuid.NewString()),
)

Replace Blocklist.GetKey if you want a different scheme, and call DefaultBlocklistKey rather than reimplementing it. That advice is not theoretical. A storage backend written against this package returned c.ID unconditionally, without the fallback. Every token without a jti therefore mapped to the empty string, so revoking one session wrote to the key "" and the existence check for every other session without a jti read from "". One logout blocked every session in the system.

The in-memory Blocklist used to fail the same way, only more quietly. Has refuses an empty key with ErrMissing, so an entry stored under one matched nothing: InvalidateToken returned nil, the entry sat in the map, and ValidateToken let the token straight through. A revocation that reports success and does nothing is worse than one that fails, so InvalidateToken now refuses an empty key and says which two things to do about it.

GetKey is an exported field read outside the mutex, so set it before the blocklist is in use, not while requests are arriving. The clock is different. Garbage collection reads it on every tick from a goroutine NewBlocklist starts before it returns, so a field could never be assigned without racing that goroutine, and it goes in through SetClock instead, which is safe to call at any time. Both fall back inside the type, so a zero-value Blocklist works rather than panicking.

Tokens with no expiry

An entry is stored with the token’s expiry, and swept once that time passes. A token with no exp has no such time, and the obvious implementation stores a zero.

That is what this package did, and it meant InvalidateToken returned nil and the entry was deleted on the very next sweep, because a zero expiry reads as “expired in 1970”. The caller was told the session was revoked. A tick later it was live again, and nothing anywhere reported a problem.

Such entries are now stored as never expiring, and GC skips them. That is the only answer consistent with the token: one that never expires needs a revocation that never expires.

The consequence is a memory cost you should know about. Those entries are never collected, so the blocklist grows with the number of revoked non-expiring tokens and never shrinks. If that worries you, the fix is upstream: give tokens an expiry. RequireExpiry on the verifying side turns the assumption into a check.

Where it sits in the validator chain

Chapter 8 covered the rule: Verify runs validators in order and stops at the first one that returns an error. A blocklist is a validator, so its position decides what it sees.

Put it last, after any validator that might reject the token for a cheaper reason:

verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token,
	jwt.Skew(time.Minute),
	jwt.Expected{Issuer: "auth.example.com"},
	blocklist,
)

There is a reason beyond tidiness. A blocklist lookup may be a network call to Redis, and an expired token does not need one. Ordering the cheap checks first means a flood of expired tokens costs you nothing downstream.

ValidateToken also cleans up after itself. When it is the first validator and the token has genuinely expired, it removes the entry on the way past and returns ErrExpired unchanged, because the claim check refuses that token anyway. Revoking a token and then verifying it after expiry takes Count from one back to zero, which is worth knowing before it surprises you on a graph.

A distributed blocklist

The in-memory blocklist is per process. Two instances behind a load balancer do not share one, so a logout handled by instance A does not stop instance B. For anything beyond a single process you need shared storage, and this package gives you the interface rather than the implementation:

type TokenBlocklist interface {
	TokenValidator

	InvalidateToken(token []byte, c Claims) error
	Del(key string) error
	Has(key string) (bool, error)
	Count() (int64, error)
}

Accept that rather than *jwt.Blocklist, and an in-memory blocklist and a Redis one become interchangeable. Here is the shape of a Redis-backed implementation:

type RedisBlocklist struct {
	client *redis.Client
	prefix string
	Clock  func() time.Time
	GetKey func(token []byte, c jwt.Claims) string
}

func (b *RedisBlocklist) key(token []byte, c jwt.Claims) string {
	get := b.GetKey
	if get == nil {
		get = jwt.DefaultBlocklistKey // not a reimplementation
	}

	return b.prefix + get(token, c)
}

func (b *RedisBlocklist) InvalidateToken(token []byte, c jwt.Claims) error {
	if len(token) == 0 {
		return jwt.ErrMissing
	}

	// Let the store expire the entry rather than sweeping it yourself. A token with no
	// expiry gets no TTL at all, for the reason in the previous section.
	var ttl time.Duration
	if c.Expiry > 0 {
		ttl = time.Until(time.Unix(c.Expiry, 0))
		if ttl <= 0 {
			return nil // already expired; the claim check refuses it anyway
		}
	}

	return b.client.Set(context.Background(), b.key(token, c), 1, ttl).Err()
}

func (b *RedisBlocklist) ValidateToken(token []byte, c jwt.Claims, err error) error {
	if err != nil {
		if errors.Is(err, jwt.ErrExpired) {
			_ = b.Del(b.key(token, c))
		}

		return err
	}

	blocked, err := b.Has(b.key(token, c))
	if err != nil {
		// Decide this deliberately. See below.
		return err
	}
	if blocked {
		return jwt.ErrBlocked
	}

	return nil
}

Three things to get right, and the third is the one people argue about.

Use DefaultBlocklistKey. The outage described earlier came from reimplementing it.

Let the store handle expiry. A Redis TTL removes the entry for you, and no sweep is needed. A token with no expiry gets no TTL, which is the same decision the in-memory version makes.

Decide what happens when the store is unreachable. Returning the error fails closed: every request is refused while Redis is down, including from users who were never revoked. Returning nil fails open: everything works, and revoked sessions come back to life for the duration of the outage. Neither is correct in general. Pick one on purpose, write down why, and make sure the choice is visible in a dashboard rather than buried in a helper.

Revoking a refresh token with its access token

SignPair links the two halves: the refresh token’s origin_jti names the access token’s jti. That link exists for this chapter.

Revoking an access token on its own accomplishes little if the refresh token that mints its replacement is still good. With the link, one lookup finds the other:

pair, err := jwt.SignPair(jwt.HS256, key, claims, jwt.PairOptions{
	AccessOptions:  []jwt.SignOption{jwt.MaxAge(15 * time.Minute)},
	RefreshOptions: []jwt.SignOption{jwt.MaxAge(7 * 24 * time.Hour)},
})

// pair.RefreshClaims.OriginID == pair.AccessClaims.ID

Store the pairing when you issue it, and on revocation block both identifiers. The alternative, blocking only what the user presented, leaves whichever half they did not present working.

Summary

A JWT verifies locally, which is why it is fast and why it cannot be withdrawn. Short lifetimes are the first answer and bound the damage without any infrastructure. A blocklist covers what the window does not, at the cost of a lookup on every request and a store to keep.

Give every token a jti, or the entry key is the whole token and you are keeping bearer credentials in memory. Call DefaultBlocklistKey rather than reimplementing it, because returning the jti unconditionally maps every token without one to the same empty key and one logout blocks everybody.

A revocation for a token with no expiry is kept forever, because the token is valid forever. That is correct and it is a memory cost, and the fix is to give tokens an expiry rather than to shorten the revocation.

Put the blocklist last in the validator chain, so the cheap checks run first, and decide on purpose what happens when a shared store is unreachable.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7519 section 4.1.7: the jti claim, and the uniqueness it is expected to have.
  • RFC 7009: OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation: the endpoint shape for accepting a revocation request, if you are exposing one.
  • RFC 9068: a profile for JWT access tokens in OAuth 2.0, including what it says about token lifetime.
