  • sync.RWMutex: what the in-memory blocklist uses, and why a sweep that releases the lock between reading and deleting can lose a write.

Chapter 10

Tokens over HTTP

A token has to travel from the client to your handler, and there are three places it can ride: a header, a query string, or a cookie. Each leaks differently, and the twenty lines that pull the token back out are the lines every service rewrites from memory. This chapter covers the extractors this package ships, a middleware that compiles, the mapping from a verification failure to a status code, and the token pair a login endpoint hands back.

Where a token lives in a request

Location Sent by the browser on its own What it costs you
Authorization: Bearer ... No The client must store the token and attach it
?access_token=... No Written to every access log and to browser history
Cookie: session=... Yes, on every request to the origin CSRF protection of its own

The Authorization header with the Bearer scheme is the default answer, and RFC 6750 defines it. It is sent only when the client chooses to send it, so a form submitted from another origin cannot carry it, and proxies do not log request headers by default. The cost is that whatever can read the client’s storage reads the token: in a browser, any script on the page.

A query parameter is the option to reach for last. A URL is written to the access log of every proxy and web server between the client and you, and it stays in browser history and in the address bar. There are places where nothing else works: an EventSource connection cannot set a header, and neither can a download link the browser follows on its own. FromQuery exists for those, and such a token should expire before anyone reads the log.

A cookie is sent automatically, which is the convenience and also the whole problem. A form on an unrelated site can point at your endpoint and the browser attaches the cookie. That is cross-site request forgery, and no amount of signature checking catches it, because the token really is yours and really is valid. The mitigations sit outside this package: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax or Strict, and an anti-forgery token for what SameSite misses.

The extractors

Four declarations cover all three locations:

type TokenExtractor func(r *http.Request) []byte
const BearerPrefix = "Bearer"

func FromHeader(names ...string) TokenExtractor
func FromQuery(names ...string) TokenExtractor
func FromCookie(name string) TokenExtractor
func ExtractToken(r *http.Request, extractors ...TokenExtractor) []byte

Each returns nil when the request carries no token where it looked, and ExtractToken returns the first non-empty result. FromHeader() reads Authorization, FromQuery() reads access_token and then token, and ExtractToken with no extractors behaves as though you passed FromHeader().

token := jwt.ExtractToken(r)
verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token)

No nil check sits between those two lines because Verify returns ErrMissing for an empty token, so an absent credential and a forged one reach the same handler rather than two. Pass extractors when a token can arrive in more than one place, as in jwt.ExtractToken(r, jwt.FromHeader(), jwt.FromCookie("session")): the first one that finds something wins, and a nil entry is skipped rather than dereferenced.

What FromHeader gets right

Two details in the header parser are the reason it is worth using rather than rewriting. The first is that the scheme comparison ignores case: RFC 7235 section 2.1 says the scheme is case-insensitive, so bearer, Bearer and BEARER are the same and clients send all three, while a parser built on strings.HasPrefix(value, "Bearer ") rejects two of them. The second is that the value is split on the first space only:

scheme, token, found := strings.Cut(value, " ")
if !found {
	return []byte(value) // A bare token with no scheme. Several gateways send this.
}
if !strings.EqualFold(scheme, BearerPrefix) {
	continue
}
if token = strings.TrimSpace(token); token != "" {
	return []byte(token)
}

strings.Cut returns everything after the first space, whatever is in it. The alternative people write, strings.Split(value, " ") followed by taking element one, truncates at the second space and hands verification a token missing its tail. The signature then fails, the log says the signature failed, and whoever is debugging it goes to look at keys.

Three hand-written versions of this parser across two codebases disagreed about exactly that. One truncated, one did not, and the third accepted a bare token with no scheme while the others rejected it, so the same credential was valid on one service and invalid on the next. That is a missing primitive rather than three separate bugs. Accepting a bare token is itself a leniency, since some gateways strip the scheme before forwarding; if your own edge always sends Bearer, write a TokenExtractor of your own, because the type is one function.

A middleware that compiles

Extract, verify, store the claims on the request context, and read them back through a typed accessor.

package auth

import (
	"context"
	"net/http"

	"github.com/kataras/jwt"
)

// claimsKey is unexported and has a type of its own, so no other package can read this
// value out of the context or overwrite it.
type claimsKey struct{}

type UserClaims struct {
	UserID string   `json:"user_id"`
	Roles  []string `json:"roles"`
}

func Middleware(key []byte) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			token := jwt.ExtractToken(r)
			verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, key, token)
			if err != nil {
				writeAuthError(w, err)
				return
			}
			var claims UserClaims
			if err = verifiedToken.Claims(&claims); err != nil {
				writeAuthError(w, err)
				return
			}
			ctx := context.WithValue(r.Context(), claimsKey{}, claims)
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))
		})
	}
}

// ClaimsOf returns the claims the middleware stored. The second result is false when the
// request did not pass through Middleware, which is a routing mistake.
func ClaimsOf(r *http.Request) (UserClaims, bool) {
	claims, ok := r.Context().Value(claimsKey{}).(UserClaims)
	return claims, ok
}

A handler behind it writes claims, ok := auth.ClaimsOf(r) and gets a UserClaims, with no type assertion of its own. Keep the ok result even though the middleware always sets the value: it is false exactly when a route was registered without the middleware in front of it, and 401 beats a nil dereference in production.

Why the context key is not a string

context.WithValue takes an any as the key and compares keys with ==, so two string keys with the same text are equal. Store the claims under "claims" and any package in the process, including one you did not write, can read them back with Value("claims") and replace them with another WithValue under the same word. A middleware from an unrelated library that happens to use that word wins, and the collision is silent: the type assertion in your accessor fails, ok is false, and the request is refused for a reason nobody can find. go vet flags a basic type used as a context key for exactly this.

An empty struct type settles it. claimsKey{} compares equal only to another claimsKey{}, claimsKey is unexported so no other package can construct one, and an empty struct occupies zero bytes. An unexported int constant works the same way and is common in the standard library; the struct form cannot be produced by accident from an untyped constant.

From error to status code

This package returns more than a dozen sentinel errors, and enumerating them at the HTTP boundary is how the lists that drift get written: one downstream copy enumerated fifteen while the alias file it came from re-exported twelve. Classify(err error) ErrorKind collapses them into the answers an application acts on.

Kind What happened Reasonable response
KindNone No error Carry on
KindMalformed Not a usable JWT: wrong shape, bad base64, oversized 400
KindInvalid Well formed but not yours: bad signature, wrong alg, unknown kid 401
KindExpired Valid, and its time has passed or has not yet come 401
KindRejected Verified, then a policy check refused it: revoked, claim mismatch 403

Classify uses errors.Is, so a wrapped error still classifies. Anything it does not recognise, an error your own validator returned included, comes back as KindInvalid: the safe reading of an unrecognised verification failure is that the token is not acceptable.

func writeAuthError(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
	status := http.StatusUnauthorized
	switch jwt.Classify(err) {
	case jwt.KindMalformed:
		status = http.StatusBadRequest
	case jwt.KindRejected:
		status = http.StatusForbidden
	}
	w.Header().Set("WWW-Authenticate", `Bearer realm="api"`)
	http.Error(w, "unauthorized", status)
}

The body is the same string in every branch, and that is the point. Telling a caller whether the token was expired, forged or revoked is free information for whoever is probing you: “expired” confirms the token was once real, “revoked” confirms the account exists, “forged” confirms neither, and someone who can tell those apart can grind through candidates. The trade-off is real, since the status code still varies across three values; if that bothers you, return 401 for everything. Distinguishing pays with a client you wrote, since KindExpired means it can refresh rather than send the user back to a login form. Put that in a WWW-Authenticate parameter, never in a different body.

Access and refresh tokens

An access token should be short-lived, because a leaked one is valid until it expires and nothing in the token can shorten that. A short life means the client needs a way to get another one without a password prompt, which is the refresh token: a longer-lived credential presented to exactly one endpoint. The two have to be linked, because revoking an access token accomplishes nothing if the refresh token that mints its replacement still works. Before SignPair, callers built that by hand: two generated identifiers, the access token’s jti copied into the refresh token’s origin_jti, every sign option run twice against two separate Claims values, and two signings. Roughly 129 lines, plus two option wrappers whose only job was to guess which half was being signed from whether origin_jti was empty.

func SignPair(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, claims any, opts PairOptions) (SignedPair, error)
func (keys Keys) SignPair(claims any, opts PairOptions) (SignedPair, error)
func (p SignedPair) TokenPair() TokenPair

type SignedPair struct {
	AccessToken []byte
	RefreshToken []byte
	AccessClaims Claims
	RefreshClaims Claims
}

AccessClaims and RefreshClaims hold the standard claims actually written into each half, generated jti included. PairOptions has five fields and a usable zero value:

  • AccessKID and RefreshKID name the registry entries to sign each half with. Keys.SignPair uses them and the package-level SignPair ignores them; an empty RefreshKID signs both halves with AccessKID. Separate keys are worth the trouble, since the refresh key is used once per session rather than once per request.
  • AccessOptions and RefreshOptions are []SignOption applied to each half separately. This is the awkward part by hand: the two tokens want different lifetimes and one option list cannot say so.
  • GenerateID is func() (string, error) and produces the jti for each half, defaulting to 22 base64url characters, which is 128 bits. Replace it when something downstream needs a UUID or another recognisable format.
  • Unlinked leaves the refresh token’s origin_jti empty. The link is the default, because without it there is no way, given a revoked access token, to find the refresh token that replaces it.
pair, err := jwt.SignPair(jwt.HS256, key, userClaims, jwt.PairOptions{
	AccessOptions:  []jwt.SignOption{jwt.MaxAge(15 * time.Minute)},
	RefreshOptions: []jwt.SignOption{jwt.MaxAge(7 * 24 * time.Hour)},
})

The link runs one way. The refresh token’s origin_jti holds the access token’s jti, so given a refresh token you can name the access token it came with and revoke both against one blocklist; given only an access token you cannot walk back without an index of your own. The refresh token is presented rarely, so it is the half that can afford the extra claim. Custom claims go into both halves verbatim, so put nothing in a refresh token you would mind being read by whoever holds it for a week.

The response shape

TokenPair is the JSON body, and it uses the OAuth2 field names so a standard client library reads it without a custom decoder.

type TokenPair struct {
	AccessToken string `json:"access_token,omitempty"`
	RefreshToken string `json:"refresh_token,omitempty"`
	IDToken string `json:"id_token,omitempty"`
}
func NewTokenPair(accessToken, refreshToken []byte) TokenPair

The body on the wire is {"access_token":"eyJhbGci...","refresh_token":"eyJhbGci..."}. Either token may be empty, and an empty one is left out of the JSON entirely. That part is newer than the struct: the fields used to be json.RawMessage filled by a helper that returned two quote characters for no input, so an empty token was never empty as far as omitempty was concerned and the response carried "access_token":"" instead.

IDToken is the OpenID Connect field, carrying identity claims about the user rather than an authorization to call an API. Providers that issue one return all three together, and a two-field struct matched no real provider response, so callers declared their own type instead of using this one.

A refresh endpoint

The endpoint verifies the refresh token, spends it, and issues a new pair. Spending it matters: a refresh token that survives its own use is a long-lived credential an attacker who copied it can keep using alongside the real client. Server here holds SignKey and RefreshKey as []byte, a *jwt.Blocklist, and Issuer as a jwt.SignOptionFunc.

func (s *Server) Refresh(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	var body struct {
		RefreshToken string `json:"refresh_token"`
	}
	// Bound the body: this endpoint is reachable without a credential.
	dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 8*1024))
	if err := dec.Decode(&body); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "bad request", http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	}
	verifiedToken, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, s.RefreshKey, []byte(body.RefreshToken),
		jwt.Expected{Issuer: "auth.example.com"}, s.Blocklist)
	if err != nil {
		writeAuthError(w, err)
		return
	}
	var claims UserClaims
	if err = verifiedToken.Claims(&claims); err != nil {
		writeAuthError(w, err)
		return
	}
	// Spend the refresh token, and revoke the access token it was issued with, which
	// "origin_jti" names. The token argument is there only because InvalidateToken
	// refuses an empty one: the blocklist key comes from the claims.
	standard := verifiedToken.StandardClaims
	origin := jwt.Claims{ID: standard.OriginID, Expiry: standard.Expiry}
	if err = errors.Join(
		s.Blocklist.InvalidateToken(verifiedToken.Token, standard),
		s.Blocklist.InvalidateToken(verifiedToken.Token, origin),
	); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "internal error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	pair, err := jwt.SignPair(jwt.HS256, s.SignKey, claims, jwt.PairOptions{
		AccessOptions:  []jwt.SignOption{jwt.MaxAge(15 * time.Minute), s.Issuer},
		RefreshOptions: []jwt.SignOption{jwt.MaxAge(7 * 24 * time.Hour), s.Issuer},
	})
	if err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "internal error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
		return
	}
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(pair.TokenPair())
}

Three things in there are choices. A separate refresh key means this endpoint is the only place that needs it, at the price of one more key to rotate. Blocking the old access token on every refresh logs the user out of any request already in flight with it, a stream of spurious failures if clients refresh eagerly rather than on a 401. And passing s.Blocklist as a validator is what makes a spent refresh token fail; without it, InvalidateToken writes entries nothing reads. That blocklist is in-memory, so two instances do not share it, which Chapter 9 covers.

Summary

A token rides in a header, a query string, or a cookie. The header is the default. A query string is written to logs and browser history. A cookie is attached automatically, which is why it needs SameSite, HttpOnly and anti-forgery protection unrelated to JWT.

ExtractToken, FromHeader, FromQuery and FromCookie replace the twenty lines every service writes. FromHeader folds the scheme’s case and splits on the first space only, the detail three hand-written parsers disagreed about. Put the verified claims on the request context under an unexported key type, because a string key is comparable to any other string with the same text. Classify turns a dozen sentinels into five kinds: map them to status codes if you like, but send the same body every time. SignPair issues an access and a refresh token together and links them through origin_jti, so revoking one can find the other. TokenPair is the OAuth2 response shape, with IDToken there for OpenID Connect.

Further Reading

  • RFC 6750: Bearer Token Usage: the Authorization: Bearer form, the query and form-body alternatives, and the WWW-Authenticate error parameters.
  • RFC 7235 section 2.1: the authentication scheme is case-insensitive, which is why FromHeader folds case.
  • RFC 6749 section 6: refreshing an access token, including the fields TokenPair mirrors.
  • OpenID Connect Core, token response: where id_token comes from and what belongs in it.
  • OWASP CSRF Prevention: what a cookie-stored token needs on top of a signature.

Chapter 11

Encrypting the Payload

Chapter 1 made the point once and this chapter is what follows from it: a JWT payload is base64url text, and anyone holding the token can read it. Signing settles who wrote the bytes and hides nothing from the person carrying them. This package can encrypt the payload with AES-GCM before signing, which changes that, and this chapter covers how, what the result is not, and why the answer is usually to store an identifier and keep the data on your own side.

What signing does not do

A signature answers one question: did a holder of this key produce these exact bytes. It says nothing about who may read them. The payload of an ordinary token is public to every party that touches it, which is the client, the browser extension the client installed, whatever proxy the request crosses, and every log line the token lands in.

Encryption changes the audience. With an encrypted payload the claims are readable only by a party holding the AES key, so the client can present the token and the token still verifies, but the client cannot see what is inside. That is the whole feature, and it is narrower than it sounds: the header stays public, the token’s shape stays public, and the signing key still governs who can mint one. The case where this earns its place is a token that has to carry something the holder should not read and that you cannot look up server-side: a tenant-internal identifier that leaks your customer count, a routing hint that names an internal service, an entitlement flag whose name tells the holder which feature to go looking for. The last section of this chapter argues that most of what people reach for encryption to solve is solved better by leaving it out.

GCM and the two functions it returns

func GCM(key, additionalData []byte) (encrypt, decrypt InjectFunc, err error)
type InjectFunc func(plainPayload []byte) ([]byte, error)

GCM builds an AES cipher in Galois/Counter Mode and returns the two halves of it as InjectFunc values. InjectFunc is the package’s general hook for transforming a payload between marshaling and encoding; encryption is one use of it, and compression and redaction are others.

The key must be 16, 24 or 32 bytes, selecting AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256. Anything else comes back from crypto/aes as crypto/aes: invalid key size 20, which you should treat as a startup failure. There is no attack here that distinguishes AES-128 from AES-256, so use 32 bytes because it costs nothing on any processor with AES instructions, and generate it from a random source rather than a passphrase:

encKey := jwt.MustGenerateRandom(32) // AES-256
sigKey := jwt.MustGenerateRandom(32) // HMAC
encrypt, decrypt, err := jwt.GCM(encKey, nil)

Keep the two keys separate. The signing key goes wherever a token has to be verified, and the encryption key goes only where the payload has to be read; those are different sets, and if one value serves both jobs then every verifier can read every payload and the encryption bought you nothing.

Signing and verifying an encrypted token

Four functions carry the encrypt and decrypt values through:

func SignEncrypted(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, encrypt InjectFunc, claims any, opts ...SignOption) ([]byte, error)
func SignEncryptedWithHeader(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, encrypt InjectFunc, claims any, customHeader any, opts ...SignOption) ([]byte, error)
func VerifyEncrypted(alg Alg, key PublicKey, decrypt InjectFunc, token []byte, validators ...TokenValidator) (*VerifiedToken, error)
func VerifyEncryptedWithHeaderValidator(alg Alg, key PublicKey, decrypt InjectFunc, token []byte, headerValidator HeaderValidator, validators ...TokenValidator) (*VerifiedToken, error)

Apart from the extra parameter they behave exactly like Sign, SignWithHeader, Verify and VerifyWithHeaderValidator. Sign options apply the same way, validators run the same way, and VerifiedToken.Payload holds the decrypted JSON rather than the ciphertext.

claims := jwt.Map{"user_id": "12345", "role": "admin"}
token, err := jwt.SignEncrypted(jwt.HS256, sigKey, encrypt, claims, jwt.MaxAge(15*time.Minute))
verifiedToken, err := jwt.VerifyEncrypted(jwt.HS256, sigKey, decrypt, token)

The result still looks like a JWT, because it is one. Its header decodes to the usual {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, and its middle segment decodes to 96 bytes that are neither JSON nor text.

A token verified without its decrypt function does not fail cleanly. The signature checks out, because the signature covers the ciphertext. What fails is the claims parse, and the error is the internal “payload is not JSON” one that the Plain validator exists to suppress. Pass jwt.Plain and verification succeeds with Payload holding raw ciphertext and StandardClaims entirely empty, expiry included. That combination is a way to accept an expired token without noticing.

The order of operations

Encrypt, then sign. Verify, then decrypt.

On the way out, signToken in sign.go marshals the claims to JSON, hands the JSON to encrypt, and only then calls encodeToken, which base64url encodes the result and signs the header and payload together:

	if encrypt != nil {
		payload, err = encrypt(payload)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
	}
	return encodeToken(alg, key, payload, customHeader)

On the way in there are two places the decryption can happen. decodeToken in token.go is the first. Its signature check, alg.Verify(key, headerPayload, signatureDecoded), sits a few lines above what follows, so the payload is only decoded and decrypted once the signature has already held:

	payload, err = Base64Decode(payload)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, nil, err
	}
	if decrypt != nil {
		payload, err = decrypt(payload)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, nil, nil, err
		}
	}

That is the path the key registry takes, because Keys.ValidateHeader returns the matched key’s Decrypt as its third result. verifyToken in verify.go is the second: it calls decodeToken, and then applies the decrypt you passed to VerifyEncrypted before parsing the standard claims.

Encrypt-then-sign is the order that makes the signature cover the ciphertext. A modified ciphertext is rejected by the cheap signature check before the AES-GCM authentication tag is ever examined, and an attacker cannot move a payload between two tokens, because the signature is over these bytes in this token.

The two decryption sites are also a hazard worth naming. Call VerifyEncryptedWithHeaderValidator with both an explicit decrypt and a header validator that returns one, and the payload is decrypted twice: the second call fails with ErrDecrypt on plaintext that is perfectly correct. Pick one. With the registry, pass nil for decrypt and let ValidateHeader supply it.

Additional authenticated data

The second argument to GCM is additional authenticated data, and it differs from the plaintext in one important respect: it is covered by the authentication tag, it is not encrypted, and it is not stored in the ciphertext at all. Both sides supply the same bytes independently, and if they differ by one byte then Open fails with ErrDecrypt. That makes it a binding rather than a payload: it ties a ciphertext to a context.

Suppose one AES key serves several tenants, and a payload encrypted for tenant acme should be undecryptable in a request routed to tenant globex. Build the pair per tenant with jwt.GCM(encKey, []byte("tenant=acme")), and a token produced by the acme encrypt function fails against a decrypt function built from tenant=globex.

The constraint that decides whether this is usable is that the verifying side has to reconstruct the same bytes without reading the payload, since the payload is what it is trying to open. So the additional data can only come from what is visible outside the ciphertext: a header field, a hostname, a path segment, a deployment constant. If the tenant name appears only inside the encrypted claims, you cannot use it. Passing nil, which is what the key registry does, gives plain authenticated encryption with no context binding.

The nonce and the error you do not get

GCM needs a nonce that is never reused with the same key. The encrypt function generates 12 random bytes per call and prepends them, so the segment on the wire is nonce, then ciphertext, then a 16-byte tag:

ciphertext := gcm.Seal(nonce, nonce, payload, additionalData)

Decryption slices those 12 bytes back off. A ciphertext shorter than the nonce cannot carry one, and slicing it would panic, so the length is checked first:

if len(ciphertext) < gcm.NonceSize() {
	return nil, ErrDecrypt
}

Note what that returns: not ErrTooShort, not a wrapped io.ErrUnexpectedEOF, but the same ErrDecrypt a failed authentication tag returns. A distinct error there would tell an attacker the difference between a truncated payload and a forged one, which is the difference between “you cut this token short” and “your key is wrong”. One distinguishable error is one bit of feedback per attempt, and that is how padding oracles are built.

In the ordinary path an attacker never reaches the decryption step, because the signature check comes first. The uniform error matters where that is not true: a service holding the signing key but not the encryption key can mint tokens whose ciphertext it chooses, and the InjectFunc values can be called outside this package entirely.

One limit on the random nonce is worth stating in numbers. Twelve random bytes give a 96-bit nonce, and collision probability grows with the square of the message count, so NIST SP 800-38D puts the ceiling for random nonces at 2^32 invocations under one key. Four billion tokens is not a limit you meet by accident, but it is a reason to rotate the encryption key rather than treat it as permanent.

Encryption in the key registry

Key carries the two functions alongside the key material:

type Key struct {
	ID      string        // Unique identifier for this key
	Alg     Alg           // Algorithm implementation for this key
	Public  PublicKey     // Public key for verification (can be nil for HMAC)
	Private PrivateKey    // Private key for signing (required for signing)
	MaxAge  time.Duration // Optional: automatic token expiration
	Encrypt InjectFunc    // Optional: payload encryption function
	Decrypt InjectFunc    // Optional: payload decryption function
}

When they are set, Keys.SignToken and Keys.Verify use them without being asked: SignToken calls SignEncryptedWithHeader with k.Encrypt, and ValidateHeader hands k.Decrypt back to decodeToken. From the caller’s side the code is identical to the unencrypted case, which is the argument for configuring encryption here rather than threading InjectFunc values through your own call sites.

In a configuration file the field is KeyConfiguration.EncryptionKey, a hex string. KeysConfiguration.Load runs it through hex.DecodeString, calls GCM with a nil additional data argument, and stores both halves on the Key. Hex rather than base64 because a 32-byte key is 64 hex characters that survive being pasted into YAML, TOML and INI without quoting rules getting involved. The decoded length still has to be 16, 24 or 32 bytes, and a 20-byte value fails at load time rather than at the first signature. Note the nil: there is no way to set additional authenticated data through configuration.

Two restrictions follow from a key having encryption attached. Key.Configuration refuses to export it, because the InjectFunc values are closures and there is nothing to serialize. And Keys.EnrichToken refuses to enrich a token signed with such a key, because enrichment merges claims into a plain payload and the payload it has is ciphertext.

This is not JWE

RFC 7516 defines JSON Web Encryption: a five-segment compact serialization, a content encryption key wrapped per recipient, and alg and enc header fields naming the key management and content encryption algorithms. This package implements none of it. token_jwe.go exists and contains no code, only a comment beginning “TODO? Add support for JWS and JWE. Currently, Out of this package’s scope”. What you get is a three-segment JWS whose payload segment happens to be ciphertext, and four consequences follow.

Nothing else can read it. A library expecting RFC 7516 will not decrypt it, and a library expecting a plain JWT will verify the signature and then fail to parse the payload. Both ends of every exchange have to be this package, or code written against it.

The header is not encrypted. alg, typ and any kid you set are visible, so tenant or environment identifiers placed in a custom header are public.

The standard claims are inside the ciphertext. exp, iss and aud are encrypted along with everything else, so nothing without the AES key can check them. An API gateway that today rejects expired tokens at the edge stops being able to.

There is one recipient. JWE wraps a content encryption key per recipient so several parties can decrypt with different private keys. Here there is one symmetric key, so every party that can decrypt can also encrypt, and therefore forge a payload for anyone else who shares it.

What it costs

The token gets longer. Here is the same claim set both ways, measured rather than estimated:

Payload bytes Token bytes
Sign 68 172
SignEncrypted 96 209

The 28-byte payload difference is fixed, 12 bytes of nonce plus a 16-byte tag, regardless of how large the claims are, and base64url turns 28 raw bytes into 37 characters of token. For a cookie with a 4 KB budget that is noise. For a header on every request of a chatty API it is a number you can multiply out.

The bigger cost is key management. You now have two key lifecycles, and rotating either one means a window where tokens signed or encrypted under the old key are still in flight, which Chapter 6 covers for signing keys and which is the same problem again here. Symmetric encryption also has no equivalent of a public key, so with one key doing both jobs you cannot give a service the ability to verify without the ability to mint.

There is also a failure mode that only appears in production. Misconfigure the encryption key on one instance out of ten and that instance verifies signatures correctly, then fails every claims parse. The error is ErrDecrypt, Classify reports KindInvalid, the log says the token was invalid, and nothing points at the encryption key.

When to keep the data on the server instead

The usual answer is to put an identifier in the token and store the data behind it. A sub claim and a lookup gets you a payload with nothing to hide and no second key lifecycle; revocation that works, since changing a row takes effect on the next request; data you can change, rather than a role the user keeps for up to fifteen minutes after you remove it; and a verifier that can check exp and aud without being trusted with the contents.

The cost is one round trip to a store you almost certainly already query for the request. Tokens carry claims to avoid that round trip, and if a claim is sensitive enough to encrypt, the round trip is usually the right trade.

Reach for encryption when the lookup is genuinely unavailable: a stateless service with no data store, a token that has to survive an offline period, or a payload that must cross a party you do not control and cannot be reduced to an opaque identifier. Those exist. They are rarer than the number of systems encrypting JWT payloads suggests.

Summary

GCM(key, additionalData) returns an encrypt and a decrypt InjectFunc built on AES-GCM, with a key of 16, 24 or 32 bytes. SignEncrypted and VerifyEncrypted carry those through the ordinary signing and verification paths, and the WithHeader variants do the same alongside custom headers.

The order is encrypt then sign, and verify then decrypt. The encryption happens in signToken before encodeToken; the decryption happens either in decodeToken, when a header validator supplies the function, or in verifyToken, when you pass it yourself. Supplying it both ways decrypts twice and fails.

Additional authenticated data is authenticated but not encrypted and not transmitted, so both sides must derive it identically. A 12-byte random nonce is prepended to each ciphertext, and a ciphertext too short to hold one returns ErrDecrypt rather than a distinct error, so nothing distinguishes a truncated payload from a forged one. The registry does all of this through Key.Encrypt, Key.Decrypt and a hex-encoded KeyConfiguration.EncryptionKey.

None of it is JWE. It does not interoperate, the header stays public, the token grows by 37 characters, and the AES key becomes a second key management problem beside the signing one. Before taking that on, check whether an identifier in the token and the data on your server answers the same question. It usually does.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7516: JSON Web Encryption: the standard this chapter is not. Section 3 shows the five-segment serialization.
  • NIST SP 800-38D: the GCM specification, the nonce rules, and the 2^32 limit on random nonces under one key.
  • crypto/cipher.NewGCM: what Seal and Open do with the destination slice.
  • RFC 5116: authenticated encryption with associated data as an interface, where the additional data argument comes from.

Chapter 12

Sharp Edges

Every library has places where the obvious reading of an API is not what it does. Most documentation leaves you to find them. This chapter is the list for this package: the defaults that are surprising, the names that read the wrong way round, the fast paths that carry a hazard, and the things that were outright broken until recently. Some of these have been fixed and are recorded here because the fix changed behaviour you may have depended on. The rest are live, and you should know about them before they find you.

Names that read the wrong way round

Leeway is stricter, not more lenient. The word suggests tolerance for a clock that runs a little fast. What it does is reject a token that expires within the duration you give it:

func Leeway(leeway time.Duration) TokenValidatorFunc {
	return func(_ []byte, standardClaims Claims, err error) error {
		if err == nil {
			if standardClaims.Expiry > 0 {
				if Clock().Add(leeway).Round(time.Second).Unix() > standardClaims.Expiry {
					return ErrExpired
				}
			}
		}

		return err
	}
}

Leeway(time.Minute) turns away a token with fifty seconds left. It is useful when a request will take a while and you want the token to still be valid at the end of it. It is not clock-skew tolerance. Skew is.

SignWithHeader replaces the header rather than merging into it. The name suggests you are adding fields alongside the standard ones. createCustomHeader marshals what you hand it and uses the result as the entire header:

func createCustomHeader(header any) ([]byte, error) {
	b, err := Marshal(header)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return Base64Encode(b), nil
}

So SignWithHeader(HS256, key, claims, map[string]any{"kid": "k1"}) produces a token whose header is {"kid":"k1"} with no alg at all. If you use a custom header, include alg and typ yourself, or use HeaderWithKid, which has both fields.

UnverifiedToken.Enrich verifies nothing. That is what the type name says, and it is easy to skim past when the method is called Enrich and the package-level Enrich does verify. The unverified one exists for callers who have already established authenticity some other way.

Defaults that are quieter than you want

MaxAge of a second or less produces a token that never expires. Read it:

func MaxAge(maxAge time.Duration) SignOptionFunc {
	if maxAge <= time.Second {
		return NoMaxAge
	}
	// ...
}

NoMaxAge zeroes both exp and iat. So a configuration file with max_age: 0, or a duration that arrived as zero because a field name was misspelled in YAML, gives you permanent tokens and no error anywhere. RequireExpiry on the verifying side is the defence.

A zero-value Expected validates nothing. Every check inside it is guarded on the field being non-empty, so jwt.Expected{} passed to Verify returns nil for any token. It looks like validation at the call site. It is not.

LoadHMAC treats a path that does not exist as the key itself.

func LoadHMAC(filenameOrRaw string) ([]byte, error) {
	if fileExists(filenameOrRaw) {
		return ReadFile(filenameOrRaw)
	}

	return []byte(filenameOrRaw), nil
}

That is convenient when you want to accept either form. It also means a typo in a path turns the path into your HMAC secret: /etc/secrets/jwt.key is twenty bytes of guessable ASCII, and nothing errors. If the key comes from configuration, read the file yourself and fail when it is not there.

A token with no exp is valid forever. RFC 7519 makes the claim optional and this package follows the RFC. RequireExpiry is one line and worth adding.

The package-level variables

Five exported variables change behaviour for the whole process:

Variable Default Read on
Clock time.Now every claim validation
CompareHeader compareHeader every verification
ReadFile os.ReadFile every key load
Marshal a function that passes []byte through every sign
Unmarshal defaultUnmarshal every claim decode

They are useful. Clock makes time-dependent tests deterministic, ReadFile lets keys come from an embedded filesystem, and Unmarshal can be swapped for a faster codec.

They are also read without any synchronisation, on paths that run concurrently. The documented rule is to set them during startup, before any goroutine verifies anything, and nothing enforces it. Assigning jwt.Clock from a test that runs in parallel with another test that verifies a token is a data race, and the race detector will say so.

CompareHeader deserves singling out. It is the algorithm check. Any package in your dependency graph can replace it for your entire process, and nothing will report that it happened.

There is a second trap that has nothing to do with races. Anything that captures one of these at construction time, rather than calling through the variable, will not see a later change:

// This reads the variable once, when the middleware is built.
unmarshal := jwt.Unmarshal

A later jwt.Unmarshal = something has no effect on that middleware. That is a real pattern from a real codebase, and it took a while to work out why the replacement was being ignored.

Keys is a plain map

Keys is map[string]*Key. Register writes to it with no lock, and Get and ValidateHeader read from it on the verification path. Building the registry at startup and reading it afterwards is fine. Registering a key while requests are in flight is a concurrent map write, which is not a race the runtime tolerates: it is fatal error: concurrent map read and map write, and it takes the process down with no recovery.

This is deliberate. Putting a mutex inside Keys would put a lock acquisition on every verification to serve the minority of callers who rotate at runtime. KeySet from chapter 7 is the type for that case: it swaps the whole map atomically, so readers take no lock at all.

If you need to add a key to a plain Keys at runtime, build a new map and swap the reference under your own synchronisation, or use KeySet.

Merge splices JSON and can emit a duplicate key

Merge is what combines your custom claims with the standard ones. It does not unmarshal and remarshal. It takes each value, checks that it is a JSON object, strips the outer braces and joins the insides with commas:

inner := jsonBytes[1 : len(jsonBytes)-1]
parts = append(parts, inner)

That is why signing is fast. It is also why merging {"role":"admin"} with {"role":"user"} produces {"role":"admin","role":"user"}, which is legal JSON that different parsers read differently. Go’s encoding/json takes the last occurrence. Several other languages take the first. A token signed by this package can therefore mean one thing to your Go service and another to a Python service reading the same bytes.

The practical rule is to not restate a claim you have already set. If you need to override one, set it once in the value that wins for your reader, and be aware that a different reader may disagree.

Raw string and []byte values are spliced in as they are, so they are checked with json.Valid first and rejected with ErrNotJSONObject otherwise. Before that check existed, a fragment like {"broken"} was spliced in happily and the result was a properly signed token whose payload is not JSON.

The unsafe string conversion

BytesToString converts a byte slice to a string without copying:

func BytesToString(b []byte) string {
	return unsafe.String(unsafe.SliceData(b), len(b))
}

The returned string shares memory with the slice. If the slice changes, the string changes with it, which is not something a Go string is ever supposed to do. Build with -tags safe to get the allocating version instead.

The place this matters most is the blocklist. Without a jti, the entry key is the whole token, produced by exactly this conversion. Storing that string as a map key would mean a caller who reuses the buffer, which is what a pooled HTTP read buffer does, silently rewrites the contents of a live key. InvalidateToken therefore copies the key with strings.Clone before storing it, and the lookup path keeps the zero-copy version, because a map lookup does not retain the string.

If you write your own code that keeps the result of BytesToString beyond the lifetime of the bytes, copy it.

What Enrich used to be

This one is worth knowing about even though it is fixed, because it explains the shape of the current API and because you may still have code written against the old one.

Enrich adds claims to a token by re-signing it. Until v0.2.0 it took the signing algorithm from the header of the token it was given, spliced that token’s payload into the new one, reused the header verbatim, and verified nothing at all. The signature it produced was made with your private key.

So a service that enriched a token it had received would sign whatever header and payload the sender chose. parseAlg resolves the unsecured algorithm, so the sender could also ask for a token with no signature. There was no attack required beyond sending a token.

The current API takes the algorithm as its first argument, checks the signature before re-signing, and refuses the unsecured algorithm outright:

func Enrich(alg Alg, key PrivateKey, accessToken []byte, extraClaims any) ([]byte, error)

The verification costs about eight allocations. If you have already verified the token and want them back, Decode followed by UnverifiedToken.Enrich skips the second check and leaves the safety argument with you. That method builds a fresh header from alg rather than copying the one it was handed, which is why a kid on its input is dropped.

Behaviour that changed in v0.2.0

If you are upgrading, these change the bytes on the wire or the errors you get back.

What changed Before Now
The unsecured algorithm’s name NONE, which no other implementation accepts none, as RFC 7518 section 3.6 requires
Enrich and UnverifiedToken.Enrich took no algorithm and verified nothing take an Alg first and verify
Expected.Audience required equal length and identical order membership, per RFC 7519 section 4.1.3
A token with exp: -1 treated as having no expiry expired
A JWK for a key type carried empty n, e, crv members omits members that do not apply
Keys.JWKS() for an ECDSA key failed with unsupported public key type works
Keys.JWKS() ordering map order, different on every call sorted by key id
GenerateEdDSA declared ed25519.PublicKey and returned PEM returns []byte
NewTokenPair(nil, nil) {"access_token":"","refresh_token":""} {}
BytesQuote exported removed
An unknown algorithm name in a KeysConfiguration silently became RS256 an error naming the key
A structured sub claim became the string map[a:1] ErrTokenForm

The none rename is the one most likely to affect you, and only if you were producing unsecured tokens with this package and reading them back with it. Tokens carrying the old NONE header will no longer verify.

Summary

The sharp edges here cluster into four kinds. Names that suggest the opposite of what the code does, and Leeway is the worst of them. Defaults that are quiet when they should complain, of which MaxAge collapsing to no expiry and LoadHMAC turning a path into a secret are the two that have cost people real time. Fast paths that carry a hazard, specifically the unsafe string conversion and the raw JSON splice in Merge, both of which are deliberate and both of which have a rule attached. And a set of behaviour changes in v0.2.0, most of which exist because the previous behaviour was wrong rather than merely different.

None of this is an argument against the package. It is the argument for reading this chapter before you are debugging at two in the morning.

Further Reading

  • RFC 7518 section 3.6: the unsecured algorithm, and the spelling of its name.
  • RFC 7519 section 4.1.3: the audience claim, and what a recipient is asked to check.
  • unsafe.String: the conversion behind BytesToString, and the guarantees it does not make.
  • Go maps are not safe for concurrent use: why a concurrent write to Keys is a fatal error rather than a race you can survive.
  • json.Valid: the check Merge applies to raw fragments, and what it does not check.

Chapter 13

Testing

Code that signs and verifies tokens is hard to test badly and easy to test uselessly. The useless version stands up a real identity provider, waits for a real clock, and passes because the network happened to be up. This chapter is about the other kind: tests that run in milliseconds, fail for one reason, and keep failing until somebody fixes the thing they were written about. This package’s own suite works that way, so most of what follows describes code you can read in the repository.

The suite that never opens a socket

This package has 112 test functions across 28 files. Not one of them opens a socket. There is no httptest.NewServer, no net.Listen, no http.Get. The whole suite finishes in about four seconds. That is not an accident of scope: half the package fetches key material over HTTPS, refreshes it on a timer, and refetches it when a token names a key identifier nobody has seen. All of that is tested, and none of it touches the network.

Three seams make it possible, and you get all three: Clock for the current time, ReadFile for PEM files on disk, and the HTTPClient interface for the JWKS fetch. Two of them are package-level variables. That is the trade-off. A seam you can reach without threading a parameter through six call sites is also a seam any other test in the same binary can reach at the same moment.

Controlling time

Every time-based check in the package reads one variable, declared as var Clock = time.Now. Replace it and exp, nbf and iat are all evaluated against whatever you return. Save the old value, restore it from t.Cleanup so the restore survives a failure partway through:

// at moves the package clock to a fixed instant and puts it back afterwards.
func at(t *testing.T, when time.Time) {
	t.Helper()

	previous := jwt.Clock
	t.Cleanup(func() { jwt.Clock = previous })
	jwt.Clock = func() time.Time { return when }
}

Call at once before signing and again with a later instant before verifying, and the expiry rule is under test rather than the scheduler. The package’s own tests use this shape: sign_test.go copies the old value into prevClock and restores it from t.Cleanup, and claims_test.go does the same with a defer.

Clock is read without a lock. Every call to Verify reads it and your assignment writes it, which is a data race in the formal sense: the detector reports it and the compiler is entitled to do something surprising with it. So no test touching Clock may call t.Parallel(), and neither may anything running beside it. Go gives each package its own test binary, so a swap in your package cannot reach another package’s tests, but within one package the whole file set shares the variable.

Where you can, skip the swap: a test that wants an expired token needs only an exp in the past, and that version is parallel-safe. Reach for the clock when the code under test computes a timestamp rather than reads one, which is what MaxAge, SignPair and the leeway validators do.

Blocklist is the counter-example: its clock is per-instance, so two blocklists in two parallel tests hold two clocks and never notice each other. NewBlocklist(0) starts one with no background collector, b.SetClock moves it an hour forward, and b.GC() then collects exactly the entries that expired in between. Prefer that shape in your own code.

SetClock is a method rather than a field for a reason worth copying. Automatic garbage collection reads the clock from a goroutine the constructor starts before it returns, so an exported field had no safe moment left for the assignment. The library shipped that field once and its own suite tripped -race on it. Any struct that hands a caller a knob and then reads it from a goroutine of its own has the same problem.

Keys for tests

The repository keeps a fixed set of key pairs under _testfiles/: RSA, RSA-PSS, ECDSA and Ed25519 in PEM, an HMAC secret, and one deliberately corrupt PEM for the parse failures. They load through helpers that panic rather than return an error, because a missing fixture is a broken checkout rather than a condition a test should branch on:

func MustLoadRSA(privateKeyFilename, publicKeyFilename string) (*rsa.PrivateKey, *rsa.PublicKey)
func MustLoadECDSA(privateKeyFilename, publicKeyFilename string) (*ecdsa.PrivateKey, *ecdsa.PublicKey)
func MustLoadEdDSA(privateKeyFilename, publicKeyFilename string) (ed25519.PrivateKey, ed25519.PublicKey)

For HMAC there is nothing to load. func MustGenerateRandom(n int) []byte gives you a secret: 32 bytes for HS256, 48 for HS384, 64 for HS512, at 345 nanoseconds per call. For a fresh Ed25519 pair as PEM there is func GenerateEdDSA() (publicPEM []byte, privatePEM []byte, err error). Note the return order. Public comes first, the opposite of the convention nearly every other key API in Go follows, and a test that binds them the wrong way round fails at the signing call rather than at the assignment. That pair took about 20 microseconds to generate, so one per test is fine.

Do not do the same with RSA. Generating a 2048-bit key took between 73 and 115 milliseconds across three runs of thirty on the machine named in Chapter 14. Thirty tests each generating one add three seconds to a suite that otherwise runs in four, and because key generation is a search for primes the cost is random as well as large. Load _testfiles/rsa_private_key.pem instead.

The keys in _testfiles/ are published. They sit in a public repository and anybody can read them. They exist to make signatures reproducible, which is the opposite of what a signing key is normally for. Never let one reach a file a deployment might read.

Faking the network

The JWKS fetch takes its client as type HTTPClient interface { Get(string) (*http.Response, error) }, one method, and it is the method *http.Client already has. That is the whole reason the interface exists: func FetchJWKS(client HTTPClient, rawURL string) (*JWKS, error) and func WithHTTPClient(client HTTPClient) RemoteKeySetOption can both be handed something that is not a client at all. Here is a fake that answers from a canned string and remembers what it was asked for, modelled on recordingClient in jwk_fetch_test.go:

type recordingClient struct {
	status    int
	body      string
	requested []string
}

func (c *recordingClient) Get(url string) (*http.Response, error) {
	c.requested = append(c.requested, url)

	status := c.status
	if status == 0 {
		status = http.StatusOK
	}
	return &http.Response{StatusCode: status,
		Body: io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(c.body))}, nil
}

The requested slice is what makes it more than a stub. A test can loop over http://auth.example.com/keys, ftp://... and file:///etc/passwd, check that every FetchJWKS call returns an error, and then assert len(client.requested) == 0. That last line is the interesting one: it proves the scheme was refused before a request went out rather than after.

The same fake covers cases a real server makes awkward. A body larger than MaxJWKSSize, which is 1 MB, is one strings.Repeat away, and a 401 whose body carries a forged log line is a string literal.

A fake that rotates

Rotation is the case a canned answer cannot test, because the point of rotation is that the answer changes. keyset_test.go has a client that can be reconfigured mid-test and counts its calls:

type rotatingClient struct {
	mu      sync.Mutex
	body    string
	fails   bool
	fetches atomic.Int64
}

func (c *rotatingClient) Get(url string) (*http.Response, error) {
	c.fetches.Add(1)

	c.mu.Lock()
	body, fails := c.body, c.fails
	c.mu.Unlock()

	if fails {
		return &http.Response{StatusCode: http.StatusInternalServerError,
			Body: io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader("upstream is unwell"))}, nil
	}
	return &http.Response{StatusCode: http.StatusOK,
		Body: io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(body))}, nil
}

// serve replaces the answer, under the same lock Get reads it through.
func (c *rotatingClient) serve(body string, fails bool) { /* ... */ }

The mutex is not decoration. KeySet refreshes from its own goroutine, so the fake really is called concurrently, and the counter is an atomic.Int64 for the same reason. With it, a rotation becomes deterministic:

client := &rotatingClient{}
client.serve(jwksFor(t, "key-one"), false)

keySet, err := jwt.NewRemoteKeySet("https://auth.example.com/keys",
	jwt.WithHTTPClient(client),
	jwt.WithRefreshInterval(0),    // no background timer; the test drives it
	jwt.WithMinRefreshInterval(0), // and no rate limit, so the refetch is immediate
)
// verify under key-one, assert one fetch, then serve both kids and verify under key-two

Setting both intervals to zero removes the timing dependency. The background refresh never fires and the rate limit on the unknown-key refetch is off, so every fetch in the count is one the code chose to make. Now the assertion can be exact: a known key adds no fetch, an unknown one adds precisely one.

The honest limit: a fake proves how your code handles a response, not that your provider sends that response. Keep one test somewhere that fetches the real JWKS, guard it with a build tag, and run it on a schedule rather than on every commit.

Golden tests

golden_test.go records the exact bytes this package emits and compares them on every run: the encoded header for each algorithm, whole tokens for the algorithms whose signatures are deterministic, JWK and JWKS documents, PEM round trips, Merge output, and the JSON shape of a TokenPair. ECDSA and RSA-PSS randomise the signature, so only the signed input is recorded, taken as token[:bytes.LastIndexByte(token, '.')]. Everything up to the last dot is deterministic and everything after it is not. Copy that split whenever you golden something with a random component. The file regenerates from a flag, go test -run TestGolden -update.

A golden whose expectation you edited to match new output proves nothing. It records what the code did the last time somebody ran it, and if the only reason the recording changed is that you ran it again, the test has stopped being a test. That failure mode is why people distrust golden files, and it is entirely avoidable.

Regenerating is fine. The rule is that you write down the before and the after. This repository keeps that record in PASS-LEDGER.md, one row per change with the old and new values side by side, so when a reviewer asks why token/HS256 differs the answer is a line in a file rather than a memory.

Golden tests also record behaviour you know is wrong: collectGolden deliberately captures the error GenerateJWK returns for an ECDSA key, so fixing it shows up as a diff rather than as silence. A golden file describes current behaviour, not correct behaviour.

Table-driven tests for the error paths

The error paths are where the interesting behaviour lives, and a dozen of them share one shape. A table keeps that readable:

for _, tt := range []struct {
	name  string
	token []byte
	want  error
}{
	{"empty", nil, jwt.ErrMissing},
	{"two segments", []byte("header.payload"), jwt.ErrTokenForm},
	{"oversized", bytes.Repeat([]byte("a"), jwt.MaxTokenSize+1), jwt.ErrTokenSize},
} {
	t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
		if _, err := jwt.Verify(jwt.HS256, secret, tt.token); !errors.Is(err, tt.want) {
			t.Fatalf("expected %v but got: %v", tt.want, err)
		}
	})
}

Assert with errors.Is, never with err.Error() == "jwt: invalid token form". The sentinel values are part of the package’s API and will not change without a version bump. The strings around them are not, and several are wrapped with context the package is free to reword. A string comparison passes today and fails on an upgrade that changed nothing you care about. Where the error carries data, errors.As gets you the value: that is how the package checks its own *HTTPError, whose remote body is deliberately kept off the message and put on a field, because the body is chosen by the host you fetch from and ends up in whatever you log.

The limit of errors.Is is that it names the sentinel, not the call site. ErrTokenAlg comes back from four places in token.go alone. When the distinction matters, assert on something else as well: a status code, the fetch count your fake recorded, or the bytes that came out.

Testing that something is refused

A test that a forgery is rejected cannot build the forgery with Sign. Sign validates the algorithm name, refuses certain shapes outright, and always attaches a real signature. Going through it means testing the happy path with a different spelling.

Build the token by hand. enrich_security_test.go has a helper for exactly this:

func craftToken(header, payload, signature string) []byte {
	var b bytes.Buffer
	b.Write(jwt.Base64Encode([]byte(header)))
	b.WriteByte('.')
	b.Write(jwt.Base64Encode([]byte(payload)))
	b.WriteByte('.')
	b.WriteString(signature)
	return b.Bytes()
}

The header and payload are strings you write out in full, so the test says precisely what the attacker sent:

// The attacker presents a token claiming the unsecured algorithm and no signature.
forged := craftToken(`{"alg":"NONE","typ":"JWT"}`, `{"sub":"attacker"}`, "")

_, err := jwt.Enrich(jwt.HS256, secret, forged, jwt.Map{"role": "admin"})
if !errors.Is(err, jwt.ErrTokenAlg) {
	t.Fatalf("expected ErrTokenAlg but got: %v", err)
}

The same helper builds a token naming a key identifier that will never exist, which is how keyset_test.go checks that twenty such tokens trigger one refetch rather than twenty. Its signature segment is the literal string sig, because the token is refused before anything decodes it, and writing garbage there documents that fact. Three shapes belong in any suite that accepts outside tokens: an unsigned token claiming NONE, a token signed correctly with the wrong key, and a token whose payload was edited after signing.

Replacing Marshal and Unmarshal

Serialization goes through two more package variables. Marshal is a function value that passes a []byte straight through and calls json.Marshal on anything else; Unmarshal is defaultUnmarshal, a json.Decoder with UseNumber enabled. Replacing either follows the same save-and-restore discipline as Clock and carries the same parallelism warning. The usual reasons are counting how many times claims were decoded, injecting a decode failure that is otherwise hard to provoke, or checking that jwt.UnmarshalWithRequired really does reject a payload missing a required field.

A middleware that captured the variable at construction will not see your change. This is the trap, and it is easy to write by accident:

type Middleware struct{ unmarshal func([]byte, any) error }

func New() *Middleware {
	return &Middleware{unmarshal: jwt.Unmarshal} // read once, right now
}

New copies the function value out of the variable at the moment it runs. A later assignment changes the variable and leaves every already-built Middleware holding the old function. If your test constructs the middleware in a TestMain or a package-level var, the assignment happens after the capture and the test quietly measures nothing.

Two fixes exist and the second is better. Call jwt.Unmarshal at the point of use rather than storing it. Or stop reading the package variable at all: make the function an explicit field the caller sets, defaulting to jwt.Unmarshal when it is nil. That turns a global into a parameter, so two tests can want two different unmarshalers at once. The same reasoning applies in production: jwt.Unmarshal = jwt.UnmarshalWithRequired in an init works, and the same line in a request handler, after the middleware was built, may not.

The race detector

This package’s continuous integration runs the suite twice, once plainly and once with the safe build tag, and both runs pass --race. It matters more here than in most libraries, because several types are designed to be used from many goroutines while something changes underneath them: KeySet replaces its key map on refresh, Blocklist sweeps expired entries while revocations arrive, and the package variables are read on every verification.

TestKeySetIsSafeUnderConcurrentUse runs eight goroutines doing two hundred verifications each while a ninth calls Refresh fifty times. Without -race that test passes whether or not KeySet is actually safe, because a data race usually produces correct answers on the run where you are watching.

The race detector does not run everywhere. On the machine this chapter was written on:

$ go test -race ./...
-race is not supported on windows/arm64
$ echo $?
2

The supported platform list is short and windows/arm64 is not on it. The exit code is 2, so a script that checks it does notice, which is worth confirming rather than assuming: a refusal that exited zero would let a local run report success without having checked anything. Run the race build in CI on a platform that supports it; a linux/amd64 container substitutes fine.

Two costs. A race build runs several times slower and uses substantially more memory, which is why it belongs in CI rather than in your edit-compile loop. And the detector reports only races it observed: one in a path your test never exercised is invisible to it. It finds bugs, and it does not prove their absence.

Summary

The suite is hermetic because three seams exist: Clock for time, the HTTPClient interface for the JWKS fetch, and ReadFile for key files. Two are package variables read without a lock, so a test that swaps one must not run in parallel with anything else in its package, and must put the old value back through t.Cleanup. Load RSA keys from _testfiles/ rather than generating them: a 2048-bit key took 73 to 115 milliseconds to generate on the machine measured, against about 20 microseconds for an Ed25519 pair. MustGenerateRandom(32) covers HMAC, and GenerateEdDSA returns the public PEM first.

Fake the network with a one-method type: a recording fake proves a URL was never requested, a rotating fake proves a key set was refetched. Golden files pin generated bytes and are worth nothing unless the regeneration is recorded where a reviewer can read it. Build forgeries by hand with craftToken rather than through Sign, assert with errors.Is, and run the result under -race on a platform that supports it.

Further Reading

  • The testing package: t.Cleanup, t.Helper, t.TempDir and the rules that govern t.Parallel.
  • Data Race Detector: how it works, what it costs, and the exact list of supported platforms.
  • Table Driven Tests: the Go wiki page, including the argument for subtests over a bare loop.
  • The errors package: Is, As, and why %w makes them work.

Chapter 14

Performance

A JWT library sits on the request path, so its cost is paid once per request forever. This package is fast for a small number of specific reasons, each of which cost something else: a precomputed header table that a custom algorithm name walks past, a zero-copy string conversion with a real aliasing hazard, and a merge that splices JSON text instead of parsing it. This chapter measures the result on one named machine, explains each decision with the price attached, and finishes with the parts that are not worth touching.

The numbers on one machine

Every figure in this chapter was measured on a Snapdragon X X1E80100, twelve cores, Windows 11, Go 1.26.5, goos: windows and goarch: arm64. Yours will differ. The ratios travel better than the absolute times.

The package’s own benchmarks, from go test -bench=. -benchmem -run=XXX in the repository root:

BenchmarkSignWithMerge-12            455037     2425 ns/op    1520 B/op    20 allocs/op
BenchmarkSignWithoutMerge-12         444027     2947 ns/op    1705 B/op    25 allocs/op
BenchmarkMerge-12                   2047495    570.2 ns/op     432 B/op     8 allocs/op
BenchmarkStructToMapJSON-12          574880     1967 ns/op    1040 B/op    28 allocs/op
BenchmarkStructToMapReflection-12   1000000     1189 ns/op     744 B/op    15 allocs/op
BenchmarkEnrich-12                   210120     6506 ns/op    3259 B/op    43 allocs/op
BenchmarkEncodeToken-12              581425     2027 ns/op     912 B/op    15 allocs/op

The comparison suite, from the same command in _benchmarks:

BenchmarkSign_Map-12               486244     2380 ns/op    1528 B/op    23 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_Struct-12            589917     2199 ns/op    1392 B/op    21 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_jwt_go_Map-12        359260     3511 ns/op    2377 B/op    37 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_jwt_go_Struct-12     445124     2934 ns/op    1913 B/op    27 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_jwt_go_Struct2-12    437682     2831 ns/op    1833 B/op    27 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_go_jose_Map-12       249398     5897 ns/op    4584 B/op    72 allocs/op
BenchmarkSign_go_jose_Struct-12    171199     7982 ns/op    5944 B/op    93 allocs/op
BenchmarkVerify-12                 469933     2681 ns/op    1376 B/op    18 allocs/op
BenchmarkVerify_jwt_go-12          297790     4694 ns/op    3088 B/op    51 allocs/op
BenchmarkVerify_go_jose-12         128449     8416 ns/op    5896 B/op    83 allocs/op

Running that second command again, on the same machine and the same binary, moved BenchmarkSign_Map from 2380 to 3723 ns/op and BenchmarkVerify from 2681 to 2818. The byte and allocation columns did not move by a single unit. Trust the allocation counts and treat the nanosecond figures as a range. A change that removes an allocation is a real change; a change that shaves five percent off one run is probably the scheduler.

The numbers printed in _benchmarks/README.md are stale. They were measured years ago on an Intel i7-8750H under Windows 10, which is a different architecture at a different clock. Do not compare them with anything above.

Where the time goes in a verification

Verify on an HS256 token does four things: split on the dots and base64-decode the header, compare the header against a known constant, compute a MAC over the signing input and compare it against the decoded signature, then base64-decode the payload and unmarshal it.

Measuring the pieces separately, with benchmarks written for this chapter against the same token the comparison suite uses:

Piece Time Allocations
Base64Decode of one payload segment 66 ns 1
Decode of a whole token, all three segments 314 ns 5
HMAC-SHA256 over the signing input, fresh MAC per call 1416 ns 6
Unmarshal of a 47-byte payload into Claims 1269 ns 9
The whole of Verify 2512 ns 18

Those parts add up to more than the whole, which is the honest result and worth saying plainly: a microbenchmark of a 66-nanosecond function is measuring its own loop as much as the function, and the standalone MAC benchmark rebuilds state the real path reuses. Read the table for ordering, not for a decomposition.

The ordering is the useful part. Base64 is noise. The MAC and the JSON decode are the bill, and they are roughly the same size. The JSON decode grows with the number of claims, while the MAC grows only with the raw byte count and does so in 64-byte steps, so the one optimisation that always works is to put fewer claims in the token. Every claim you move out of the payload and into a lookup on your side comes off the decode time and the bytes on the wire together.

Precomputed headers

For every built-in algorithm the package builds three byte slices once, in init, and keeps them in a map:

type fixedHeader struct {
	raw      []byte // {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
	encoded  []byte // the base64url form of raw
	reversed []byte // {"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256"}
}

var fixedHeaders = make(map[string]*fixedHeader, len(allAlgs))

Signing looks the header up rather than building it:

func createHeader(alg string) []byte {
	if header := fixedHeaders[alg]; header != nil {
		return header.encoded
	}

	return Base64Encode([]byte(`{"alg":"` + alg + `","typ":"JWT"}`))
}

Verification never parses the header as JSON at all. compareHeader decodes the segment and runs bytes.Equal against the precomputed raw form, with one branch for producers that emit the fields in the other order:

if headerDecoded[2] == 't' {
	expectedHeader := createHeaderReversed(alg)
	// ...
}

That is a byte comparison against a constant instead of a JSON parse, on every request.

The cost lands in three places. A custom Alg whose Name is not in the map takes the slow path: createHeader concatenates and base64-encodes on every signature, and createHeaderRaw allocates a fresh slice on every verification. More importantly, a header this package did not produce is compared byte for byte, so a token carrying an extra header field, or the same two fields in a third order, fails with ErrTokenAlg rather than being understood. There is also a length gate: compareHeader rejects a decoded header shorter than 25 bytes unless it is exactly 15, the length of {"alg":"HS256"}. Interoperating with a producer outside those shapes means supplying your own HeaderValidator through VerifyWithHeaderValidator, which parses properly and costs what parsing costs.

Bytes to string without a copy

Converting a []byte to a string in Go allocates and copies. The package does not:

func BytesToString(b []byte) string {
	return unsafe.String(unsafe.SliceData(b), len(b))
}

The returned string points at the caller’s bytes. There is a second implementation behind the safe build tag that is a plain string(b) conversion, and the continuous integration runs the full suite under both.

The hazard is aliasing, and it is not theoretical. A string in Go is immutable by contract, not by enforcement. BytesToString hands you one whose backing array somebody else still owns, and if they write to it your string changes underneath you. The place this bites is Blocklist. When a token carries no jti, the blocklist key is the whole token, produced by BytesToString, and a map key whose contents change is a map key that can no longer be found. So InvalidateToken copies before storing:

key = strings.Clone(key)

One allocation, on a path that runs once per logout rather than once per request. Lookups keep the zero-copy form, because a lookup does not retain the string. TestInvalidateTokenDoesNotAliasTheCallerBuffer hands the blocklist a buffer, overwrites every byte of it, and checks the revocation still matches.

Measure before you assume the tag is expensive. Running the comparison suite with -tags safe gave BenchmarkVerify at 2569 ns/op, 1376 B/op, 18 allocs/op, which is inside the run-to-run variation of the default build for this workload. If you cannot audit every caller that hands this package a reused buffer, build with -tags safe and spend the difference elsewhere.

Merge splices raw JSON

func Merge(values ...any) ([]byte, error) combines claim sets. The obvious implementation unmarshals everything into a map[string]any, merges the maps, and marshals the result. This one strips the outer braces off each part and joins the insides with commas:

inner := jsonBytes[1 : len(jsonBytes)-1]
parts = append(parts, inner)
// ...
combined = bytes.Join([][]byte{[]byte("{"), bytes.Join(parts, []byte(",")), []byte("}")}, nil)

Never unmarshalled, never re-marshalled. The repository benchmarks the three approaches side by side, which is how the decision was made in the first place: BenchmarkMerge at 570 ns and 8 allocations, against 1967 ns and 28 allocations through a map, and 1189 ns and 15 allocations through reflection. End to end, BenchmarkSignWithMerge runs at 2425 ns and 20 allocations where BenchmarkSignWithoutMerge needs 2947 ns and 25.

The cost is duplicate keys. Merging {"role":"admin"} with {"role":"user"} produces {"role":"admin","role":"user"}. That is well-formed JSON, and RFC 8259 declines to say which value wins: Go’s encoding/json takes the last, and other parsers take the first. The golden file records the result under merge/duplicate-key so nobody has to guess what the package does. The rule for callers is short. Never merge two objects that can carry the same claim, and if you cannot guarantee that, put the object whose values should win last.

One check does survive. A string or []byte part is spliced in verbatim, so Merge runs json.Valid over exactly those two cases. Without it, {"broken"} passed the first-and-last byte test and produced a signed token whose payload was not JSON.

Marshal passes bytes through

The default Marshal starts with a type switch:

var Marshal = func(v any) ([]byte, error) {
	if b, ok := v.([]byte); ok {
		return b, nil
	}

	return json.Marshal(v)
}

Merge returns []byte, Sign hands its claims to Marshal, and the payload therefore reaches the encoder without a second serialization. It also means you can cache a payload: marshal your claims once, keep the bytes, and sign them repeatedly for the price of the signature alone.

The cost is that a []byte is taken at its word. Marshal does not check it is JSON, so Sign(alg, key, []byte("not json")) produces a signed token whose payload is not JSON, and the failure surfaces at whoever verifies it. Merge covers its own raw inputs with json.Valid; the direct path to Sign is yours to get right.

Base64Decode trims instead of padding

A JWT segment carries no base64 padding, and base64.URLEncoding wants input whose length divides by four. The obvious fix is to append = characters until it does, and this package did that for years. What replaced it goes the other way:

func Base64Decode(src []byte) ([]byte, error) {
	src = bytes.TrimRight(src, padStr)

	buf := make([]byte, base64.RawURLEncoding.DecodedLen(len(src)))
	n, err := base64.RawURLEncoding.Decode(buf, src)
	return buf[:n], err
}

Trimming rather than appending was a correctness fix first. bytes.Split does not cap the capacity of the last part it returns, so the signature segment of a token still owns the token’s spare capacity, and appending to it wrote past the end of the caller’s buffer. With a pooled HTTP read buffer, which is how most servers hand a token to this package, that is a write into memory the next request is about to use.

It was also faster, and by more than anyone expected. bytes.TrimRight returns a sub-slice and allocates nothing, RawURLEncoding needs no padding, and DecodedLen on the trimmed input asks for a smaller buffer than the padded form did. The recorded before and after for BenchmarkVerify: 22 allocations, 1632 B and 2821 ns became 18 allocations, 1376 B and 2455 ns. Four allocations and 256 bytes off every single verification, for a change that was made to stop a memory corruption.

Measuring your own usage

The command is the one used throughout this chapter:

go test -bench=. -benchmem -run=XXX

-benchmem adds the two columns that matter. -run=XXX gives the test filter a pattern nothing matches, so the tests do not run and their time stays out of the result. Call b.ReportAllocs() and put b.ResetTimer() after any setup, or the key you generated in the benchmark body ends up in the measurement.

The counts to expect, on the small token these benchmarks use: 18 allocations to verify with HS256, 21 to sign a struct, 23 to sign a map. If yours are much higher, look at your claims type before you look at the package. A map costs more than a struct because encoding/json sorts the keys and boxes every value. A struct with twenty fields costs more than one with four. A time.Time field costs more than an int64.

For comparing two versions of your own code, run each with -count=10 and put the output through benchstat. A single pair of runs cannot tell a five percent change from noise, and this chapter’s own second run is the proof: the same binary, the same machine, 2380 ns and then 3723 ns for the same benchmark.

What not to optimise

The signature is the floor, and with anything other than HMAC it is most of the building. Verification of the same small token, by algorithm:

Algorithm Verify Allocations
HS256 2512 ns 18
RS256 38108 ns 22
EdDSA 46887 ns 12
ES256 54032 ns 34

Signing with RS256 measured 1522261 ns, a little over 1.5 milliseconds. That is the RSA asymmetry doing its usual thing: verification uses a public exponent of 65537 and is cheap, signing uses the private exponent and is not, and the gap here is a factor of forty.

Read the RS256 row against the HS256 row. The package’s own work is identical in both and runs on the order of a microsecond; the extra 35 microseconds is the RSA verification itself, modular arithmetic in crypto/rsa. Shaving another allocation off the parsing path would move an RSA verification by well under one percent, and an RSA signing by roughly nothing.

So do not tune the library for an RSA workload. Tune the number of RSA operations. Verify once per request rather than once per handler. Give access tokens a short life and a cheap algorithm and keep RSA for the refresh path. If you control both ends, EdDSA verification costs about the same as RS256 here while using twelve allocations instead of twenty-two, and EdDSA signing measured 23348 ns against RS256’s 1522261, a factor of sixty-five.
