The other thing not worth optimising is the constant-time comparison in the HMAC path. It is there so that a wrong signature takes the same time to reject as a nearly-right one, and replacing it with bytes.Equal would buy nanoseconds and sell an oracle.

The comparison benchmarks

_benchmarks compares this package against github.com/golang-jwt/jwt v3.2.2 and github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v3 v3.0.4. Verification, from the run quoted above:

Package Verify Bytes Allocations
kataras/jwt 2681 ns 1376 18
golang-jwt/jwt 4694 ns 3088 51
go-jose/go-jose 8416 ns 5896 83

The second run gave 2818, 5198 and 8624 for the same three. The timing ratio is not a fixed multiple and this book will not quote one. The allocation ratio held exactly across both runs, and that is the number worth carrying: a little over a third of golang-jwt’s allocations and under a quarter of go-jose’s.

Two caveats belong next to those figures. go-jose’s ParseSigned does not verify anything; the benchmark has to call Claims afterwards to force the signature check, so the two sides are not calling equivalent APIs. And golang-jwt/jwt v3.2.2 is an old major version, kept because that is what the benchmark module pins. A current v5 would be a fairer comparison and has not been measured here.

Summary

Signing a struct with HS256 took about 2.2 microseconds and 21 allocations on the machine named above; verifying took about 2.7 microseconds and 18 allocations. Timings moved by up to a third between two runs of the same binary while allocation counts did not move at all, so allocations are the metric to hold a change to.

Inside a verification, base64 decoding is noise and the MAC and the JSON unmarshal are roughly equal halves of the cost. Four decisions buy the rest: a precomputed header table, which a custom algorithm name and an unusual field order walk past; a zero-copy BytesToString, which aliases the caller’s buffer and forces a strings.Clone in the blocklist; a Merge that splices raw JSON and therefore emits duplicate keys rather than resolving them; and a Base64Decode that trims padding, which removed four allocations from every verification and fixed a write past the end of the caller’s buffer at the same time.

Above HMAC, the signature dominates everything else. RS256 verification measured 38 microseconds against HS256’s 2.5, and RS256 signing 1.5 milliseconds. Optimise the number of those operations rather than the code around them.

Further Reading

  • Benchmarks in the testing package: what b.N, b.ResetTimer and b.ReportAllocs actually do.
  • benchstat: the tool for deciding whether two sets of benchmark runs differ.
  • Profiling Go Programs: -cpuprofile and -memprofile, and how to read what comes out.
  • unsafe.String: the exact contract, including the rule that the bytes must not be modified while the string is alive.
  • RFC 8259 section 4: the paragraph that leaves duplicate object names up to the implementation.

Epilogue

The library this book describes is about four thousand lines of Go with no dependencies. It does one thing. That should make it simple, and mostly it is: Sign and Verify are two functions, and the format is three base64url segments joined by dots.

What is not simple is everything around those two functions, and that is what took most of the pages. Which algorithm, and therefore who can mint a token as well as read one. Which key, and what happens on the day it has to be replaced without a maintenance window. What a claim means when a service in another language reads the same bytes. What to do about a session that has to end before its token does.

The pattern worth taking away

Almost every defect this package has had, and there have been a number, was the same shape: something reported success while failing.

A revocation that returned nil and then evaporated on the next garbage collection tick. A build tag that was documented for years and had never compiled. A key set generator that returned an error for every ECDSA key, so a service published a /.well-known/jwks.json with a key missing from it. An expiry claim that overflowed to a negative number, failed a greater-than-zero test, and produced a token that never expired. An enrichment path that signed an attacker’s header with your private key and handed back a perfectly valid token.

None of those threw. None of them showed up in a log. Each one needed somebody to sit down with the source and ask what the code does rather than what it says it does.

If you take one habit from this book, take that one. When something in an authentication path looks like it worked, check what it actually did. The failures that announce themselves are the cheap ones.

What this package is not going to do for you

It signs and verifies tokens. It does not decide who your users are, what they may do, or whether a token that verifies should be honoured. A signature proves that a holder of a key produced some bytes. Everything from there is yours: the audience check, the issuer check, the revocation list, the session model, and the decision about what a claim entitles somebody to.

It also will not stop you putting a password in a payload, granting a token a year of life, or sharing an HMAC key with a service you do not control. Chapter 12 lists the places where the library is quieter about that than it might be.

Contributing

The repository is at github.com/kataras/jwt. The test suite is hermetic and runs in about four seconds, so there is no excuse for a change without a test. If you find something in this book that does not match the source, the source is right and the book is wrong: open an issue and say which page.

Two things are worth knowing before you send a change. The library keeps no dependencies, and that is not negotiable; the book and the brand kit are separate modules for exactly that reason. And performance is a feature here, so a change that adds an allocation to Sign or Verify needs to say what it buys.

Thanks

To everyone who filed an issue against this package with a reproducer attached, which is rarer and more useful than it sounds. To the authors of RFC 7515, 7517, 7518 and 7519, who wrote specifications precise enough to implement from and honest enough to say where the danger is. And to the people who ran this code in production and reported what broke, which is the only way any of the defects in chapter 12 were ever found.

Go build something, and give your tokens an expiry.

Colophon

A working guide to github.com/kataras/jwt: what a JSON Web Token actually is, how this package signs and verifies one, how to choose an algorithm, rotate keys, publish and consume a JWKS, revoke a token that is still inside its lifetime, and where the sharp edges are. Every signature in this book was checked against the source.
